title: Spanish C1
description: The fifth step in Latin American Spanish, from B2 to CEFR level C1, the level of the Instituto Cervantes DELE C1 exam. Lessons cover register and style from Mexican colloquial speech to formal writing, tact, euphemism and irony, the norm and its common doubts (dequeísmo, impersonal haber, anglicisms), verbs whose meaning changes with the mood, the reduplicated and Latin American concessives, the subjunctive on its own, comparison and proportion, formal connectors of contrast, cause and condition, cohesion and reference in long texts, argumentation and fallacies, idioms and proverbs, pronominal verbs and verbs with prepositions, collocations and precise vocabulary, academic hedging, participle and gerund constructions, summarizing and mediating, reports from graphics and formal letters, spelling and punctuation doubts, emphasis and word order, and the integrated tasks of the DELE C1. Honors lessons add plain language, other varieties of Spanish, humor, rhetoric, translation, the language of the internet and of business, and classics from Don Quixote and Sor Juana to the novel of the Revolution and the Boom. About 620 new words build on the roughly 3,300 from Spanish A1 to B2, with Mexican usage as the standard and Spain's and other regions' words noted. Conjugation drills keep all fifteen forms of the earlier courses, and a reading list suggests books, magazines, podcasts and official exam material for this level. Unlocks when Spanish B2 is complete.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Según con quién: register and politeness at C1
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At B2 you learned the forms of Spanish. At C1 the question is which form to choose, for whom, and
why. This module is about that choice: register and style.

This lesson puts B1 lesson 20 (*tú* and *usted*, formal letters) and B2's passive *se* (14) and
nominal style (18) on one scale, adds Mexican forms of address and office conventions, and tells
one piece of news three times. The theme is protocol: ceremonies, graduations and official events, with A2's
*la ceremonia*, *el anfitrión* (host) and *el brindis* (toast).

## Register is a scale, not a switch

**[[Register]]** is the level of formality you choose for a situation and keep throughout (B1's *el
registro*). Think of it as a scale with four steps:

- the **[[colloquial register]]**: friends, family, voice notes, chats (*coloquial*; *vulgar* is
  reserved for crude language);
- the neutral register: a colleague, an ordinary e-mail;
- the **[[formal register]]**: speeches, official letters, anyone you treat with *deferencia*
  (deference);
- specialized registers: law, science and administration, with their own fixed words.

![A horizontal scale with four steps, from coloquial on the left through neutral and formal to especializado on the right. Above the scale, one message at each step: Me salió una chamba; Conseguí trabajo; Obtuve un empleo; Fui designado para ocupar el puesto. Below it, arrows show what changes along the scale: tú to usted, short sentences to long ones with nouns, and everyday words to fixed formulas.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The same content moves along the scale: *Me salió una chamba* (I got a gig, B1's *la chamba*) →
*Conseguí trabajo* (I got a job) → *Obtuve un empleo* (I obtained employment) → *Fui designado
para ocupar el puesto* (I was appointed to the post). Nothing in the first is wrong; it is out of
place in a job application, as the last would be in a chat. This *variación* (variation) is
normal: everyone moves along the scale daily. What matters is *la adecuación*, the
fit between language and situation. A choice that misses it is *inapropiado* (inappropriate), not
*incorrecto*.

## What moves along the scale

Four things change together.

| | Neutral | Formal |
|---|---|---|
| words | *pedir, empezar, ayudar, decir* | *solicitar, iniciar, apoyar, comunicar* |
| requests | *¿Me pasas la lista?* | *¿Me podría pasar la lista? / Le agradecería que me enviara la lista.* |
| notices | *No estacionarse.* | *Favor de no estacionarse.* (Mexico) / *Se ruega puntualidad.* |
| grammar | *Vamos a entregar los diplomas a las once.* | *La entrega de diplomas se realizará a las once.* |

- Requests soften with the conditional or the imperfect of courtesy: *Quería pedirle un
  favor* (I wanted to ask you a favor) is less direct than *quiero*.
- Notices in Mexico usually use *Favor de* + infinitive (*Favor de apagar su celular*, Please
  turn off your cell phone). *Se ruega puntualidad* (Punctuality is requested) is formal and more usual in
  Spain, though Mexican invitations use it too.
- Grammar: formal texts hide the doer with *se* (*Se informa a los asistentes que…*,
  Attendees are informed that…) and pack actions into nouns.

## Forms of address in Mexico

B1's rule of thumb still holds: start with *usted* and let the other person offer *tú*. The finer
points:

- Many younger offices use *tú* among colleagues, but government offices, universities and
  traditional companies often keep *usted*, especially upward. *Hablar de usted* (also *tratar de
  usted*) is to address someone as *usted*; its opposite is A1's *tutear*.
- The older or senior person usually offers *tú*: *Háblame de tú, por favor* or *¿Nos hablamos
  de tú?* Switching on your own can be *descortés* (discourteous); refusing an invitation can
  sound cold.
- Titles are far more common than in the US, in speech and writing: *Buenas tardes, licenciada;
  Estimado Ing. Robles:*. Leaving one out where it's expected can look like a lack of *decoro*
  (propriety).

| Title | Abbreviation | Who |
|---|---|---|
| *licenciado / licenciada* (A1) | Lic. | a university graduate |
| *ingeniero / ingeniera* | Ing. | an engineer |
| *maestro / maestra* | Mtro. / Mtra. | a teacher; also someone with a master's degree |
| *doctor / doctora* | Dr. / Dra. | a physician or a PhD |

## Politeness: mitigating and intensifying

**[[Politeness]]** is the set of strategies speakers use to protect each other's feelings and
standing. Being *cortés* (courteous, from B1's *la cortesía*) at C1 means using three of them:

- Indirectness: *¿No tienes frío?* can mean "May I close the window?"
- **[[Mitigation]]**: softening what could hurt or impose, with *un poquito*, *si no es molestia*,
  *a lo mejor* (maybe) and the conditional: *¿Me podrías ayudar un poquito, si no es molestia?*
  — Could you help me a little, if it's no trouble?
- **[[Intensification]]**: strengthening thanks and praise: *Muchísimas gracias; Fue sumamente
  amable* — You were extremely kind.

Lesson 04 returns to both. Ceremonial Spanish is also warm: *la cordialidad* (warmth) and *la formalidad* go together, and
*la cercanía* (closeness) can coexist with *la solemnidad*.

## The vocabulary of protocol

*El protocolo* is official etiquette. *La etiqueta* is formal manners (also a label: B2's
*etiquetar*); *de etiqueta* on an invitation means formal dress.

- *La investidura* is the act of receiving a title or office: *la investidura como doctor honoris
  causa*. For officials, Mexico usually says *la toma de protesta*.
- *La condecoración* is a state honor; *condecorar* is to confer one. The Secretaría de
  Relaciones Exteriores describes the *Orden Mexicana del Águila Azteca* as the highest
  distinction the Mexican government gives to foreigners.
- *El presídium* is the head table of guests of honor in Mexican ceremonies.

## Written formulas beyond B1

- *Distinguido/a* is more distant than *Estimado/a*, for someone of high rank you don't know:
  *Distinguida doctora Paz:* (greetings end with a colon).
- *Me dirijo a usted para…* (I am writing to you to…) uses *dirigirse a*. A letter *dirigida al
  director* is addressed to him.
- A *fórmula de cortesía* (courtesy formula) closes the text: *Sin otro particular, le envío un
  cordial saludo* (With nothing further, I send you my warm regards), then *Atentamente* (A1).

Mexican offices also write *el oficio*, an official letter between offices or to a person in an
institution. It has *el membrete* (letterhead), a reference number, *Asunto*, the addressee's name
and post in capitals followed by *PRESENTE* (a traditional formula; some offices write *EDIFICIO* for internal mail), a copy line
(*c.c.p.*, *con copia para*) and room for *el acuse de recibo* (acknowledgment of receipt), the
stamp showing when it arrived. An *oficio* says *por medio del presente* (*el oficio*); a letter
says *por medio de la presente* (*la carta*).

![A Mexican oficio on letterhead. At the top, the university's name and a round logo. On the right, the reference number CEI/087/2026, the subject line Cambio de fecha y sede de la ceremonia de graduación, and the place and date. On the left, the addressee's name and post in capitals, then PRESENTE. Then lines of text, the closing ATENTAMENTE, the signature, name and post of the sender, a copy line c.c.p., and a received stamp with a date in the bottom corner.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## One event, three registers

Laura Medina organizes events at a university in Pachuca. The engineering graduation has to move,
and she tells three people.

### 1. A voice note to her friend Caro (colloquial)

```dialogue
# Nota de voz
Laura: ¡Quiúbole, Caro! Oye, nomás para avisarte que siempre no es el viernes la graduación de mi hermano. La cambiaron al sábado a las once, y ya no va a ser en el jardín sino en el auditorio, porque dicen que va a llover. Y es de etiqueta, ¿eh? O sea, nada de tenis. Mi mamá ya está bien nerviosa con lo del protocolo, porque va a estar el rector y le van a dar una medalla a una exalumna. Total, que te aparto un lugar en la tercera fila. Avísame si siempre sí vienes, ¿sale?
= Hey, Caro! Listen, just to let you know that my brother's graduation isn't on Friday after all. They moved it to Saturday at eleven, and it won't be in the garden anymore but in the auditorium, because they say it's going to rain. And it's formal dress, OK? I mean, no sneakers. My mom is already really nervous about the protocol thing, because the university president will be there and they're giving a medal to a former student. So anyway, I'll save you a seat in the third row. Let me know if you're coming after all, deal?
```

*Quiúbole* is a very informal Mexican greeting; *siempre no / siempre sí* means "not / yes after
all"; *nomás* (just) and *¿sale?* (deal?) are lesson 02's words.

### 2. An e-mail to a colleague (neutral)

> Asunto: Cambio de fecha de la graduación de Ingeniería
>
> Hola, Javier:
>
> Te escribo para avisarte que la ceremonia de graduación se pasó al sábado 13 de junio a las
> 11:00. Será en el Auditorio Central y no en la explanada, porque el pronóstico anuncia lluvia
> para el viernes.
>
> ¿Les podrías comentar el cambio a tus grupos de último semestre? Recuérdales que la vestimenta
> es formal y que deben llegar media hora antes para la foto. Además, el rector va a entregar la
> medalla al mérito a Rosa Elena Tapia, que fue alumna tuya, ¿verdad?
>
> ¿Me confirmas el jueves si vas a estar en el presídium? Necesito el número exacto de lugares.
>
> Gracias y saludos,
>
> Laura

> Subject: Change of date for the Engineering graduation. Hi, Javier: I'm writing to let you know
> that the graduation ceremony has been moved to Saturday, June 13, at 11:00. It will be in the
> Central Auditorium and not on the esplanade, because the forecast says rain for Friday. Could you
> mention the change to your final-semester groups? Remind them that the dress is formal and that
> they should arrive half an hour early for the photo. Also, the university president is going to
> present the merit medal to Rosa Elena Tapia, who was a student of yours, right? Can you confirm
> on Thursday whether you'll be at the head table? I need the exact number of seats. Thanks and best
> wishes, Laura

### 3. An *oficio* to the director (formal, administrative)

> UNIVERSIDAD AUTÓNOMA DEL ALTIPLANO · Facultad de Ingeniería · Coordinación de Eventos
> Institucionales
>
> Oficio núm. CEI/087/2026. Asunto: Cambio de fecha y sede de la ceremonia de graduación.
> Pachuca, Hgo., a 2 de junio de 2026.
>
> DR. ERNESTO VILLASEÑOR GARZA, DIRECTOR DE LA FACULTAD DE INGENIERÍA. PRESENTE
>
> Por medio del presente, me permito informarle que, por acuerdo del Comité Organizador y en
> atención al pronóstico meteorológico, la ceremonia de graduación de la Generación 2022-2026 se
> celebrará el sábado 13 de junio a las 11:00 horas en el Auditorio Central, y no el viernes 12 en
> la explanada, como se había anunciado.
>
> Asimismo, le comunico que el código de vestimenta será de etiqueta y que, conforme al protocolo
> institucional, el Rector presidirá la ceremonia, en la cual se entregará la Medalla al Mérito
> Académico a la Ing. Rosa Elena Tapia Montes, egresada de esta Facultad.
>
> Mucho le agradecería que hiciera extensiva esta información al personal docente y que nos
> confirmara la asistencia de los integrantes del presídium a más tardar el 8 de junio.
>
> Sin otro particular, aprovecho la ocasión para enviarle un cordial saludo.
>
> ATENTAMENTE. Mtra. Laura Medina Ochoa, Coordinadora de Eventos Institucionales. c.c.p.
> Secretaría Académica.

Summary: citing the organizing committee and the forecast, Laura informs the director that the
ceremony moves from Friday on the esplanade to Saturday the 13th at 11:00 in the Central
Auditorium. Dress is formal; the president will present the Academic Merit Medal to a graduate. She asks him to pass the news to the teaching staff and confirm the head-table guests by
June 8. Glosses: *me permito informarle* (I take the liberty of informing you), *en atención a*
(in view of), *hacer extensiva* (to pass on), *el personal docente* (teaching staff), *a más tardar* (at the latest), *egresada*
(graduate).

### What changed

| | Voice note | E-mail | *Oficio* |
|---|---|---|---|
| address | *Caro*, *tú* | *Javier*, *tú* | title, full name and post, *usted* |
| the news | *la cambiaron al sábado* | *se pasó al sábado* | *se celebrará el sábado* |
| the reason | *dicen que va a llover* | *el pronóstico anuncia lluvia* | *en atención al pronóstico meteorológico* |
| the request | *Avísame, ¿sale?* | *¿Me confirmas…?* | *Mucho le agradecería que… confirmara* |
| linking | *o sea, total* | *además* | *asimismo, conforme a* |

The facts never change; only the register does.

## Your turn: rewrite for another reader

The e-mail and the *oficio* above are your models. Check your text against this list:

- One form of address throughout: *usted*, with *le* and *su* to match.
- A greeting with a title and a colon, a purpose sentence, the facts, the request, a closing
  formula and a sign-off.
- No colloquial words or fillers.
- The request mitigated: the conditional or *Le agradecería que* + imperfect subjunctive.
- Every fact kept (who, what changed, when, where, why); anything not *pertinente* (relevant) to
  the new reader, such as jokes, left out.

```assignment
writing: es5-m1-register-shift
```

## Pronunciation

- *condecoración*: con-de-co-ra-CIÓN, five syllables; *c* before *i* is said as *s*.
- *investidura*: in-ves-ti-DU-ra, five syllables.
- *deferencia*: de-fe-REN-cia, four syllables; *-cia* is one syllable.
- *descorteses*: des-cor-TE-ses, four syllables, with no written accent in the plural.
- *membrete*: mem-BRE-te, three syllables; the final *e* is pronounced, as in *meh*.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing *tú* and *usted*: *Estimado doctor: Te escribo…* Keep one, with its pronouns and
  possessives.
- Formal words in casual talk. *Le agradecería que me pasara la sal* at dinner sounds
  sarcastic.
- A comma after the greeting. Spanish letters use a colon: *Estimada licenciada:*.
- *Vulgar* for "colloquial". *Vulgar* means crude; an informal word is *coloquial*.

## Key points

- Register is a scale: colloquial, neutral, formal, specialized. Fit the language to the
  situation.
- Words, requests, notices and grammar move together: *pedir → solicitar*; *¿Me pasas…? → ¿Me
  podría…? → Le agradecería que…*; *Favor de* + infinitive on Mexican notices.
- In Mexico, titles are used in speech and writing, and the senior person offers *tú*.
- Formal Spanish mitigates requests and criticism and intensifies thanks.
- An *oficio* has a letterhead, a number, *Asunto*, the addressee with *PRESENTE*, a copy line
  and room for the acknowledgment of receipt.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Ni modo: colloquial conversation in Mexico
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 placed register on a scale. This lesson stays at the informal end, where most real
conversation happens. Informal Spanish isn't "bad"
Spanish: it has its own grammar, built for speed, shared knowledge and keeping the floor.

You know some of it already: A2's *la muletilla* (filler word), B1's *la neta*, *la chamba*, *el
cuate* and *¡Qué oso!*, B1 21's interjections, and B2 17's *total* and *en fin*. Here you'll see
how they work together, and meet the words a C1 listener needs to follow friends talking in
Mexico City. The theme is *la sobremesa*: the long *plática* (informal talk, A2's *platicar*) that
goes on at the table after a meal, when nobody is in a hurry to leave.

## How informal conversation is built

### Fillers and backchannels

A **[[filler]]** fills a pause while the speaker plans: *este…* (um, the most Mexican of all), *pues*,
*bueno*, *o sea* (I mean), *¿cómo se llama?* (what's it called). Listeners keep the speaker going
with backchannels: *ajá*, *sí, sí*, *¿en serio?*, *no manches* (no way, very informal), and tags
such as *¿no?* and *¿verdad?* that invite agreement:

- *Este… llegamos como a las nueve, ¿no?* — Um… we got there around nine, right?

Fillers aren't errors in speech; a conversation without any would sound like a lecture. In
writing, and in a DELE oral exam, use few.

### Discourse markers of speech

A **[[discourse marker]]** tells the listener how to take what comes next. Speech has its own set:
*bueno* opens or changes a topic (*Bueno, ¿y qué onda con la fiesta?*); *pues* starts an answer
(*Pues por eso*, Well, that's why); *o sea* reformulates; *total* (B2) jumps to the outcome; *y
luego* moves a story on; *más bien* corrects.

### Vague language

Friends don't need precision, so they wave at a category: *y eso* (and stuff), *o algo así* (or
something like that), *y cosas así* (and things like that), *como que* (kind of, sort of):
*Había botana, música y eso* — There were snacks, music and stuff. *Como que no quería* — I sort
of didn't want to.

### Ellipsis and short answers

Shared context lets speakers drop whatever is obvious: *—¿Y la cartera? —En la chamarra de Toño.*
(And the wallet? In Toño's jacket.) *—¿Fuiste? —Obvio.* (Obviously.)

### Reported speech, informally

Telling a story, many young Mexicans report their own reaction with *y yo de* + a quote: *Y yo
de: "¿En serio? ¿Un martes?"* (And I was like, "Seriously? On a Tuesday?"). Others use *y yo,
así de…* or just *y yo:*. This is heard, not taught as standard: in neutral Spanish, *le dije* or
*pensé*.

### Intensifiers

*Bien* + adjective (*bien bonito*, really pretty), *súper* (A2), *de a tiro* (totally: *quedé de
a tiro cansado*), *muy muy*, and the prefix *requete-* (*requetebién*, really well). *Re-*
(*rebueno*) is heard too, but it is most typical of the Río de la Plata.

![A chart titled Rasgos de la conversación with five columns. Muletillas: este, pues, bueno, o sea. Señales de escucha: ajá, ¿en serio?, ¿no?, ¿verdad?. Lenguaje vago: y eso, o algo así, y cosas así, como que. Elipsis: ¿Y la cartera? En la chamarra. ¿Fuiste? Obvio. Intensificadores: bien cansado, súper, de a tiro, requetebién.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Mexican colloquial words and grammar

Some forms are Mexican or American and mean something you might not expect:

- *Nomás* means "just, only": *Nomás tomé dos cervezas.* The DLE marks this sense as American, where it
  is also written *no más*; in Spain *no más* usually means "no more".
- *Hasta* can mean "not until" in Mexico: *El taxi llegó hasta las tres* = the taxi didn't arrive
  until three. The *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* (DPD, 2005, online, entry *hasta* §2) notes
  that in Mexico, Central America, Colombia and coastal Ecuador the *no* is dropped, which can
  confuse other speakers (*Se abre hasta las tres* could mean it closes at three, or that it opens
  then). Recognize it; in formal writing put the *no* back: *No llegó hasta las tres*.
- *¿A poco?* (really? no way?) shows surprise: *—Ya me pagaron. —¿A poco?*
- *Luego luego* means "right away": *Me contestó luego luego.* (A single *luego* is "later".)
- *¡Sale!* (deal!, OK!) agrees; *¡Ándale!* urges (come on!) or confirms (that's it!).
- *Ni modo* (oh well, nothing to be done) accepts what can't be changed.
- *Aventarse* (*me aviento*, like *pensar*) is to go for it, to dare: *Me aventé a cantar.* Its
  literal sense is to throw oneself.
- *Apapachar* is to cuddle or comfort: *Ven, te apapacho.*

And nouns and adjectives of a night out: *la onda* (vibe: *¿Qué onda?*, What's up?; *buena onda*,
nice, cool), *la lana* (bucks; literally wool), *el compa* (pal, *la compa*; from *compadre* or
*compañero*), *la palomilla* (your gang of friends), *la pachanga* (a lively party), *el antro*
(a nightclub; in Spain, a seedy bar), *la botana* (snacks served with drinks), *la cruda* (a
hangover; Spain *la resaca*), *el relajo* (rowdy fun, a commotion: *echar relajo*), *el cotorreo*
(banter) and *cotorrear* (to shoot the breeze), and *chafa* (shoddy, lousy; the same for both
genders: *una canción chafa*).

All of this is *la jerga* of a group, its slang. *La carcajada* is a belly laugh (*reírse a
carcajadas*), and *el sarcasmo* is saying the opposite to mock.

### How informal is it?

| Label | Examples | Safe with |
|---|---|---|
| informal | *nomás, ni modo, ¿a poco?, ¡sale!, la plática, la botana, apapachar* | almost anyone you call *tú*; many are fine with *usted* too |
| very informal | *¿Qué onda?, la lana, el compa, chafa, la cruda, el cotorreo, aventarse* | friends and family |
| rude | words you'll hear but this course doesn't teach | nobody you don't know well |

One word deserves a note. *Güey* (also spelled *wey*) is an extremely common term of address among
friends, especially young men, in much of Mexico, and the *Diccionario del español de México* of
El Colegio de México includes it (Excélsior, March 13, 2020). It originally meant something like
"dimwit", it is still an insult in many settings, and it never belongs in front of strangers,
older people or at work. Recognize it; don't start using it.

## Text: una sobremesa en la colonia Roma

Four friends have finished lunch at Lupita's apartment in Mexico City. Nobody has moved.

```dialogue
# Sobremesa
Dani: Esta sobremesa ya va para tres horas, ¿eh?
Fer: Bueno, ¿y qué onda con la pachanga de tu prima, Memo? Nomás vi las fotos.
Memo: Ay, no, ni me digas. O sea, estuvo buenísima, pero acabé de a tiro mal.
Lupita: ¿A poco? Si tú casi no tomas.
Memo: Pues por eso. Este… llegamos a casa de mi prima como a las nueve, ¿no? Había botana, música y eso. Y luego la palomilla de mi prima dijo: "Vámonos al antro". Y yo de: "¿Al antro? ¿Un martes?".
Dani: Ajá, y fuiste, obvio.
Memo: Obvio. Mi prima es de las que no aceptan un no.
Fer: ¿Y qué tal el lugar?
Memo: Pues un antro chafa, la verdad, pero la onda estaba bien. Y ahí empezó el relajo. Había karaoke, y mis primos: "¡Ándale, Memo, échate una!". Yo como que no quería, pero me aventé.
Fer: ¡No es cierto! ¿Cantaste?
Memo: Canté una de José José, o algo así, y la neta me salió bien chafa. Todo el antro muerto de risa.
Lupita: ¡Te hubiera grabado!
Memo: Pues alguien sí me grabó, porque luego luego me llegó el video.
Dani: ¿Y la cartera? Tu mamá me dijo algo de una cartera.
Memo: Ah, sí. Cuando ya nos íbamos, que no encuentro la cartera. Sin lana, sin tarjeta, sin nada. Y el taxi llegó hasta las tres, porque nadie quería ir a Tlalpan.
Fer: ¿Y ya apareció?
Memo: Al otro día. Estaba en la chamarra de mi compa Toño: me la guardó y se le olvidó.
Lupita: Qué buena onda tu compa, ¿eh? Guardártela toda la noche…
Memo: Sí, súper buena onda. Total, que al día siguiente traía una cruda espantosa, y nomás me había tomado dos cervezas. Creo que fue la pena, más bien.
Dani: Ay, pobre. Ven, te apapacho.
Memo: Ni modo, ya pasó. Pero no vuelvo a cantar, ¿eh?
Fer: Sí, cómo no. En la próxima pachanga te aventamos al micrófono.
Lupita: Bueno, ya, dejen de cotorrear, que se enfría el café. ¿Quedamos el sábado? Memo trae la botana.
Memo: ¡Sale! Pero canta Fer.
```

Summary: Fer asks Memo about his cousin's party. Memo says it was great but he ended up in a bad
way. At nine there were snacks and music; then his cousin's friends went to a club on a Tuesday (a
shabby one, but with a good vibe), and at the karaoke his cousins pushed him to sing. He did, badly, and someone filmed it and sent
him the video at once. Leaving, he couldn't find his wallet, and the taxi didn't come until three.
The next day it turned up in his friend Toño's jacket. Lupita and Memo praise Toño with obvious
sarcasm. Memo had a terrible hangover after only two beers, probably from embarrassment. Dani
offers a hug; the friends tease him and plan the next get-together. Glosses: *ni me digas* (don't
even ask), *échate una* (sing one), *muerto de risa* (dying of laughter), *que no encuentro la
cartera* (and I can't find my wallet: *que* introduces a sudden event in a story), *traía una
cruda* (I had a hangover), *la pena* (embarrassment, as in Mexico).

Notice the fillers, tags, vague language, *y yo de*, intensifiers, sarcasm (*Qué buena onda tu
compa*) and *hasta* meaning "not until".

![Four friends sitting around a table after a meal, with coffee cups, a plate of pan dulce and a bowl of snacks. Each has a speech bubble. Top left: Este… llegamos como a las nueve. Top right: ¿A poco? Bottom left: Había botana, música y eso. Bottom right: Quedé de a tiro cansado.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### The same story in neutral Spanish

> Guillermo fue a la fiesta de su prima un martes. Esa noche, los amigos de ella
> decidieron ir a un bar con karaoke y, aunque él no quería, se animó a cantar; según él, lo hizo
> muy mal, y alguien lo grabó. Al salir, no encontraba su cartera, y el taxi no llegó hasta las tres
> de la mañana. Al día siguiente supo que un amigo se la había guardado y había olvidado
> devolvérsela. Además, amaneció con un fuerte malestar, aunque solo había tomado dos cervezas.

> Guillermo went to his cousin's party on a Tuesday. That night, her friends decided to go to a
> karaoke bar and, although he didn't want to, he plucked up the courage to sing; by his account, he
> did it very badly, and someone recorded him. When they left, he couldn't find his wallet, and the
> taxi didn't arrive until three in the morning. The next day he learned that a friend had kept it
> for him and had forgotten to give it back. On top of that, he woke up feeling very unwell,
> although he had only had two beers.

The fillers, tags and slang are gone; *Memo* becomes *Guillermo*; *el antro* becomes *un bar*; *no
llegó hasta* replaces Mexican *llegó hasta*; *la cruda* turns into *un fuerte malestar*.

## Pronunciation

- In fast speech *pues* often sounds like *pos* or *pus*, and *para* like *pa'*: *pa' que veas*.
  Understand them; write *pues* and *para*.
- *¿A poco?* rises on *po* and falls again; said flat, it sounds bored rather than surprised.
- *apapachar*: a-pa-pa-CHAR, four syllables. *aventarse*: a-ven-TAR-se, four.
- *carcajada*: car-ca-JA-da, four syllables; the *j* is a breathy sound from the throat, as in A1.
- *Este…* as a filler stretches the last vowel: *esteee…*. The word *este* (this) doesn't.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *hasta* the wrong way. In Mexico, *Abren hasta las diez* usually means they *don't*
  open until ten.
- Overdoing slang. A learner who says *¿Qué onda, compa?* to a stranger in an office sounds
  odd. Match the other person's register, and let them go first.
- Translating *ni modo* as "no way". It means "oh well, too bad". "No way!" is *¿A poco?* or
  *¡No manches!*
- Writing *nomás* in a formal text. Use *solo* or *solamente*.

## Key points

- Informal speech has its own system: fillers (*este, pues, o sea*), backchannels and tags (*ajá,
  ¿no?, ¿verdad?*), speech markers (*bueno, pues, total*), vague language (*y eso, o algo así,
  como que*), ellipsis and *y yo de* for reported reactions.
- Mexican colloquial grammar: *nomás* (only), *hasta* = "not until" (write *no… hasta* in formal
  texts), *¿a poco?*, *luego luego*, *¡sale!*, *¡ándale!*, *ni modo*.
- Know each word's label: informal, very informal or rude. *Güey* is common among friends and
  rude elsewhere.
- Retelling a colloquial story in neutral Spanish means removing fillers and slang and putting
  back full sentences.

lessons.title: ¿Se dice así? Norm, usage and the language authorities
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 01 and 02 asked which Spanish fits a situation. This one asks a different question: who
decides what counts as correct at all? At C1 you will hear forms that textbooks never taught
(*habían muchas personas*, *me di cuenta que*, *checar*), and you need to know which are standard,
which are frequent but avoided in careful writing, and which are accepted regional usage. You'll
also learn to look a doubt up yourself.

## Who describes the norm

The **[[norm]]** is the set of forms that educated speakers accept as correct in careful use. For
Spanish it is described by the language academies:

- the Real Academia Española (RAE), founded in 1713;
- the Academia Mexicana de la Lengua, founded in 1875;
- the Asociación de Academias de la Lengua Española (ASALE), founded in 1951 at a congress in
  Mexico, which now joins 23 academies, from Spain and the Americas to the Philippines and
  Equatorial Guinea (ASALE's brochure, 2016).

Their main works, all prepared jointly: the *Diccionario de la lengua española* (DLE, online at
dle.rae.es), the *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* (DPD, 2005; a revised second edition came out
in print in February 2025, but this course cites the 2005 text online), the *Nueva gramática de la
lengua española* (2009, with a volume on phonetics in 2011) and the *Ortografía* (2010). Beside
them, FundéuRAE, a foundation that the RAE and the news agency EFE relaunched under that name in
2020, publishes quick usage recommendations, mostly for journalists.

The academies present this norm, the *norma* each *academia* helps to describe, as shared by every
Spanish-speaking (*hispanohablante*) country, aiming at "unity
within diversity", in ASALE's words. In practice that means the educated usage of Mexico is as
standard as that of Madrid or Bogotá: seseo, *ustedes* for "you all", *el carro*, *checar*.

## Prescriptive and descriptive

A **[[prescriptive]]** view says how people should speak or write; a *normativo* (prescriptive) work
gives advice: "use this, avoid that". A **[[descriptive]]** view records how people do speak, without
judging. A *lingüista* (linguist) studying Mexican speech works descriptively; a style guide works
prescriptively. Modern academic works do both: the DPD describes a usage, says where it is
frequent, and then recommends.

Two attitudes fall outside both. *El purismo* (purism) rejects change and foreign influence; a
*purista* (purist) sees every *neologismo* (new word) as damage. And linguistic prejudice treats
some *variedades* as "bad Spanish". Linguists agree that every **[[variety]]** (a form of a language
shared by a region or group) has a full, regular grammar. Some forms carry *prestigio*; others
carry *estigma*, and people *estigmatizan* (stigmatize) their speakers. That is a social
judgment, not a linguistic one: a *prestigioso* (prestigious) accent is no more correct from a *lingüístico* (linguistic)
point of view, and *la lingüística* (linguistics) studies all varieties alike. Languages *evolucionan*: today's error can be tomorrow's norm.

## The common doubts

Each doubt below is described as the DPD and the *Nueva gramática* treat it. "Frequent" means
common in speech; careful writing, and this course's answers, use the standard form.

| Doubt | Standard | Frequent in speech | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[[dequeísmo]]** | *Pienso que tienes razón.* | *Pienso de que…* | rejected by the norm |
| **[[queísmo]]** | *Me di cuenta de que…* | *Me di cuenta que…* | very widespread; avoided in careful writing |
| impersonal *haber* | *Había muchas personas.* | *Habían muchas personas.* | very frequent in Latin American speech; the norm keeps it singular |
| *haber* with "us" | *Somos muchos los que…* | *Habemos muchos que…* | a *vulgarismo* (nonstandard form) |
| past of impersonal *haber* | *Hubo dos accidentes.* | *Hubieron dos accidentes.* | the norm keeps it singular |
| *le* for *les* | *Les dije a mis papás.* | *Le dije a mis papás.* | very common everywhere; write *les* in formal texts |
| *tú* preterite | *dijiste, fuiste* | *dijistes, fuistes* | nonstandard |
| subjunctive of *haber* | *Ojalá que haya tiempo.* | *haiga* | strongly stigmatized |

### Dequeísmo and queísmo

**[[Dequeísmo]]** is adding a *de* that the verb doesn't take: *~~Pienso de que~~ tienes razón*.
**[[Queísmo]]** is the opposite, dropping a *de* the verb needs: *Me di cuenta que* for *Me di cuenta
de que*. The test is to turn the clause into a question or replace it with *eso*:

- *¿Qué piensas?* → *Pienso eso* → *Pienso que…* (no *de*)
- *¿De qué te diste cuenta?* → *Me di cuenta de eso* → *Me di cuenta de que…* (keep *de*)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Deciding between que and de que
  accDescr: Start with a verb followed by a que clause. Replace the clause with eso, or make a question. If the verb takes de before eso, as in me di cuenta de eso, write de que; dropping it is queísmo. If it doesn't, as in pienso eso, write que alone; adding de is dequeísmo.
  A["Verb + que clause"] --> B["Replace the clause with eso, or ask a question"]
  B --> C{"Does the verb take de? (acordarse de eso)"}
  C -- Yes --> D["Write de que: Me acuerdo de que…"]
  C -- No --> E["Write que: Pienso que…"]
  D --> F["Dropping de is queísmo"]
  E --> G["Adding de is dequeísmo"]
```

Some verbs work both ways with a change of meaning or construction: *Me alegra que vengas*
(it pleases me) and *Me alegro de que vengas* (I'm glad) are both standard. *Informar*, *avisar*
and *advertir* (A2) also allow both in their usual senses (*Le avisé que / de que venía*), but
*advertir* meaning "to notice" takes *que* alone. Queísmo is so widespread in
Mexican speech that calling it "wrong" in conversation would be unfair; in a DELE text or a formal
letter, keep the *de*. Queísmo often goes unnoticed; dequeísmo stands out more and is corrected more often.

### Agreement doubts

*La concordancia* (agreement) explains the *haber* cases. In *Había muchas personas*, *muchas
personas* is the object of impersonal *haber*, not its subject, so the verb stays singular, as in
*hay* and *hubo*. Speakers feel the noun as a subject and make it plural, very often in Latin American speech;
the academies still recommend the singular.
The same goes for *habemos*: the standard is *somos* or *hay*.

## Anglicisms, calques and loanwords

An **[[anglicism]]** (*el anglicismo*) is a word or use taken from English. Some come as a **[[calque]]**
(*el calco*), a loan translation that copies English structure with Spanish words; others as a
**[[loanword]]** (*el extranjerismo*), a foreign word adopted whole or adapted.

| Form | What it is | Status (DPD 2005 unless noted) | Careful alternative |
|---|---|---|---|
| *aplicar a una vacante* | calque of "apply for" | very common in Mexican speech (B2 17) | *postularse, solicitar* |
| *hacer sentido* | calque of "make sense" | avoided in careful use | *tener sentido* |
| *tomar lugar* | calque of "take place" | avoided in careful use | *tener lugar, celebrarse* |
| *checar* | adaptation of "check" | "In Mexico the variant *checar* is used"; *chequear* can't be censured | also *revisar, comprobar* |
| *rentar* (A1) | influenced by "to rent" | established in educated use in some American countries, especially Mexico; the DPD prefers *alquilar* | *alquilar* |
| *fútbol, escáner, tuit* | adapted loanwords | in the DLE with Spanish spelling | — |

So *checar* and *rentar* are accepted Mexican usage, not errors; *hacer sentido* is a calque that
careful writers still *desaconsejan* (advise against). An *incorrección* (an incorrect usage) is
a form the norm rejects, not merely one you don't like.

## Looking a doubt up

1. The DLE gives each *acepción* (sense) a number and marks: *Méx.* (Mexico), *Am.*
   (America), *coloq.* (colloquial), *p. us.* (rarely used), *vulg.* (vulgar).
2. The DPD explains doubts in prose and recommends.
3. FundéuRAE answers current questions (new words, headlines) in short notes.

![A dictionary entry drawn as a card. At the top, the headword checar in bold. Next to it, its origin in brackets: from English to check. Below, the grammar label tr., then sense 1 with the country mark Méx. and the definition comprobar o revisar algo. An example sentence in italics follows: Checa que la puerta esté cerrada.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The card is our own simplified model of an entry, not a copy of the DLE's.

## Text: *Dudas al aire*

A radio phone-in. The host, Ramiro, takes calls for the language columnist Ofelia Rentería, a
*lingüista* and *académica* (academician).

```dialogue
# Dudas al aire
Ramiro: Buenas noches, bienvenidos a Dudas al aire. Hoy nos acompaña la doctora Ofelia Rentería, lingüista y miembro de la Academia Mexicana de la Lengua. Tenemos la primera llamada. Adelante, Sandra.
Sandra: Buenas noches. Mi jefe dice "pienso de que" y yo siento que está mal. ¿Tengo razón?
Ofelia: Tiene razón. Es dequeísmo. Pregúntese "¿qué pienso?": si la pregunta no lleva "de", la oración tampoco. Se dice "pienso que". Eso sí, corríjalo con tacto.
Ramiro: Segunda llamada. Héctor, desde Monterrey.
Héctor: Qué tal. A mí me corrigieron "me di cuenta que". ¿También es dequeísmo?
Ofelia: Al revés: es queísmo. "Darse cuenta" lleva "de": uno se da cuenta de algo. Lo normativo es "me di cuenta de que". Es muy frecuente en el habla, en México y en todas partes, pero en un texto cuidado conviene escribir el "de".
Ramiro: Tenemos a Lucía, de Puebla.
Lucía: Buenas noches. En mi oficina todos dicen "habían muchas personas". ¿Ya se acepta?
Ofelia: Es una pregunta muy común. Con el "haber" que significa existir, la norma pide el singular: "había muchas personas", igual que "hay". El plural es frecuentísimo en el habla de América, y no es raro que lo diga gente culta, pero las academias siguen recomendando el singular.
Ramiro: Ahora, Daniel, desde Mérida.
Daniel: Una prima de España se burla de mí porque digo "checar". ¿Es un error?
Ofelia: No. "Checar" es la forma que se usa en México, y el Diccionario panhispánico de dudas lo registra. Lo mismo pasa con "rentar". Son usos establecidos en México, no incorrecciones. Su prima dice "alquilar", y también está bien.
Ramiro: Última llamada. Mariana, desde Guadalajara.
Mariana: Hola. En el trabajo escribo mucho "hace sentido" porque trabajo en inglés todo el día. ¿Está bien?
Ofelia: Es un calco del inglés "make sense". Se entiende, pero en español decimos "tiene sentido". Los calcos no son un crimen: la lengua evoluciona con ellos. Pero si quiere sonar cuidada, se lo desaconsejo.
Ramiro: Doctora, ¿hay un español mejor que otro?
Ofelia: No. Hay usos más formales y menos formales, y hay prestigio y estigma, que son cosas sociales. Pero ninguna variedad es "mal español". El español de Mérida y el de Madrid tienen una gramática igual de completa.
Ramiro: Muchas gracias, doctora. Nos escuchamos el próximo jueves.
```

Summary: the host introduces the linguist. Sandra's boss says *pienso de que*: dequeísmo, and the
question test shows why; correct him tactfully. Héctor was corrected for *me di cuenta que*: that
is queísmo, very frequent in speech, but careful texts keep *de*. Lucía asks about *habían muchas
personas*: existential *haber* stays singular, though the plural is very common in Latin America,
even among educated speakers. Daniel's Spanish cousin teases him for *checar*: it's the established
Mexican form, recorded by the DPD, like *rentar*. Mariana writes *hace sentido* from English:
it's a calque; *tiene sentido* is better in careful Spanish. Finally, no variety is "bad Spanish";
prestige and stigma are social. Glosses: *con tacto* (tactfully), *al revés* (the other way round),
*se burla de mí* (makes fun of me), *nos escuchamos* (until next time, on the radio).

## Pronunciation

- *lingüística*: lin-GÜÍS-ti-ca, four syllables. The dieresis on *ü* means the *u* is pronounced:
  *gwee*.
- *hispanohablante*: his-pa-no-a-BLAN-te, six syllables; the *h* of *habla* is silent.
- *dequeísmo*: de-que-ÍS-mo, four syllables; *que* sounds like *keh*. *queísmo*: que-ÍS-mo, three.
- *neologismo*: ne-o-lo-GIS-mo, five syllables; each vowel of *neo* is its own syllable.

## Common mistakes

- Overcorrecting. Afraid of dequeísmo, learners drop needed *de*s: *Me acuerdo de que*, *Estoy
  seguro de que* and *Me alegro de que* are all standard.
- Calling every Mexicanism an error. *Checar*, *rentar*, *el carro* and *ahorita* are standard
  Mexican Spanish.
- Treating *le* for *les* as a speech error. It's normal in speech everywhere; just write *les*
  in formal texts.
- Thinking the DLE is Spain's dictionary. It is prepared by all the academies and marks
  Mexican senses (*Méx.*) as such.

## Key points

- The norm is described by the academies (RAE 1713, Academia Mexicana 1875, ASALE 1951) in the
  DLE, the DPD, the *Nueva gramática* and the *Ortografía*; FundéuRAE gives quick advice.
- Prescriptive works recommend; descriptive work records. No variety is "bad Spanish".
- Dequeísmo adds a *de*, queísmo drops one; test with a question or *eso*.
- Impersonal *haber* stays singular (*había, hubo*); *habemos*, *-stes* and *haiga* are nonstandard;
  *le* for *les* is common in speech.
- *Checar* and *rentar* are accepted in Mexico; *hacer sentido* and *tomar lugar* are calques to
  avoid in careful writing.

lessons.title: Con todo respeto: tact, euphemism and irony
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 introduced mitigation and intensification as tools of politeness. This lesson uses them
where they matter most: refusing, disagreeing with someone above you, criticizing, giving bad news
and apologizing. It also covers the opposite skill, reading what people don't say outright:
euphemism, irony and litotes. The theme is diplomacy, where *el tacto* (tact) is a profession.

## Five delicate speech acts

| Act | Formulas | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| refusing | *Te lo agradezco mucho, pero me temo que no voy a poder.* | Thanks a lot, but I'm afraid I won't be able to. |
| refusing in writing | *Lamentablemente, me veo en la necesidad de declinar su amable invitación.* | Unfortunately, I find myself obliged to decline your kind invitation. |
| disagreeing upward | *Con todo respeto, creo que…; Si me permite…; Entiendo su punto, pero…* | With all due respect, I think…; If I may…; I see your point, but… |
| criticizing | *No es por nada, pero…; Sin ánimo de ofender…* | Don't take this the wrong way, but…; No offense meant, but… |
| bad news | *Lamento comunicarle que…; Por desgracia…; Me temo que…* | I regret to inform you that…; Unfortunately…; I'm afraid that… |
| apologizing | *Le ruego disculpe las molestias; Le pido una disculpa.* | Please excuse the inconvenience; I apologize to you. |

*Declinar* (to decline politely) is formal and written; in speech, *no voy a poder* does the job. A
refusal is *una negativa*: *Recibimos una negativa*. *Le ruego disculpe* drops the *que* (*le ruego
que disculpe*), as formal letters often do. *Le pido una disculpa* is the usual Mexican formal
apology.

Notice the shape: thanks or a softener first, the unwelcome part second, often a reason or an
alternative after it. That shape *suaviza* (softens) the message without hiding it.

## How Spanish mitigates

To *atenuar* (tone down) a statement, Spanish has more than *un poco*:

- The conditional distances an opinion: *Yo diría que el plan es arriesgado* — I'd say the
  plan is risky. *¿No sería mejor esperar?* — Wouldn't it be better to wait?
- The imperfect of courtesy makes a request less direct: *Quería comentarle algo* — I wanted
  to mention something to you.
- The future of concession grants the other side before disagreeing: *Será lo que tú digas,
  pero yo no lo veo así* — It may be as you say, but I don't see it that way. *Tendrá sus razones,
  pero…* — He must have his reasons, but…
- Impersonal forms take the blame away from the listener: *Se cometió un error* instead of
  *Usted cometió un error*.
- Diminutives and hedges: *un poquito, a lo mejor, como que, medio* (*Está medio caro*, It's
  kind of expensive).

Intensification works the other way, on praise and thanks: *Le agradezco infinitamente; Es un
trabajo extraordinario.* Pile it on criticism and you get an insult.

![A dial with a needle. The left half is labeled atenuar, with examples a lo mejor, un poquito, yo diría que, ¿no sería mejor…?. The right half is labeled intensificar, with examples muchísimo, sumamente, de verdad, infinitamente. Under the left half: peticiones y críticas. Under the right half: agradecimientos y elogios.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Euphemism

A **[[euphemism]]** (*el eufemismo*) replaces a word felt as harsh with a milder one:

| Direct | Euphemism | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *morir* | *fallecer* (B2) | to pass away |
| *el viejo* | *el adulto mayor* (lesson 15's word: senior citizen) | older adult |
| *el indigente* | *la persona en situación de calle* | person experiencing homelessness |
| *los despidos* | *el ajuste de personal* | staff adjustment (layoffs) |
| *subir los precios* | *actualizar las tarifas* | to update the rates |

Some euphemisms are respectful, and official Mexican usage prefers them (*adulto mayor*, *persona
en situación de calle*). Others hide something: an *ajuste de personal* is still people losing
their jobs. A C1 reader notices the difference.

## Irony and litotes

**[[Irony]]** (*la ironía*) says one thing and means the opposite, trusting the listener to notice.
**[[Litotes]]** is a kind of understatement: denying the opposite to affirm something strongly.

- *No está nada mal.* — It's not bad at all. (= It's very good: litotes.)
- *No es tonto.* — He's no fool. (= He's clever.)
- *¡Qué oportuno!* — How timely! (said of something that came at the worst moment: irony)
- *Muy bonito, ¿no?* — Very nice, huh? (a reproach: irony)

Intonation marks them: an ironic *¡Qué oportuno!* is drawn out and flat, often with a pause before
it. Context does the rest: if the bus breaks down in the rain, *¡Qué suerte!* is *irónico*. Lesson
02's *el sarcasmo* is irony meant to hurt or mock.

## Indirectness: a note on Mexican politeness

Many English speakers find Mexican politeness indirect, and our observation is that refusals are
often softened until they no longer sound like refusals. *Sí, cómo no, luego lo vemos* (Yes, of
course, we'll see later), *A ver si puedo* (I'll see if I can) or a warm *Te aviso* (I'll let you
know) can all mean "probably not". It isn't dishonesty: a direct *no* can feel *descortés*
(lesson 01), so speakers protect the relationship. Some listeners are more *susceptibles*
(touchy) than others, and a frank *No me gustó* that sounds normal in some countries may cause
*incomodidad* (awkwardness) in Mexico. This is a tendency, not a rule: plenty of Mexicans value
*la franqueza* (frankness), especially among close friends.

## Diplomacy in Mexico

*La diplomacia* is the art of *negociar* (negotiating) between states, and *la negociación* its
work. An *embajador* (ambassador; *la embajadora*) heads B1's *embajada*; a *cumbre* is a summit
meeting of leaders (B2's *la cima* is a mountain top); a *tratado* is a treaty. When two sides are
stuck, a *mediador* (mediator) offers *la mediación*: to *mediar* is to mediate, in a
*conciliador* (conciliatory) tone.

Mexico's foreign ministry is the Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (SRE). Its best-known
principle is the *Doctrina Estrada*, issued by the diplomat Genaro Estrada and published on
September 27, 1930: Mexico would not pass judgment on other governments by "recognizing" them, and
would simply keep or withdraw its diplomats, in defense of non-intervention and self-determination.
Principles of this kind were written into the Constitution (article 89, section X) by a reform
published on May 11, 1988 (to confirm against the official text).

![A round summit table seen from above, with a small flag stand at each seat, all flags left blank. One seat at the head is marked with a nameplate, a document lies in the middle of the table, and two microphones stand at the seats facing each other. In a corner, away from the table, a person holds a notepad.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Text: one disagreement, two registers

Two cultural attachés in Bogotá are preparing a photography exhibition. The Chilean attaché writes
first; the Mexican attaché, Valeria Arriaga, answers. Then Valeria calls her friend Pato.

### The e-mails

> Asunto: Exposición *Miradas del Sur y del Norte*: propuesta de ajustes
>
> Estimada licenciada Arriaga:
>
> Le escribo en relación con la exposición que nuestras embajadas inaugurarán en el Museo de la
> Ciudad. Tras revisar el espacio, el museo nos sugiere adelantar la inauguración al 3 de marzo y
> reducir la sección mexicana de cuarenta a veinticinco fotografías, a fin de dar cabida a una sala
> de video. Entiendo que se trata de un cambio delicado, por lo que le agradecería que me hiciera
> llegar sus comentarios antes del viernes.
>
> Reciba un cordial saludo,
> Tomás Echeverría, Agregado Cultural, Embajada de Chile

> Asunto: RE: Exposición *Miradas del Sur y del Norte*
>
> Estimado Tomás:
>
> Muchas gracias por su mensaje y por el trabajo que usted y el museo han dedicado a este proyecto.
>
> Con todo respeto, quisiera plantearle algunas dudas. Adelantar la fecha no sería un problema; sin
> embargo, reducir la sección mexicana a veinticinco obras nos obligaría a dejar fuera a tres de los
> fotógrafos invitados, a quienes ya se les confirmó su participación. Me temo que eso podría
> generar cierta incomodidad.
>
> Si me permite una sugerencia, ¿no sería posible reducir ambas secciones en la misma proporción, o
> bien instalar la sala de video en el vestíbulo? Así se mantendría el equilibrio que acordamos.
>
> Quedo a sus órdenes para conversarlo por teléfono cuando le resulte conveniente.
>
> Un saludo cordial,
> Valeria Arriaga, Agregada Cultural, Embajada de México

Summary: Tomás explains that the museum wants to open earlier, on March 3, and to cut the Mexican
section from forty photographs to twenty-five to make room for a video room. He calls the change
delicate and asks for comments by Friday. Valeria thanks him, accepts the earlier date, and objects
that the cut would leave out three photographers already confirmed, which could cause
awkwardness. She suggests cutting both sections in the same proportion or putting the video room
in the lobby, and offers to talk by phone. Glosses: *dar cabida a* (to make room for), *plantear
dudas* (to raise concerns), *dejar fuera* (to leave out), *o bien* (or else), *quedo a sus
órdenes* (I remain at your disposal, Mexico).

### The phone call

```dialogue
# Llamada
Pato: ¿Qué onda, Vale? ¿Cómo va lo de la expo?
Valeria: Ay, ni me preguntes. Hoy me escribió el agregado chileno, súper amable, ¿eh?, para decirme que me quitan quince fotos.
Pato: ¿Quince? ¡Qué oportuno, a tres semanas de inaugurar!
Valeria: Ándale. Y todo para meter una sala de video. Yo quería contestarle "¿Estás loco?", pero le escribí "Con todo respeto, quisiera plantearle algunas dudas".
Pato: Muy diplomática.
Valeria: Pues es mi chamba. La neta, él no es mala onda: el que presiona es el museo. Él nomás está mediando.
Pato: ¿Y qué le propusiste?
Valeria: Que recorten las dos secciones igual. Si les quitan fotos a los chilenos también, a ver si siguen tan entusiasmados con el video.
Pato: Qué sutil. ¿Y si te dice que no?
Valeria: Pues tendrá sus razones, pero no voy a dejar fuera a tres fotógrafos que ya invité. Sin ánimo de ofender a nadie, eso sí sería una falta de respeto.
Pato: Oye, no está nada mal tu estrategia.
Valeria: Ya veremos. Mañana lo hablamos por teléfono. Deséame suerte.
```

Summary: Valeria tells Pato, with irony (*súper amable, ¿eh?*), that the Chilean attaché wants to
remove fifteen of her photos; Pato answers with more irony (*¡Qué oportuno!*). She admits she
wanted to write something rude and chose a diplomatic formula instead. She doesn't blame Tomás:
the museum is pushing, and he's only mediating. Her proposal, equal cuts for both sides, is a
*sutil* (subtle) test of the museum's enthusiasm. Pato approves with a litotes (*no está nada
mal*). Glosses: *la expo* (the exhibition, informal), *meter* (to fit in), *no es mala onda* (he's
not a bad guy), *la falta de respeto* (disrespect).

Compare the *sutileza* (subtlety) of the e-mail with the *franqueza* of the call: the same
objection, mitigated in one, ironic and blunt in the other.

## Pronunciation

- *diplomacia*: di-plo-MA-cia, four syllables; *diplomático*: di-plo-MÁ-ti-co, five.
- *eufemismo*: eu-fe-MIS-mo, four; *eu* is one syllable, like *eh-oo* said quickly.
- *atenuar*: a-te-NUAR, three syllables; but *atenúo*: a-te-NÚ-o, four, because the written
  accent splits *ú-o*.
- *ironía*: i-ro-NÍ-a, four syllables; the accent on *í* splits it from the *a*.

## Common mistakes

- Translating "I'm sorry, but no" word for word. *Lo siento, pero no* is blunt; add thanks and
  a reason: *Te lo agradezco, pero me temo que no voy a poder.*
- Missing a litotes. With a smile, *No está nada mal* is praise, not faint
  approval.
- Calling a euphemism a lie. Many are just respectful (*adulto mayor*); judge by what they
  hide.
- Declinar in speech. *Declino su invitación* in conversation sounds stiff; it belongs in
  writing.

## Key points

- Refusals, disagreements, criticism and bad news follow a shape: softener, message, reason or
  alternative.
- Spanish mitigates with the conditional, the imperfect of courtesy, the future of concession
  (*Será lo que tú digas, pero…*), impersonal forms and small hedges.
- Euphemisms soften (*fallecer, adulto mayor*) or hide (*ajuste de personal*).
- Irony and litotes (*¡Qué oportuno!, No está nada mal*) depend on intonation and context.
- Mexican politeness often softens refusals; read *a ver si puedo* and *te aviso* with care.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Lenguaje claro: rewriting official texts
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 showed how a message climbs the register scale into the formal Spanish of an *oficio*.
This lesson goes back down, but not to the colloquial end. *El lenguaje claro* (plain language) is
formal, correct and respectful, and still easy to read on the first try. It is the answer to a
complaint as old as offices: that official Spanish is written for the people who write it, not
for the people who must act on it.

You met legal style in B2 12h1 (the future for obligations, long nominal subjects, conditions
stacked after the rule). Here you'll take two original texts of that kind, one notice and one
contract clause, and rewrite them step by step. Then you'll ask the harder question: what can't be
simplified without losing *precisión* (precision)?

## What plain language is

Plain-language organizations usually define it by its results rather than by rules: a text is in
plain language when the people it's written for can find what they need, understand it, and use
it. *La claridad* (clarity) is measured on the reader, not on the writer's intentions.

That definition has practical consequences:

- Short sentences, one idea each, usually under about 25 words.
- Active voice and a visible doer: *Cortaremos el agua*, not *Se llevará a cabo la suspensión
  del servicio*.
- Verbs instead of nouns: *revisar* rather than *llevar a cabo la revisión* (B2 18's support
  verbs).
- The reader's words: *el dueño* before *el arrendador*; when a *tecnicismo* (technical term)
  is needed, explain it the first time.
- The most important thing first, then the details.
- Layout: headings, lists, dates and numbers where the eye finds them.

None of this means writing like a chat. A plain notice still uses *usted*, still says *Le
recomendamos* and not *Oye*. Plain language moves a text toward neutral on lesson 01's scale and
keeps it there.

## A movement, not a fashion

The plain-language movement grew from the 1970s onward in several English-speaking countries, and
in June 2023 the International Organization for Standardization published ISO 24495-1, *Plain
language — Part 1: Governing principles and guidelines*.

In Spanish:

- Mexico launched its *Lenguaje Ciudadano* (citizens' language) initiative in 2004, under the
  Secretaría de la Función Pública. A federal manual circulated in 2021 calls Mexico the first
  Latin American country to take such a step and recommends knowing the reader, writing simply,
  avoiding jargon and using a clear layout.
- Spain's Ministry of Justice presented the report of its Comisión para la Modernización del
  Lenguaje Jurídico to the Council of Ministers in September 2011. It noted that citizens found
  legal language cryptic and recommended ordering ideas, shorter paragraphs, fewer chained
  subordinate clauses and less abuse of gerunds and the passive. A new commission on the clarity and
  modernization of legal language held its first session in June 2023.

Several Latin American courts and governments have plain-language guides of their own; look for
*guía de lenguaje claro* with the name of a country.

## The habits of bureaucratic Spanish

*La burocracia* (bureaucracy, red tape) has a style. A *burocrático* (bureaucratic) text often
shows these habits:

| Habit | Example | Plain version |
|---|---|---|
| nouns for actions | *la realización de trabajos de mantenimiento* | *vamos a dar mantenimiento* |
| empty formulas | *Se hace del conocimiento de los usuarios que…* | *Le informamos que…* |
| hidden doer | *se llevará a cabo la suspensión del servicio* | *cortaremos el agua* |
| *redundancia* (needless repetition) | *en el periodo comprendido entre… y…* | *del… al…* |
| ornamental synonyms | *el vital líquido* (for water) | *el agua* |
| one long sentence | nearly 100 words before the first period | several short sentences |

To *simplificar* (simplify) and *reformular* (rephrase) such a text, work in order: find the
message, put it first, unpack the nouns, name the doer, cut the repeats, then lay it out.

## Example 1: a water-cut notice

An original notice in the style of a municipal water office:

> AVISO. Se hace del conocimiento de los usuarios del servicio de suministro de agua potable que,
> con motivo de la realización de trabajos de mantenimiento preventivo en la red de distribución,
> se llevará a cabo la suspensión temporal del servicio en las colonias Centro, San Rafael y Las
> Flores, en el periodo comprendido entre las 08:00 horas del día martes 14 y las 18:00 horas del
> día miércoles 15 del mes en curso, por lo que se exhorta a la ciudadanía a efectuar el
> almacenamiento del vital líquido con la debida anticipación, a efecto de evitar contratiempos.

> NOTICE. Users of the drinking-water supply service are hereby informed that, owing to the
> carrying out of preventive maintenance work on the distribution network, a temporary suspension
> of service will be carried out in the Centro, San Rafael and Las Flores neighborhoods, in the
> period between 08:00 on Tuesday the 14th and 18:00 on Wednesday the 15th of the current month,
> and therefore citizens are urged to store the vital liquid in due time, so as to avoid setbacks.

Step 1: find the message. Who is affected? Three neighborhoods. What happens? No water. When?
From Tuesday 8:00 to Wednesday 18:00. Why? Maintenance. What should the reader do? Store water.

Step 2: put the most important first. The reader's question is "Will I have water?", so the
heading answers it.

Step 3: unpack the nouns and name the doer. *La realización de trabajos de mantenimiento* →
*vamos a dar mantenimiento*; *se llevará a cabo la suspensión* → *no habrá agua*; *efectuar el
almacenamiento* → *guardar agua*.

Step 4: cut the redundancy. *Temporal* is implied by the dates; *en el periodo comprendido
entre* becomes *desde… hasta*; *el vital líquido* is just *agua*; *a efecto de evitar
contratiempos* adds nothing.

Step 5: lay it out.

> **Sin agua el martes 14 y el miércoles 15**
>
> Vamos a dar mantenimiento a la red de agua potable. Por eso no habrá agua en las colonias
> Centro, San Rafael y Las Flores:
>
> - desde el martes 14 a las 8:00
> - hasta el miércoles 15 a las 18:00
>
> Le recomendamos guardar agua antes del martes. ¿Dudas? Llame al 771 555 0142.

> No water on Tuesday the 14th and Wednesday the 15th. We are going to do maintenance on the
> drinking-water network. Because of this there will be no water in the Centro, San Rafael and Las
> Flores neighborhoods: from Tuesday the 14th at 8:00 until Wednesday the 15th at 18:00. We
> recommend that you store water before Tuesday. Questions? Call 771 555 0142.

One sentence of 96 words has become five short ones. Nothing the reader needs is lost, and one
thing is added: a phone number, which every notice of this kind should give.

![Two versions of the same notice side by side. On the left, labeled Antes, a single dense block of small text under the word AVISO. On the right, labeled Después, a bold heading Sin agua el martes 14 y el miércoles 15, a short sentence, two bullet points with the start and end times, a recommendation, and a phone number at the bottom. Arrows between them point to three changes: el mensaje primero, verbos, no sustantivos, and listas y fechas visibles.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Example 2: a lease clause

Contracts are harder, because every word may matter in court. Here is an original clause in the
style of a Mexican lease (invented for this lesson; not legal advice):

> CLÁUSULA OCTAVA. En caso de que el ARRENDATARIO incurra en mora en el pago de dos o más
> mensualidades consecutivas de la renta pactada, el ARRENDADOR podrá, a su elección, exigir el
> cumplimiento forzoso del presente contrato o darlo por rescindido, sin perjuicio del cobro de los
> intereses moratorios que se generen a razón del 3 % (tres por ciento) mensual sobre el saldo
> insoluto.

> EIGHTH CLAUSE. Should the TENANT fall into arrears in the payment of two or more consecutive
> monthly installments of the agreed rent, the LANDLORD may, at his option, demand enforced
> performance of this contract or declare it rescinded, without prejudice to collecting the default
> interest generated at the rate of 3% (three percent) per month on the unpaid balance.

Step 1: the message. If the tenant misses two months in a row, the landlord chooses between
two remedies, and interest is owed either way.

Step 2: decide what stays. *Incurrir en mora* (to fall into arrears) can become *dejar de
pagar*. But *rescindir* is a *tecnicismo*: ending a contract because the other side broke it, not
just "ending" it. And *saldo insoluto* (unpaid balance) is exact. Keep the legal meaning; explain
the term.

Step 3: write and lay out.

> **8. Si usted no paga la renta**
>
> Si usted deja de pagar dos meses seguidos de renta, el dueño (el arrendador) puede elegir:
>
> a) exigirle que cumpla el contrato y pague, o
>
> b) rescindir el contrato, es decir, terminarlo porque usted no cumplió.
>
> En los dos casos, usted deberá pagar además un interés del 3 % al mes sobre la cantidad que deba.

> 8. If you don't pay the rent. If you stop paying two months of rent in a row, the owner (the
> landlord) can choose: a) to demand that you comply with the contract and pay, or b) to rescind
> the contract, that is, to end it because you didn't comply. In both cases, you will also have to
> pay interest of 3% a month on the amount you owe.

Notice what didn't change: the numbers, the two options, the word *rescindir*. A contract that
addresses the tenant as *usted* should define who *usted* is (often in a first clause: *En este
contrato, "usted" es el arrendatario*).

## What can't be simplified

Simplifying is not the same as shortening. Three limits:

- Terms of art. *Rescindir, la prescripción, el saldo insoluto* have exact legal meanings.
  Replace them and you may change the law, not just the style. Keep them and explain them.
- New ambiguity. *La ambigüedad* (ambiguity) can be created by simplifying. *El dueño puede
  terminar el contrato si usted no paga dos meses* could mean any two months or two in a row. The
  original *consecutivas* prevented that; the plain version keeps it as *seguidos*.
- Necessary length. A *conciso* (concise) text says everything needed in as few words as
  possible, not fewer. A notice that drops the times to look short has failed.

The test is always the reader: can the tenant, or the neighbor in San Rafael, act correctly after
one reading?

## Common mistakes

- Plain = colloquial. *Oigan, no va a haber agua* is clear but wrong for an official notice.
  Stay neutral and keep *usted*.
- Removing every technical word. Some must stay; explain them with *es decir* or a parenthesis.
- Splitting without linking. Five short sentences still need connectors: *por eso, además, en
  los dos casos*.
- Shortening by deleting facts. Check that every date, number and condition survives.

## Key points

- Plain language is defined by the reader: they can find, understand and use what they need.
- Mexico's *Lenguaje Ciudadano* began in 2004; Spain's commission on legal language reported in
  2011; ISO 24495-1 appeared in 2023.
- Rewrite in order: message, most important first, verbs for nouns, a visible doer, no redundancy,
  clear layout.
- Keep terms of art and explain them; don't create new ambiguity; concise doesn't mean incomplete.

lessons.title: Honors: Oír otros españoles: Spain, the Caribbean, the Andes and the Río de la Plata
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 03 said that no **[[variety]]** of Spanish is "bad Spanish". This lesson is about hearing that
variety. The Instituto Cervantes' specification for the DELE C1 (in force since 2024) says that the
texts and recordings of the reading and listening tests come from at least three geographic
varieties, so a C1 listener trained only on Mexican Spanish will meet sounds that throw them.

B1 24h1 taught regional words and B2 24h1 taught *voseo*. This lesson is about sound: the
features you'll hear in Spain, the Caribbean, the Andes and the Río de la Plata, described for
recognition. You don't need to imitate any of them. Mexican pronunciation, which this course
teaches, is understood everywhere.

A note on the listening questions. The app speaks with a Mexican voice (es-MX), and no
synthetic voice reproduces real regional speech. So this lesson's listening questions play a
sentence in that Mexican voice and ask what it would sound like elsewhere. To hear the real
accents, listen to radio, podcasts and television from each country; the descriptions below tell
you what to listen for.

## Two features most speakers share

Start with what Mexico has in common with most of the Spanish-speaking world.

- **[[Seseo]]** (*el seseo*): *z* and *c* before *e, i* are pronounced as *s*, so *casa* (house) and
  *caza* (hunt) sound the same. It is the norm in all of Latin America, in the Canary Islands and
  in parts of Andalusia.
- **[[Yeísmo]]** (*el yeísmo*): *ll* and *y* are pronounced alike, so *calló* (fell silent) and
  *cayó* (fell) sound the same. It is the majority pronunciation in Spain and the Americas.

What changes from one region to another is how that shared sound is made, and a handful of other
*rasgos* (distinguishing features). The map shades whole countries for simplicity; the features
belong to regions and groups of speakers, not to borders.

```map
base: world
title: Four listening areas (simplified)
view: 60, -120 to -56, 10
region: Spain | Peninsular Spanish
region: Cuba, Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico | Caribbean Spanish
region: Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia | Andean Spanish
region: Argentina, Uruguay | Río de la Plata Spanish
region: Mexico | Mexican Spanish (this course)
point: Madrid | 40.42, -3.70 | Peninsular Spanish
point: Sevilla | 37.39, -5.98 | Peninsular Spanish
point: San Juan | 18.47, -66.11 | Caribbean Spanish
point: Caracas | 10.49, -66.88 | Caribbean Spanish
point: Quito | -0.18, -78.47 | Andean Spanish
point: La Paz | -16.50, -68.15 | Andean Spanish
point: Buenos Aires | -34.60, -58.38 | Río de la Plata Spanish
point: Montevideo | -34.90, -56.16 | Río de la Plata Spanish
point: Ciudad de México | 19.43, -99.13 | Mexican Spanish (this course)
caption: Countries are shaded as wholes. Caribbean features are also heard on the coasts of Venezuela and Colombia (Caracas is marked), Andean features in the highlands of Colombia, and southern Spain (Sevilla) shares several features with the Caribbean.
```

## Spain: *distinción*, seseo and ceceo

Most of Spain, including Madrid and the north, uses **[[distinción]]** (*la distinción*): *z* and *c*
before *e, i* are said like English *th* in *thin*, and *s* is an *s*. So *casa* and *caza* differ:
*CA-sa* and *CA-tha*. *Gracias* sounds like *GRA-thias*. It isn't a lisp: the same speaker says
*s* perfectly well in *sí*.

The south complicates the picture. Parts of Andalusia and the Canary Islands use seseo, like
Mexico. Other parts of southern Spain use *el ceceo*: the *th* sound for both letters, so *casa*
and *caza* both sound like *CA-tha*. Ohio State University's *Dialectos del español* project
describes ceceo as characteristic of many parts of southern Spain, and also records it in parts of
Nicaragua, El Salvador and Honduras.

Other things you'll hear in Spain:

- A *j* (and *g* before *e, i*) that is often harsher and further back in the throat than
  Mexico's: *jamón*, *gente*.
- In the south, the *s* at the end of a syllable weakened to a breath, as in the Caribbean.
- *-ado* reduced to *-ao*, very common in relaxed speech across Spain: *cansado* → *cansao*.

*Peninsular* (from the Iberian Peninsula) is how Latin Americans often describe Spain's Spanish:
*el español peninsular*.

## The Caribbean: aspiration and lost s

Caribbean Spanish (*el español caribeño*) is spoken in Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican
Republic and along the coasts of Venezuela and Colombia. Its best-known feature is **[[aspiration]]**:
an *s* at the end of a syllable becomes a breath, like English *h*, or disappears. Ohio State's
project records both, in southern Spain and in coastal and lowland America.

- *los ojos* → *loh ojoh*; *¿Cómo estás?* → *¿Cómo ehtá?*
- *mismo* → *mihmo*; *las casas* → *lah casa*

Other Caribbean features:

- L and r may swap at the end of a syllable: *puerta* can sound like *puelta*, especially in
  Puerto Rico; the reverse (*alma* like *arma*) is heard in some areas.
- The *j* is a soft breath, *h* rather than a scrape: *trabajo* → *trabaho*. (Ohio State also
  records this in Central America, Colombia and Bolivia.)
- Final *n* is said at the back of the mouth, like *-ng* in *sing*: *pan* → *pang*.
- *-ado* → *-ao* and *para* → *pa'*, as in relaxed speech elsewhere.

The overall impression is fast, with consonants softened and vowels carrying the words.

## The Andes: firm consonants, weak vowels

Andean Spanish (*el español andino*), in the highlands of Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia and southern
Colombia, often sounds the opposite of Caribbean Spanish to learners:

- The *s* is kept firmly at the end of syllables: *los ojos* has two clear *s* sounds.
- Unstressed vowels weaken, sometimes almost disappearing: *pues* can sound like *ps*, *buenos
  días* like *buens días*. Ohio State notes this in Mexico too, which is why central Mexican and
  Andean speech can sound alike in this one way.
- The *r* is often assibilated, with a buzz like the *s* in *measure*: *carro*, *ropa*. Ohio
  State records this in the Andes and also in Paraguay, Chile, Costa Rica, Guatemala and parts of
  Mexico.
- Some speakers keep *ll* and *y* apart (no yeísmo): *llama* with an *ly*-like sound, *yate*
  with *y*. In Quito, *ll* (but not *y*) may sound like the *s* in *measure*.

Its *cadencia* (cadence, the rhythm of speech) is often described as slow and measured.

## The Río de la Plata: *sh* and *zh*

Buenos Aires and Montevideo share the *rioplatense* variety (from the Río de la Plata, the River
Plate). Two features stand out:

- Sheísmo and zheísmo: *ll* and *y* are said like *sh* in *shoe* or like the *s* in *measure*:
  *calle* → *CA-she*, *yo* → *sho*, *llegué* → *she-GUÉ*. Many younger speakers in Buenos Aires
  use the *sh* sound.
- Aspiration before a consonant: *mismo* → *mihmo*, *los dos* → *loh dos*.

Its intonation is often compared to Italian, and many link that to the large Italian immigration
of the late 19th and early 20th centuries; take this as a common description, not a measured fact.

## What you'll hear: one sentence, five ways

The sentence: *Los chicos ya llegaron a la plaza, ¿vas a venir?* (The kids have already gotten to
the square; are you going to come?) The spellings in the middle column imitate speech; they aren't
written Spanish.

| Variety | How it may sound | Features |
|---|---|---|
| Mexico City | *Los chicos ya llegaron a la plasa, ¿vas a venir?* | seseo, yeísmo, firm *s* |
| Madrid | *Los chicos ya han llegado a la platha, ¿vas a venir?* | *distinción*: *plaza* with *th*; Spain often uses the perfect here (B1) |
| San Juan, Puerto Rico | *Lo' chico' ya llegaron a la plasa, ¿va' a venil?* | final *s* aspirated or lost; *r* → *l* |
| La Paz | *Los chicos ya llegaron a la plasa, ¿vas a venir?* (buzzing *r*, short unstressed vowels) | firm *s*, assibilated *r* |
| Buenos Aires | *Loh chicos sha shegaron a la plasa, ¿vas a venir?* | *sh* for *y* and *ll*; *s* aspirated before a consonant |

![A chart with four columns, one for each variety: Peninsular, Caribeña, Andina, Rioplatense. Under each, a cloud with an example word and how it sounds: Peninsular, gracias said GRA-thias; Caribeña, los ojos said loh ojoh; Andina, carro with a buzzing r; Rioplatense, calle said CA-she. Below each cloud, the name of the feature: distinción, aspiración de la s, r asibilada, sheísmo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Example 1: decoding a Caribbean sentence

You hear, from a speaker in Santo Domingo: *Mi'ja, ehtamo' cansao, vamo' a dehcansá un rato.*

1. Restore the *s* sounds. A breath or a gap before a consonant, or at the end of a word, is
   usually an *s*: *ehtamo'* → *estamos*; *vamo'* → *vamos*; *dehcansá* → *descansar*.
2. Restore *-ado*: *cansao* → *cansados* (the plural *s* was lost too: *estamos* tells you it's
   plural).
3. Restore final *r*: *dehcansá* lost its *r* as well, which happens at the end of infinitives.
4. Contractions: *mi'ja* is *mi hija*, an affectionate term of address.

Result: *Mija, estamos cansados, vamos a descansar un rato.* — Honey, we're tired, let's rest for a
while.

## Example 2: decoding a *rioplatense* sentence

You hear, from a speaker in Buenos Aires: *Sho me shamo Lucía y shegué ashé de Montevideo.*

1. Every *sh* is a candidate for *ll* or *y*. Try both: *sho* → *yo*; *me shamo* → *me
   llamo*; *shegué* → *llegué*. *Ashé* could be *allé* (no such word) or *ayé*: *ayer*, with the
   final *r* weakened.
2. Check the grammar. *Yo me llamo Lucía y llegué ayer de Montevideo* makes sense: a time word
   fits between *llegué* and *de*.

Result: My name is Lucía and I arrived yesterday from Montevideo. When a sound confuses you, ask
which written letters could make it, and let the grammar choose.

## Why this matters for the DELE C1

Because the exam's recordings come from at least three varieties, a C1 candidate has to follow a
Caribbean or Argentine speaker without help. Three strategies:

- Expect the features, so they don't distract you: lost *s* in the Caribbean, *sh* in Buenos
  Aires, *th* in Madrid.
- Listen for meaning, not sounds. Grammar and context restore most of what you miss.
- Expose yourself early. A few minutes a day of radio or podcasts from each area does more
  than any description.

## Common mistakes

- Calling *distinción* a lisp. It is the standard pronunciation of most of Spain.
- Thinking Spain's Spanish is "more correct". The norm is shared (lesson 03); Mexican seseo is
  as standard as Madrid's *th*.
- Expecting every speaker to fit the label. Not every Argentine says *sh*, and many educated
  Caribbean speakers keep more *s* sounds in formal speech.
- Imitating. A learner who adopts a few features at random sounds odd everywhere. Recognize
  them; speak your own variety consistently.

## Key points

- Seseo and yeísmo are shared by most of the Spanish-speaking world, Mexico included.
- Spain: *distinción* (*th* for *z, ce, ci*) in the center and north; seseo and *ceceo* in parts of
  the south.
- The Caribbean: aspiration or loss of syllable-final *s*, *l / r* exchange, a soft *j*, final *n*
  as *-ng*.
- The Andes: firm *s*, weak unstressed vowels, an assibilated *r*, some *ll / y* distinction.
- The Río de la Plata: *sh* or *zh* for *ll* and *y*, aspiration before consonants.
- The app's voice is Mexican: use real recordings to train your ear.
