lessons.title: Siento que…: when the mood changes the meaning
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In B1 and B2 you learned which expressions trigger the subjunctive. At C1, ask instead "what am
I doing with this clause?" Several common verbs take either mood, and the mood changes what
they mean: *Dice que viene* reports a fact, *Dice que vengas* passes on a request. B2 lesson 13
showed this with *decir, advertir* and *insistir*; this lesson covers the whole family, the
cases where both moods are right, and the way the indicative takes a fact for granted.

The theme: perception, illusions and false memories.

## The principle: information or something else

The **[[indicative]]** presents what the clause says as information: something stated, reported,
perceived or remembered as true. The **[[subjunctive]]** presents it as something else: a request,
a reaction to a fact, a possibility, or a fact mentioned only as background. **[[Mood]]** is the
name for this choice of verb forms (Spanish has three moods: indicative, subjunctive and
imperative).

So a verb with two senses, one about information and one about influence or feeling, takes
both moods, one per sense. Neither is "wrong"; they say different things.

![A chart titled "Same verb, two meanings" with three columns: the verb, its meaning with the indicativo, and its meaning with the subjuntivo. Decir: reports a statement, Dice que viene; passes on a request, Dice que vengas. Sentir: perceive, Siento que hace frío; regret, Siento que no puedas venir. Entender: take in, Entiendo que estás molesto; sympathize, Entiendo que estés molesto. Temer: polite bad news, Me temo que no hay boletos; fear, Temo que no haya boletos. Suponer: assume, Supongo que ya llegó; imagine a case, Supongamos que no llegue. Recordar: remember, Recuerdo que lo dijo; remind someone to, Recuérdale que traiga las llaves. Admitir: accept a fact, Admito que me equivoqué; allow, No admito que me hables así.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The verbs

### *Decir* and other verbs of saying: report or request

- *Dice que viene a las cinco.* — She says she's coming at five. (a statement)
- *Dice que vengas a las cinco.* — She says you should come at five. (a request)
- *Avísale que llegamos tarde.* — Let him know we'll be late. *Avísale que nos espere.* — Tell
  him to wait for us.

The same split works with *escribir, gritar, repetir* and *avisar*.

### *Sentir*: perceive or regret

- *Siento que hace frío aquí.* — I feel that it's cold in here.
- *Siento que no puedas venir.* — I'm sorry you can't come.

With the indicative, *sentir* is a sense or a hunch (*Siento que alguien me observa* — I sense
someone is watching me); with the subjunctive, it's regret, like *lamentar*.

### *Comprender, entender*: take in or sympathize

- *Entiendo que estás molesto.* — I gather you're upset. (I've registered it.)
- *Entiendo que estés molesto.* — I understand your being upset. (I accept it as reasonable.)

Both are correct and close: the indicative is about information received, the subjunctive adds
sympathy.

### *Temer*: fear, or soften bad news

- *Temo que no haya boletos.* — I'm worried there may be no tickets.
- *Me temo que no hay boletos.* — I'm afraid there are no tickets.

*Temer* and *tener miedo de que* express fear: subjunctive. *Me temo que* usually announces,
politely, something the speaker knows: indicative. (*Me temo que* + subjunctive also occurs,
for a genuine worry.)

### *Suponer*: assume or imagine

- *Supongo que ya llegó.* — I suppose he's already arrived.
- *Supongamos que no llegue / no llega.* — Let's suppose he doesn't arrive.

*Supongo que* states an assumption: indicative. After *supongamos que* or *supón que*, both
moods are heard; the subjunctive sounds more hypothetical.

### *Pensar, recordar, esperar*

- *Pienso que es buena idea.* — I think it's a good idea. *Pienso ir.* — I'm planning to go.
- *Recuerdo que lo dijo en la junta.* — I remember he said it at the meeting.
- *Recuérdale que traiga las llaves.* — Remind him to bring the keys.
- *Espero que llegue a tiempo.* — I hope she gets here on time.

*Esperar* is the odd one. The DPD (2005 edition, *esperar*, §2) defines it as hoping that
something will happen *or believing that it will*. The subjunctive is the usual choice in both
senses, but in the "expect" sense you'll also hear the future indicative, *Espero que llegará a
tiempo*, presenting the arrival as a forecast. Recognize it; use the subjunctive yourself.

### *Insistir, aceptar, admitir*

- *Insiste en que es inocente / en que lo acompañemos.* — He insists he's innocent / that we go
  with him.
- *Admito que me equivoqué.* — I admit I was wrong.
- *No admito que me hables así.* — I won't allow you to talk to me like that.
- *Acepto que el plan tiene fallas.* — I accept that the plan has flaws. *No acepto que me
  traten así.* — I won't accept being treated like this.

## Verbs of perceiving and knowing

The lesson's new verbs report what the mind registers, so in the affirmative they take the
indicative: *Percibí que estaba nervioso* (I noticed he was nervous). *Intuyo que algo anda mal*
(I sense something's wrong). *Se percató de que lo seguían* (He became aware he was being
followed). *Captar* usually takes a noun (*No captó la ironía* — He didn't grasp the irony);
*discernir* takes *entre* (*discernir entre lo real y lo imaginado* — tell the real from the
imagined).

![An optical illusion under the question ¿Cuál es más larga? Two horizontal lines of exactly the same length, one above the other. The top line has arrowheads pointing outward at both ends; the bottom line ends in fins that open outward, like arrow tails, and looks longer. Dashed lines drop from the ends of both to a ruler, with the caption Miden lo mismo (they're the same length).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In this classic *ilusión óptica* (the Müller-Lyer illusion, published in 1889), the lines are
equal, yet most people *perciben* the lower one as longer: the brain makes an *inferencia* from
cues. In *la sinestesia*, one sense triggers another: some people see colors when they hear
notes. A 2006 survey of 500 people in Scotland (Simner and colleagues, in the journal
*Perception*) put its prevalence at about 4%. *El olfato* is often described as the sense most
closely tied to *la memoria*.

## Taking a fact for granted

After a verb of knowing or perceiving, even a negated one, the indicative tells the listener
that the fact is true:

- *No sabía que estabas aquí.* — I didn't know you were here. (You are.)
- *No me di cuenta de que ya era tarde.* — I didn't realize it was already late.

The subjunctive appears when the speaker doesn't vouch for the fact or denies seeing it:

- *No veo que haya ningún problema.* — I don't see that there's any problem. (There isn't one,
  as far as I can tell.)
- *No sabía que tuvieras hermanos.* — I didn't know you had brothers and sisters. (Also
  correct; it sounds surprised, as if the fact were still sinking in.)

If you accept the fact as true, the indicative is the safe choice.

### Questions with opinion verbs

B2 showed both moods in questions; now use the difference:

- *¿Crees que es verdad?* — Do you think it's true? (an open question; you may lean toward yes)
- *¿Crees que sea verdad?* — Do you really think it could be true? (more doubtful)

Both are correct; the subjunctive is very common in Mexican speech.

## *El hecho de que* and a *que* clause first

Both moods are standard here; choose the nuance:

- *El hecho de que recuerdes algo con detalle no significa que sea cierto.* — The fact that you
  remember something in detail doesn't mean it's true. (The subjunctive, the usual choice: the
  fact is a topic for comment.)
- *El hecho de que el testigo mintió quedó demostrado.* — The fact that the witness lied was
  proven. (The indicative: the fact itself is the news.)
- *Que la memoria nos engañe no debería sorprendernos.* — That memory fools us shouldn't
  surprise us.
- *Que la memoria nos engaña lo sabe cualquier psicólogo.* — Any psychologist knows that memory
  fools us.

A fronted *que* clause usually takes the subjunctive; the indicative is natural when the main
verb asserts knowledge (*lo sabe*).

## Reading: *Tres testigos, tres verdades*

> **Tres testigos, una esquina y tres verdades**
>
> Un martes a las ocho de la mañana, en una esquina de la colonia Narvarte, una camioneta de
> reparto y un taxi chocaron. No hubo heridos. Una hora después, tres personas que habían visto
> el accidente le contaron a una reportera lo que recordaban.
>
> Doña Teresa, que esperaba el camión, aseguró que el taxi «venía volando» y que se había pasado
> el alto. Julián, un estudiante que cruzaba la calle con audífonos, dijo que, por una
> distracción, no se percató del choque hasta oír el golpe, pero que la camioneta «seguramente» iba rápido, «porque esas camionetas siempre van rápido». La
> tercera testigo, una enfermera que salía de su turno, recordaba un detalle que nadie más
> mencionó: un perro que cruzó corriendo justo antes del impacto. Los tres eran sinceros. Y,
> como constató después el video de una cámara de la calle, los tres se equivocaban en algo: el
> semáforo estaba en amarillo, la camioneta iba despacio y el perro existía, pero había cruzado
> un minuto antes.
>
> ¿Mentían? No. Su memoria había hecho lo que hace siempre: reconstruir. Desde los años setenta,
> la psicóloga estadounidense Elizabeth Loftus ha mostrado en decenas de experimentos que el
> recuerdo no funciona como una grabación. En un estudio clásico de 1974, ella y John Palmer les
> mostraron a unos estudiantes el video de un choque. A unos les preguntaron a qué velocidad
> iban los autos cuando «se estrellaron»; a otros, cuando «se golpearon». Quienes oyeron el verbo más violento calcularon velocidades más altas y, una
> semana después, más de ellos dijeron haber visto vidrios rotos, aunque en el video no había
> ninguno. Una sola palabra bastó para cambiar el recuerdo.
>
> Más tarde, Loftus fue más lejos: en un experimento publicado en 1995, logró que algunos
> participantes recordaran un episodio que nunca vivieron, haberse perdido de niños en un centro
> comercial. Alrededor de una cuarta parte llegó a recordarlo, al menos en parte. Un recuerdo
> falso así no es una mentira ni una alucinación: quien lo tiene lo siente tan real como
> cualquier otro.
>
> ¿Qué ocurre? Lo que sabemos, lo que esperamos y lo que otros nos cuentan rellena los huecos de
> lo que percibimos, y el subconsciente no discierne bien entre lo que vimos y lo que inferimos
> después. Doña Teresa da por hecho que los taxistas manejan mal; Julián, que las camionetas van
> rápido. Cada uno, sin saberlo, completó la escena con su propio sesgo cognitivo.
>
> Nada de esto significa que los testigos no sirvan. Significa que conviene tratar cada
> testimonio como una inferencia razonable, no como una prueba definitiva, y entrevistar pronto,
> con preguntas abiertas. A los demás nos queda una lección de humildad: cuando digo que
> recuerdo algo «perfectamente», a lo mejor debería decir que lo recuerdo… aparentemente.

**Summary.** (1) A delivery van and a taxi collide at a corner in Mexico City; three witnesses
talk to a reporter. (2) Each is sincere and each is wrong about something: the light, the van's
speed, the dog's timing, as a street camera later shows. (3) Elizabeth Loftus's 1974 study
with John Palmer: a more violent verb in the question raised speed estimates and "memories" of
broken glass. (4) A 1995 experiment planted a childhood memory of being lost in a mall in about
a quarter of participants. (5) Expectations fill gaps; each witness's bias completed the scene.
(6) Treat testimony as inference and be humble about memory.

**Glosses:** *venía volando* = was going really fast; *se había pasado el alto* = had run the
red light; *se estrellaron / se golpearon* = smashed / hit; *los huecos* = the gaps; *da por hecho* = takes for granted.

## Pronunciation

- *percepción*: three syllables, *per-cep-CIÓN*; the *p* is a real, light *p* before the *c*
  (which, with seseo, sounds like *s*).
- *consciente, inconsciente, subconsciente*: in Latin America *sc* before *e* is a single *s*
  sound: *con-SIEN-te*, *in-con-SIEN-te*, *sub-con-SIEN-te*. *Conciencia* has three syllables:
  *con-CIEN-cia*.
- *discernir*: *di-ser-NIR*; the stress moves in *discierno*: *di-SIER-no*.
- *espejismo*: *es-pe-JIS-mo*; the *j* is breathed from the back of the throat.

## Common mistakes

- Using the subjunctive for every *decir*: *Dice que está cansada* reports a fact. Only a
  request takes *esté*.
- Translating "I'm sorry that…" with the indicative: *Siento que no puedes venir* means "I sense
  you can't come". Regret needs *puedas*.
- Using the subjunctive after *percatarse, constatar* or *darse cuenta* in the affirmative:
  they report facts (*Se percató de que llovía*).

## Key points

- Information takes the indicative; requests, regret, sympathy and permission take the
  subjunctive: *decir* (report / request), *sentir* (perceive / regret), *entender* (take in /
  sympathize), *recordar* (remember / remind to), *admitir* (accept a fact / allow).
- *Me temo que* + indicative softens bad news; *supongamos que* takes either mood.
- *Espero que* + subjunctive is the usual choice; *espero que llegará* is heard.
- After negated knowledge, the indicative presupposes the fact (*No sabía que estabas aquí*).
- Both moods are correct in questions with *creer*, after *el hecho de que* and in a *que*
  clause at the start of a sentence.

lessons.title: Quieras o no: concession at C1
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

B2 lesson 07 gave you *aunque* in four tenses, *por más que, por muy… que, a pesar de que, si
bien, aun cuando, y eso que* and *aun* + gerund. A **[[concessive clause]]** admits an obstacle and
says it doesn't change the outcome. This lesson adds the structures that make concession sound
native: the repeated verb of *hagas lo que hagas*, *quieras o no*, *ni aunque*, *con lo caro que
está*, and the Latin American *así* + subjunctive. It also sharpens the mood after *aunque*.

The theme is entrepreneurship and failure, with B1's *emprender, el emprendedor, invertir, la
inversión, el fracaso, arriesgarse* and *endeudarse*. For scale: according to INEGI (press
release of February 18, 2015, based on its economic censuses), a business opening in Mexico in
manufacturing, commerce or services had a life expectancy of 7.7 years, and about 64 in 100
survived their first year.

## The reduplicated concessive

The **[[reduplicated concessive]]** repeats a verb in the subjunctive around a relative word: *hagas
lo que hagas* (whatever you do). It means "no matter what / where / who…", and it covers every
possible case at once. B1's honors lessons met a few as fixed phrases (*pase lo que pase, cueste
lo que cueste, digan lo que digan*); at C1 you build them yourself.

| Pattern | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| verb + *lo que* + verb | *hagas lo que hagas* | whatever you do |
| verb + *donde* + verb | *vayas donde vayas* | wherever you go |
| verb + *como* + verb | *lo hagas como lo hagas* | however you do it |
| verb + *cuando* + verb | *llegue cuando llegue* | whenever it arrives |
| verb + *quien* + verb | *venga quien venga* | whoever comes |
| verb + *lo que* + verb | *cueste lo que cueste* | whatever it costs |

- *Hagas lo que hagas, revisa los números cada mes.* — Whatever you do, check the numbers every
  month.
- *Venga quien venga, la junta empieza a las nueve.* — Whoever comes, the meeting starts at
  nine.
- *Vayas donde vayas, vas a encontrar competencia.* — Wherever you go, you'll find competition.
- *Te van a criticar decidas lo que decidas.* — They'll criticize you whatever you decide.

Three rules:

1. The same verb, tense and person both times: *digan lo que digan*, never ~~digan lo que
   dicen~~. A pronoun goes with both verbs: *lo hagas como lo hagas*.
2. Present subjunctive for now and the future; imperfect subjunctive in the past (the
   **[[sequence of tenses]]**): *Hiciera lo que hiciera, el negocio no despegaba.* — Whatever he did, the business wouldn't take off.
   (The *-se* forms, *hiciese lo que hiciese*, are also correct.)
3. A comma separates it when it comes first; at the end it can follow the main clause
   directly, as in *decidas lo que decidas* above.

This is also how Spanish encourages someone: *Pase lo que pase, aquí estamos.* — Whatever
happens, we're here for you.

## *Quieras o no*, *llueva o no*

Two alternatives, both in the subjunctive, mean "whether… or not":

- *Quieras o no, los números no mienten.* — Like it or not, the numbers don't lie.
- *Llueva o no, el tianguis se pone.* — Rain or shine, the street market goes ahead.
- *Te guste o no, hay que pagar impuestos.* — Whether you like it or not, taxes have to be paid.

The person changes with the subject (*quiera o no, queramos o no*), and the past uses the
imperfect subjunctive: *Quisiera o no, tuvo que cerrar.*

## *Ni aunque*: not even if

*Ni aunque* rejects a condition as not enough, however extreme. The tense follows B2's *aunque*
rule: present subjunctive for a real possibility, imperfect for an unlikely or imaginary one.

- *No vuelvo a abrir un restaurante ni aunque me lo regalen.* — I'm not opening a restaurant
  again, not even if they give me one.
- *—¿Y si te ofrecieran un socio con capital? —Ni aunque me pagaran el doble.* — "And if they
  offered you a partner with capital?" "Not even if they paid me double."

## *Con lo* + adjective + *que*: given how…, for all…

*Con lo* + adjective or adverb + *que* + indicative points to a degree everyone can see. It is
often causal (given how…), and becomes concessive when the result is the opposite of what you'd
expect, often introduced by *y*:

- *Con lo caro que está todo, no sé cómo le hacen.* — With everything as expensive as it is, I
  don't know how they manage. (causal)
- *Con lo trabajadora que es, y el negocio no levanta.* — Hardworking as she is, the business
  isn't taking off. (concessive)

The adjective agrees with its noun (*con lo cara que está la renta*), and *con lo que* + verb
works the same way: *Con lo que invirtió, y todavía no ve ganancias.* — For all he invested,
he still isn't seeing a profit.

## *Por mucho / más / poco que*

From B2: *por más que* and *por mucho que* + subjunctive (however much), or + indicative for a
known fact (*Por más que insiste, no le dan el préstamo* — however much he insists, and he does).
*Por poco que* is the mirror image: *Por poco que ahorres, algo se junta.* — However little you
save, it adds up.

## *Así* + subjunctive: "even if" in Latin America

In much of Latin America, Mexico included, you'll hear *así* + subjunctive meaning "even if":

- *No acepto, así me ofrezcan el doble.* — I won't accept, even if they offer me double.
- *Voy a terminar la carrera, así me tarde diez años.* — I'm going to finish my degree, even if it
  takes me ten years.

It is common, especially in speech, but speakers from elsewhere may not expect it, so it is
for recognition here. In your own writing, *aunque* is the safe choice; if you use *así*, no
answer in this course marks it wrong.

## *Mal que bien* and *aun* + gerund

*Mal que bien* (somehow or other, despite everything) sums up a result reached with difficulty;
it takes no verb of its own: *Mal que bien, salimos adelante.* — One way or another, we pulled
through. B2's *aun* + gerund concedes in one phrase: *Aun ganando poco, no se rinde.* — Even
earning little, she doesn't give up.

## *A pesar de lo que* + either mood

*A pesar de lo que* takes the mood of the content: indicative for something actually said or
done, subjunctive for whatever may be said.

- *A pesar de lo que dicen los expertos, el café se llenó.* — Despite what the experts say, the
  café filled up. (They do say it.)
- *A pesar de lo que digan, voy a intentarlo.* — Whatever they may say, I'm going to try.

## *Aunque* with a fact you both know

B2 taught *aunque* + indicative for a fact you're telling the listener. At C1, notice the
subjunctive with a fact the listener *already knows*: you grant it and move on.

- *Aunque sea tu socio, no tiene razón.* — He may be your partner, but he isn't right.
- *Aunque es tu socio, no tiene razón.* — Although he's your partner, he isn't right.

Both are correct. The indicative asserts the fact as information; the subjunctive treats it as
known and beside the point, the usual choice when the listener obviously knows it.

![A chart titled "Concession at C1: structure and mood". Rows: hagas lo que hagas (reduplicated), subjuntivo, whatever you do. Quieras o no, subjuntivo, like it or not. Ni aunque, subjuntivo, not even if. Con lo caro que está, indicativo, given how / for all. Por más que, por poco que, subjuntivo, or indicativo for a known fact. Así me paguen, subjuntivo, even if, Latin America, recognize. A pesar de lo que, either mood. Aunque sea tu socio, a known fact, either mood. Mal que bien, no verb, somehow or other.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Podcast: *Fracasar para emprender*

![A line chart of a fictional café's monthly customers over 24 months. The line rises from about 300 at opening to a peak of about 2,400 in month 10, falls sharply from month 13 and drops to nearly zero by month 18, marked "quiebra"; the peak is marked "el mejor mes". The chart is titled Clientes al mes (datos ficticios). A second, dashed line labeled "segundo intento" starts in month 20 and climbs to about 900 in month 24.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```dialogue
# Fracasar para emprender (episodio 34)
Conductor: Bienvenidos a «Fracasar para emprender». Hoy platicamos con Mariana Robles, fundadora de una cafetería en Puebla que cerró a los dieciocho meses y de una empresa emergente de logística que hoy da empleo a veinte personas. Mariana, ¿qué pasó con la cafetería?
Mariana: Pues el primer año fue increíble. Teníamos fila en la puerta. Pero yo confundía clientes con ganancias. Con lo llena que estaba la cafetería, nunca revisé los costos, y cuando subieron la renta y el precio del café, ya era tarde.
Conductor: ¿No tenías plan de negocios?
Mariana: Tenía uno precioso, de cuarenta páginas, que no volví a abrir. Mi socio me decía que lo actualizáramos cada mes, y yo le contestaba que no había tiempo. Quieras o no, los números te alcanzan.
Conductor: ¿Cómo viviste la quiebra?
Mariana: Con vergüenza. En México todavía se ve el fracaso como algo personal. Dijera lo que dijera mi familia, yo sentía que había fallado. Me endeudé, vendí el carro y durante meses no quise ni oír la palabra «emprender». Pero, mal que bien, salí adelante.
Conductor: ¿Y qué te hizo volver?
Mariana: Una amiga me invitó a una incubadora de la universidad. Ahí entendí que un tropiezo no es el final si aprendes algo. Esta vez empecé al revés: primero el modelo de negocio, luego los clientes y, al final, el local.
Conductor: Muchos oyentes nos escriben que tienen miedo de arriesgarse. ¿Qué les dirías?
Mariana: Que el miedo no se va, hagan lo que hagan. Pero que una cosa es arriesgarse y otra es apostar a ciegas. Por poco que vendan, que lleven las cuentas desde el primer día.
Conductor: ¿Qué fue lo más difícil de aprender?
Mariana: Aceptar las pérdidas a tiempo. Yo quería salvar la cafetería a toda costa y le seguí metiendo dinero meses después de que dejó de ser rentable. La perseverancia es buena, pero no cuando te impide ver los números. Y en Puebla el mercado del café es muy competitivo.
Conductor: ¿Buscaste capital de riesgo para la segunda empresa?
Mariana: Sí, y al principio nadie me quería escuchar. Un inversionista me dijo que no metía dinero en alguien que ya había quebrado. Le contesté que precisamente por eso yo sabía lo que no había que hacer. Al final, contra viento y marea, conseguimos dos inversionistas.
Conductor: ¿Volverías a abrir una cafetería?
Mariana: ¡Ni aunque me la regalaran! No, es broma. A lo mejor algún día, pero esta vez rentable desde el primer mes.
Conductor: Mariana, gracias por tu tenacidad y por contarlo.
Mariana: Gracias a ti. Y a quien esté pensando en cerrar: cueste lo que cueste, aprende de los números antes de que te alcancen.
```

**Summary.** Mariana Robles, from Puebla, tells a podcast host how her café, packed in its first
year, closed after eighteen months: she confused customers with profit, never updated her
business plan, and was caught by rising rent and coffee prices. She felt the bankruptcy as a
personal shame, went into debt and sold her car. Her hardest lesson: accept losses in time
instead of saving a business at all costs. A university incubator brought her back; her
second business, a logistics startup, started from the business model. Her advice: fear never
goes away, but keep accounts from day one. Investors doubted her, yet she found two. Would she
open a café again? Maybe, if it's profitable from month one.

**Glosses:** *platicamos* = we're chatting (Mexico); *teníamos fila* = we had a line; *los
números te alcanzan* = the numbers catch up with you; *apostar a ciegas* = to bet blindly;
*meter dinero en* = to put money into.

The chart above the interview (fictional numbers) shows the shape of her story: a fast rise, a
fall to *la quiebra* and a slower second climb.

## Pronunciation

- *emprendimiento*: five syllables, *em-pren-di-MIEN-to*; *ie* is one syllable.
- *inversionista*: five syllables, *in-ver-sio-NIS-ta*; *io* is one syllable.
- *rentabilidad*: five syllables, *ren-ta-bi-li-DAD*, stressed on the last; the final *d* is
  very soft.
- *quiebra*: two syllables, *QUIE-bra*; the *u* is silent, so it starts with a *k* sound.
- *tenaz, tenaces*: *te-NAZ, te-NA-ces*; with seseo both *z* and *c* sound like *s*.

## Common mistakes

- Changing the verb or the tense in the repeated pattern: ~~hagas lo que haces~~, ~~dijera lo
  que dice~~. Same verb, same tense, same person.
- Using the indicative after *ni aunque*: it takes the subjunctive.
- Forgetting agreement in *con lo… que*: *con lo cara que está la renta*, not ~~lo caro~~ when
  the adjective describes *la renta*.
- Adding a verb to *mal que bien*: it's a fixed phrase on its own.
- Expecting *así* + subjunctive everywhere: it means "even if" in much of Latin America; elsewhere,
  Spain included, it is much less common.

## Key points

- Reduplicated concessive: subjunctive + *lo que / donde / como / cuando / quien* + the same
  verb: *hagas lo que hagas*; past *hiciera lo que hiciera*.
- *Quieras o no, llueva o no*: two alternatives in the subjunctive.
- *Ni aunque* + subjunctive (present or imperfect): not even if.
- *Con lo* + adjective + *que* + indicative: causal or, against expectations, concessive.
- *Así* + subjunctive (Latin America) = even if: recognize it; write *aunque*.
- *A pesar de lo que* and *aunque* + a known fact take either mood.

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: ¡Quién pudiera!: the subjunctive on its own
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Most subjunctives hang on a main verb: *quiero que, es posible que, aunque*. The
**[[independent subjunctive]]** stands in a main clause of its own, with no verb above it: *¡Ojalá llueva!, ¡Que te
vaya bien!, ¡Quién pudiera!* B1 lesson 04h1 taught *que* + subjunctive wishes and a few fixed
phrases, and B2 used *ojalá* for regrets. This lesson puts all of it together: the four tenses
of *ojalá*, exclamations with *quién* and *ni que*, commands passed on with *que*, blessings and
curses, and the adverbs of doubt that can take either mood.

The theme is popular beliefs in Mexico: charms, the evil eye, *limpias*, *mandas* and
pilgrimages. They are described here as practices many people keep, without any claim about
whether they work.

## *Ojalá* in four tenses

A wish expressed by the verb itself is called **[[optative]]**: *ojalá* (or *ojalá que*, very common
in Mexico) is the optative word par excellence, and in standard Spanish it always takes the
subjunctive. Its tense says how possible the wish is and when it is set.

| *ojalá* + | The wish is about… | Example |
|---|---|---|
| present | something possible, now or later | *Ojalá no llueva mañana.* — I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow. |
| perfect | a past you don't know about yet | *Ojalá haya llegado bien.* — I hope she got there safely. |
| imperfect | something unlikely or impossible now | *Ojalá tuviera más tiempo.* — I wish I had more time. |
| pluperfect | a past that can't be changed | *Ojalá me hubieras avisado.* — I wish you'd told me. |

The middle two need care. The perfect looks back at something already decided but unknown to
you (the exam, the trip). The imperfect is for what you think won't happen, or can't: *Ojalá el
abuelo estuviera aquí* (I wish Grandpa were here; he died). For the future, present and
imperfect can both be right, and the choice shows your hopes: *Ojalá gane* (she may well win)
vs *Ojalá ganara* (I wish she'd win, but I doubt it).

![A chart titled "Ojalá: likelihood and time" with two columns, Pasado and Presente o futuro, and two rows, Posible and Poco probable o imposible. Possible in the past: ojalá + perfect, Ojalá haya llegado bien. Possible now or later: ojalá + present, Ojalá no llueva. Unlikely or impossible now or later: ojalá + imperfect, Ojalá tuviera más tiempo. Impossible in the past: ojalá + pluperfect, Ojalá me hubieras avisado. A note under the chart: the -se forms (tuviese, hubiese) are also correct.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## *¡Quién* + imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive!

*¡Quién* + subjunctive! is a wish about yourself, phrased as "who could…!". The imperfect is
for now, the pluperfect for the past:

- *¡Quién pudiera viajar así!* — If only I could travel like that!
- *¡Quién tuviera tu suerte!* — I wish I had your luck!
- *¡Quién lo hubiera dicho!* — Who would have thought it!

*Quién* carries an accent mark, as in a question.

## *¡Ni que* + imperfect subjunctive!

*¡Ni que…!* rejects an exaggeration: "as if…!". It takes the imperfect subjunctive (or the
pluperfect for the past):

- *¡Ni que fuera millonario!* — As if I were a millionaire!
- *¡Ni que hubieras visto un fantasma!* — Anyone would think you'd seen a ghost!

## *Que* + subjunctive: commands passed on and wishes

Alone, *que* + subjunctive passes on a command to someone not addressed, or makes a wish:

- *¡Que pase el siguiente!* — Next, please! (literally, may the next one come in)
- *—Dice Paco que lo esperes. —¡Que me llame él!* — "Paco says to wait for him." "He can call
  me!"
- *¡Que te vaya bien! ¡Que descanses!* — Take care! Rest well!

Mexico also says *¡Que te vaya bonito!* (B1 04h1). Religious blessings follow the same pattern:
*Que Dios te bendiga* (God bless you), with *bendecir*, and B1's *Dios quiera que…* (God willing).

### Curses with *así* (recognize only)

In curses, *así* + subjunctive is a traditional formula: *¡Así se le caiga la casa encima!* (May
the house fall down on him!). You'll meet it in songs, films and novels, said in anger; it is
not something to say to a person. *Maldecir* is to curse; *una maldición* is a curse.

### *Vaya usted a saber*

A fixed independent subjunctive: *¿Por qué lo hizo? Vaya usted a saber.* — Why did he do it?
Goodness knows. (Informal: *vete tú a saber*.)

## *Quizás, tal vez, acaso*: either mood

These adverbs of doubt take either mood when they come *before* the verb; the subjunctive
sounds a little more doubtful:

- *Quizás viene mañana. / Quizás venga mañana.* — Maybe she'll come tomorrow.
- *Tal vez tiene razón. / Tal vez tenga razón.* — Maybe he's right.

*Quizá* and *quizás* are both correct. After the verb, use the indicative: *Vendrá quizás
mañana.* *Acaso* is literary in this use; in speech it mostly appears in rhetorical questions:
*¿Acaso no te lo dije?* (Didn't I tell you?). *Posiblemente* and *probablemente* also take either
mood, while *a lo mejor* (B2 lesson 08) takes the indicative: *A lo mejor viene.*

## *Siquiera*: if only, at least

- *Si siquiera me hubiera llamado…* — If only he had called me… (with *si*, a regret)
- *Dame siquiera una pista.* — At least give me a clue.

*Ni siquiera* means "not even": *Ni siquiera me saludó.*

## Wishing, regretting and doubting in conversation

```dialogue
# Antes de la entrevista
Sofía: ¿Ya leíste tu horóscopo? Dice que hoy es tu día.
= Have you read your horoscope? It says today's your day.
Daniel: ¡Ni que yo fuera supersticioso! Aunque traigo mi amuleto, por si acaso.
= As if I were superstitious! Although I've got my lucky charm on me, just in case.
Sofía: ¡Quién tuviera tu calma! Yo, en tu lugar, estaría temblando.
= I wish I had your calm! In your place, I'd be shaking.
Daniel: Ojalá me hubiera preparado más. Tal vez me pregunten por mi último trabajo.
= I wish I'd prepared more. Maybe they'll ask me about my last job.
Sofía: Pues prende una veladora. Mi mamá es muy devota de San Judas, el santo de las causas difíciles.
= Well, light a votive candle. My mom is very devoted to Saint Jude, the saint of difficult causes.
Daniel: ¡Ni que necesitara un milagro! Bueno… quizás sí.
= As if I needed a miracle! Well… maybe I do.
Sofía: Que te vaya muy bien. Y avísame, ¿eh?
= Good luck. And let me know, OK?
```

## In the market

![A market stall with a striped awning. On the counter, left to right, each with a label: a red bracelet with a round charm, el amuleto; four tall glass candles, las veladoras; two small painted tin pictures leaning against a crate, los exvotos; a figure of a saint in a brown robe with a halo, el santo; a newspaper page with stars, el horóscopo. Bundles of green herbs hang from the awning, labeled las hierbas.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At many Mexican markets you'll find a stall like this one: *amuletos* (a red bracelet against *el
mal de ojo* for babies is a common one), *veladoras* in tall glasses, painted *exvotos* (also
called *retablos*) that thank a saint for a favor, and herbs for a *limpia*, a ritual cleansing
done by a *curandero* or *curandera*. A *manda* is a promise to a saint or the Virgin, often paid
with a *peregrinación*: the best known is the pilgrimage to the Basílica de Guadalupe in Mexico
City around December 12, her feast day. For December 2024, Mexico City's government reported
more than 11 million visitors in the days around the 12th (figures as reported in the press).

## Reading: *La veladora de la abuela*

> La mañana de la boda, la abuela Cuca se levantó antes que nadie, le prendió una veladora a
> San Antonio y le dio las gracias en voz baja. Hacía años que le pedía un buen marido para su
> nieta, y aunque Valeria se reía de esas cosas, la abuela estaba segura de que el santo había
> hecho su parte.
>
> —Ojalá no llueva —dijo Valeria al ver el cielo gris.
>
> —Ojalá llueva —la corrigió la abuela—. Novia mojada, novia afortunada.
>
> Valeria no discutió. Con su abuela, discutir de augurios era perder el tiempo. Cuca no barría
> de noche, no abría el paraguas dentro de la casa y nunca ponía la bolsa en el suelo, «porque se
> va el dinero». Cuando nació Valeria, le puso una pulsera roja contra el mal de ojo, y todavía
> la guardaba en un cajón como si fuera un tesoro.
>
> —Abuela, ¿de veras crees en todo eso?
>
> —Yo no creo ni dejo de creer, mija. Pero por si acaso.
>
> A las once llegó la tía Lupe con una noticia de mal agüero: al novio se le había roto un espejo
> en el hotel.
>
> —¡Ni que fuera el fin del mundo! —dijo Valeria, aunque sintió un escalofrío.
>
> —Que no se entere tu abuela —susurró la tía.
>
> Demasiado tarde. Cuca ya buscaba su rosario.
>
> —Quizás no pase nada —dijo, más para sí misma que para las demás—. Ojalá ya se le haya pasado
> el susto a ese muchacho. Pero que alguien le lleve una ramita de pirul, por si las dudas.
>
> La ceremonia fue a las cinco. A las cinco y diez empezó a llover. La abuela, en la primera
> fila, sonrió como quien gana una apuesta. Más tarde, mientras los novios bailaban, Valeria se
> sentó a su lado.
>
> —Ojalá el abuelo estuviera aquí.
>
> —Ojalá te hubiera visto así de bonita. ¡Quién pudiera volver a tener veinte años! Tu abuelo y
> yo nos casamos sin un peso y sin fiesta, y fuimos felices cuarenta años. Toco madera por
> ustedes.
>
> Y tocó la mesa, que era de plástico. Las dos se rieron.
>
> Al final de la noche, la abuela le confesó que había hecho una manda: si la boda salía bien,
> iría caminando a la Basílica el próximo 12 de diciembre.
>
> —Abuela, tienes ochenta y dos años.
>
> —Por eso. Dios quiera que me dé fuerzas. Y tú, que te vaya bonito, mija. Que te vaya muy
> bonito.

**Summary.** On Valeria's wedding morning, her grandmother Cuca lights a votive candle to Saint
Anthony, who she believes found Valeria a husband. Valeria hopes it won't rain; her grandmother
hopes it will, since a wet bride is a lucky bride. Cuca keeps many small superstitions and still
has the red bracelet she put on baby Valeria against the evil eye. An aunt brings bad news: the
groom broke a mirror. Valeria shrugs it off; the grandmother prays and sends a sprig of pepper
tree for a cleansing. It rains during the ceremony. At the party they miss the late grandfather,
and Cuca reveals a vow: she'll walk to the Basílica on December 12.

**Glosses:** *novia mojada, novia afortunada* = a wet bride is a lucky bride (a traditional
saying); *mija* = my dear (from *mi hija*); *un escalofrío* = a shiver; *el pirul* = the pepper
tree, used in *limpias*; *por si las dudas* = just in case (Mexico); *sin un peso* = penniless.

## Pronunciation

- *ojalá*: three syllables, *o-ja-LÁ*, stressed on the last; the *j* is breathed from the
  throat.
- *agüero*: *a-GÜE-ro*; the two dots mean the *u* is pronounced, like *w*: *a-GWE-ro*.
- *peregrinación*: five syllables, *pe-re-gri-na-CIÓN*.
- *exvoto*: *ex-VO-to*, with *x* as *ks*.
- *¡Quién pudiera!*: *quién* is one syllable; the *u* is silent.

## Common mistakes

- *Ojalá* + indicative: ~~ojalá viene~~. Standard Spanish requires the subjunctive: *ojalá
  venga*.
- Using the present for a past wish: *Ojalá llegue bien* is about the future; for a trip that's
  already over, *Ojalá haya llegado bien*.
- *¡Ni que* + indicative: ~~ni que era~~. It's *¡Ni que fuera!*
- The subjunctive after a postposed *quizás*: ~~Venga quizás~~. After the verb, *Vendrá quizás*.
- *Quien* without the accent in *¡Quién pudiera!*

## Key points

- *Ojalá (que)* + present: possible; + perfect: unknown past; + imperfect: unlikely or
  impossible now; + pluperfect: past regret.
- *¡Quién pudiera / tuviera…!* wishes for yourself; *¡Quién lo hubiera dicho!*
- *¡Ni que* + imperfect subjunctive! = as if!
- *¡Que* + subjunctive! passes on commands and makes wishes: *¡Que pase el siguiente!*
- *Así* + subjunctive in curses: recognize only.
- *Quizás, tal vez*: either mood before the verb, indicative after it; *a lo mejor* +
  indicative.

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Cuanto más entreno…: comparison and proportion at C1
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A2 lesson 11 taught *más… que, más de* + a number and *tan… como*; B2 added the superlative with
a subjunctive relative (*el mejor atleta que haya tenido el país*). At C1 comparison becomes a
tool for argument and analysis: proportion (*cuanto más entrenas, más rápido corres*),
comparisons with a whole clause (*corre más de lo que crees*), the difference between *no… más
que* and *no… más de*, and the intensifiers a sports journalist uses (*de lo más, a cual más,
sumamente*). This module is about mood, and mood appears here too: a future proportion takes the
subjunctive.

The theme is elite sport: records, rivalries, sponsorship and doping. Mexico's best Olympic
medal count is still the nine it won as host in 1968; at Paris 2024 its team won five, three
silver and two bronze (final medal table as reported by the Mexican press).

## *Cuanto más…, más…*: proportion

A **[[correlative comparison]]** links two comparatives so that one grows or shrinks with the other:
"the more…, the more…". Spanish uses *cuanto* in the first half and a comparative in the second:

- *Cuanto más entreno, más rápido corro.* — The more I train, the faster I run.
- *Cuanto menos duermes, peor rindes.* — The less you sleep, the worse you perform.
- *Cuanto antes empieces, mejor.* — The sooner you start, the better.

Three details:

1. *Cuanto* agrees with a noun that follows *más / menos*: *Cuantas más horas entrena, más se
   cansa* (the more hours she trains…); *Cuantos más patrocinadores tiene, más presión siente* (the
   more sponsors she has, the more pressure she feels). Before a verb, an adjective or an adverb it doesn't change: *cuanto más rápido.*
2. *Tanto* may open the second half in formal writing: *Cuanto más alto es el nivel, tanto
   mayor es la exigencia* (the higher the level, the greater the demands). It is optional.
3. Mood: a habit or a general truth takes the indicative (*cuanto más entreno*); a future
   proportion takes the subjunctive, like *cuando* + future: *Cuanto más practiques, mejor te va
   a ir.* — The more you practice, the better it'll go for you.

Mexico's variants. In Mexico you'll hear *mientras más… más* (*Mientras más practicas, más
fácil es*: the more you practice, the easier it is) and, very often, *entre más… más* (*Entre
más corro, más hambre me da*: the more I run, the hungrier I get). The RAE's
*Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* (online second edition, provisional version, *más*, §1.8a)
calls *mientras más* an acceptable colloquial variant, and says *entre más* is normal in Mexico
and Central America among speakers of all levels, while educated usage elsewhere rejects it. So:
*cuanto más* is the form for every audience, *mientras más* is fine in conversation, and *entre
más* is everyday Mexican Spanish to understand (and accepted in this course's answers).

![A diagram titled "Cuanto más…, más…" with two pairs of bar staircases joined by double arrows. Top pair, both rising: entreno, entreno más, mucho más; and corro rápido, más rápido, mucho más; caption: Cuanto más entreno, más rápido corro. Bottom pair, both falling: duermo poco, menos, mucho menos; and rindo bien, peor, mucho peor; caption: Cuanto menos duermo, peor rindo. A footnote: México: mientras más… más; entre más… más.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Comparing with a whole clause

A **[[comparative]]** (*más… que, menos… que, tan… como*) compares two things. When what you compare with is a quantity or degree expressed by a clause, Spanish uses *de* +
article + *que*:

- With a verb or an adjective, neuter *de lo que*: *Corre más de lo que crees.* — She runs faster
  than you think. *Fue más difícil de lo que esperaba.* — It was harder than I expected.
- With a noun, the article agrees with it: *del que, de la que, de los que, de las que*: *Ganó más
  medallas de las que esperaba.* — She won more medals than she expected. *Tenemos menos
  tiempo del que parece.* — We have less time than it seems. Neuter *de lo que* is also used
  with a noun, above all after verbs like *creer* or *esperar* (*más medallas de lo que
  esperaba*); the agreeing form is the more common choice in writing.

*Que lo que* is a different structure: it compares two things, not two amounts: *Me gusta más
esta pista que lo que vimos ayer* (I like this track better than what we saw yesterday).

## *No… más que* vs *no… más de*

These look alike and mean different things (DPD, *más*, §1.20):

- *No tiene más que dos medallas.* — She has only two medals. (*no… más que* = only)
- *No tiene más de dos medallas.* — She has no more than two medals. (two at most; perhaps
  fewer)

The same goes for *menos*: *No pesa menos de cincuenta kilos* (at least fifty). In everyday
Mexican Spanish, "only" is also *nada más* or *nomás*: *Nada más le faltan dos segundos* (she's
only two seconds off).

## Intensifiers: *de lo más, a cual más, sumamente*

- *de lo más* + adjective = extremely: *Fue una final de lo más emocionante* (it was an
  extremely exciting final). The adjective usually agrees: *dos rivales de lo más simpáticas*
  (two really nice rivals).
- *a cual más* + adjective = each one more… than the next, all very…: *Tres corredoras a cual
  más rápida* (three runners, each faster than the next). The adjective is singular and agrees
  in gender.
- *sumamente, extremadamente* + adjective: formal, common in the press: *una prueba sumamente
  exigente* (an extremely demanding event).
- *la mar de* (colloquial Spain, to recognize): *Está la mar de contenta.* — She's really happy.

## Superlatives

- Relative **[[superlative]]** + relative clause: B2's *Es la mejor atleta que haya tenido México*
  (the subjunctive, very common, frames it as the best of all possible cases). The indicative is
  also correct when you state a fact: *la mejor marca que ha logrado este año* (the best mark
  she has achieved this year). Lesson 08h1 looks at this choice more closely.
- Absolute superlative: *-ísimo* (*rapidísimo, larguísimo, riquísimo, felicísimo*: note *g →
  gu, c → qu, z → c*) or *sumamente* + adjective. A few learned forms belong to literary and
  formal writing: *paupérrimo* (very poor), *celebérrimo* (very famous), *antiquísimo* (very old,
  also everyday). You need to recognize the first two; *pobrísimo* is the everyday form.
- *Igual de… que* (as… as) is very common in speech; *tan… como* is the usual choice in formal
  writing: *Es igual de rápida que su hermana / Es tan rápida como su hermana* (she's as fast as
  her sister).

![A three-step podium in a stadium, each part labeled. Three athletes with medals stand on the blocks numbered 1, 2 and 3; the winner, in the middle, holds a bouquet, and the athlete in second place is labeled la medallista. The medal on the third-place athlete is labeled la medalla, and the blocks el podio. Behind them, a scoreboard showing the time 4:05.71 and a star is labeled el récord; a banner with a blank logo is labeled el patrocinador; a flag on a pole at the right is labeled la bandera.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: *Dos caminos al podio*

| Temporada | Ximena Rocha (1500 m) | Daniela Ibarra (1500 m) |
|---|---|---|
| 2021 | 4:21.30 · campeona nacional juvenil | 4:15.80 · 6.ª en el Mundial juvenil |
| 2022 | 4:12.45 · bronce panamericano | 4:09.10 · lesión, sin podio |
| 2023 | 4:08.02 · plata centroamericana | 4:10.60 · eliminada en semifinal |
| 2024 | 4:05.71 · récord nacional | 4:11.95 · se retira de la pista |
| 2025 | 4:06.10 · finalista mundial | maratón: 2:29:40 en su debut |

> **Dos caminos al podio**
>
> A los dieciséis años, Daniela Ibarra era la gran promesa del atletismo mexicano. Corría el
> 1500 en menos tiempo del que necesitaban muchas adultas, y su entrenador repetía que cuanto
> antes la llevaran al circuito internacional, mejor. Ximena Rocha, de la misma edad, entrenaba
> en Toluca con un club modesto y no tenía más que un patrocinador local: una panadería. Hoy,
> cinco temporadas después, la historia es otra.
>
> La tabla lo dice todo. Daniela empezó más rápido de lo que nadie esperaba, pero cuantas más
> carreras sumaba, más lesiones acumulaba. En 2022 una fractura por estrés la dejó fuera de la
> temporada; en 2023 volvió, quedó eliminada en la semifinal del nacional y, en 2024, anunció que
> se retiraba de la pista. Ximena, en cambio, nunca fue la favorita, pero bajó su marca cada
> temporada hasta 2024, cuando batió el récord nacional, y en 2025 se clasificó a la final del
> Mundial.
>
> ¿Qué explica dos caminos tan distintos? Los especialistas en alto rendimiento coinciden en una
> idea: cuanto antes se le exige a una atleta, más riesgo hay de que se queme. Daniela compitió
> en la élite antes de terminar de crecer; Ximena tuvo una cantera paciente que la dejó correr
> poco y entrenar mucho. «No es la más talentosa que haya visto», admite su entrenadora, «pero sí
> la más tenaz. Y la deportividad que tiene con sus rivales es de lo más rara en este deporte».
>
> El dinero también cuenta. Cuando Daniela se lesionó, perdió el patrocinio de una marca
> deportiva en cuestión de semanas; a Ximena, en cambio, cada medalla le trajo un patrocinador
> nuevo. «Cuantos más resultados tienes, más fácil es que te apoyen, y cuantos menos tienes, más
> sola te quedas», resume Ximena, que lleva dos temporadas invicta en el circuito nacional.
>
> La rivalidad entre las dos, que llenó estadios cuando eran juveniles, se ha convertido en
> amistad. Daniela, que ahora prepara maratones, corrió en 2025 su primer maratón en menos de
> dos horas y media y no descarta volver a un podio. «Me retiré de la pista, no del atletismo»,
> dice. «Y ninguna de las dos ha tenido nunca un problema de dopaje, cosa que hoy no es poca».
>
> Lo que muestra su historia es que el palmarés de los dieciséis años predice menos de lo que
> creemos. La proeza de Ximena no fue un día perfecto, sino cinco años sin rendirse. Y la de
> Daniela, quizás, fue saber parar a tiempo.

**Summary.** (1) At sixteen, Daniela Ibarra was Mexico's great middle-distance prospect, rushed
into international racing; Ximena Rocha trained at a modest club with a bakery as her only
sponsor. (2) Daniela's injuries grew with her races and she left the track in 2024; Ximena, never
the favorite, improved every season up to her national record in 2024 and reached a world
final in 2025. (3) Experts say pushing young athletes raises the risk of burnout; Ximena's coach praises
her tenacity and sportsmanship. Sponsors left Daniela when she was injured and followed Ximena's
medals. (4) The rivals are now friends; Daniela runs marathons and both
have clean records. (5) Early results predict less than we think.

**Glosses:** *la promesa* = the prospect; *una fractura por estrés* = a stress fracture; *que se
queme* = that she burns out; *no descarta* = doesn't rule out; *cosa que hoy no es poca* = which
is no small thing nowadays. The runners and their times are fictional.

## Pronunciation

- *atleta*: *a-TLE-ta*. In Mexico *tl* stays together at the start of a syllable, as in
  *Tlaxcala*; in Spain many speakers split it, *at-LE-ta*.
- *récord, récords*: *RÉ-cord*, stressed on the first syllable, with a soft final *d*.
- *palmarés*: *pal-ma-RÉS*, stressed on the last syllable.
- *eliminatoria*: six syllables, *e-li-mi-na-TO-ria*; *ia* is one syllable.
- *cuanto*: two syllables, *CUAN-to*; it has no accent mark in these comparisons (it isn't a
  question).

## Common mistakes

- ~~Cuanto más horas~~: before a noun, *cuanto* agrees: *cuantas más horas, cuantos más
  días*.
- ~~El más entrenas, el más corres~~ (a calque of English "the more"): use *cuanto más…, más*.
- ~~Corre más que lo que crees~~ when comparing amounts: *más de lo que crees*.
- Mixing up *no… más que* (only) and *no… más de* (at most).
- ~~Más mejor~~: *mejor, peor, mayor* and *menor* are already comparatives.

## Key points

- *Cuanto más / menos…, (tanto) más / menos / mejor…*; *cuanto* agrees with a noun; future
  proportion → subjunctive (*Cuanto antes lo hagas, mejor*).
- Mexico: *mientras más* (colloquial, accepted) and *entre más* (everyday Mexican, recognized).
- *más / menos de lo que* + verb; *del que, de la que, de los que, de las que* with a noun.
- *No… más que* = only; *no… más de* = no more than.
- *de lo más* + adjective; *a cual más* + adjective; *sumamente*; Spain's *la mar de*.
- Superlative + *que haya…* (subjunctive, common) or + indicative for a stated fact; *-ísimo*;
  *tan… como* in formal writing.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Zonas grises: when both moods are right
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 05 to 08 kept meeting the same situation: a context where the indicative and the
subjunctive are both correct. Exercises in textbooks rarely admit it, but real Spanish is full of
these gray zones, and at C1 you're expected to read them as nuance, not as error. This honors
lesson explains *why* they exist, using two ideas from linguistics, **[[presupposition]]** and the
**[[factive verb]]**, and gives you a method for any "both possible" question. It doesn't repeat
lesson 05's verbs with two meanings; it looks at cases where the meaning stays almost the same
and only the speaker's stance shifts.

The examples follow the description of mood in the RAE and ASALE's *Nueva gramática de la lengua
española* (2009); the notes for this lesson list what was checked.

## Presupposition: what a sentence takes for granted

A **[[presupposition]]** is information a sentence treats as already known, so that it survives
even if you negate the sentence or turn it into a question. Compare:

- *Lamento que hayas perdido el vuelo.* — I'm sorry you missed your flight.
- *No lamento que hayas perdido el vuelo.* — I'm not sorry you missed your flight.
- *¿Lamentas que haya perdido el vuelo?* — Are you sorry I missed my flight?

In all three, the flight was missed. That fact is presupposed: *lamentar* *presupone* it. The
sentence doesn't assert it; it builds on it.

A **[[factive verb]]** is a verb that presupposes the truth of its clause in this way. There are two
groups, and they behave differently with mood:

| Group | Verbs | Mood | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| factive of knowing | *saber, darse cuenta de, descubrir, olvidar, recordar, constatar* | indicative | *Descubrió que la llave estaba en su bolsa.* |
| factive of feeling or judging | *lamentar, alegrarse de, molestar, sorprender, es una pena, es lógico* | subjunctive | *Le sorprendió que la llave estuviera en su bolsa.* |

That table settles a myth: the subjunctive does not mean "not real". After *me sorprende que*,
the fact is as real as after *descubrió que*. What changes is what the sentence is about: the
knowing verbs present the fact as information gained; the feeling verbs take it as background
and comment on it. Most gray zones live exactly here, where a fact is both true and in the
background.

## Gray zone 1: a known fact as a topic

### *El hecho de que*

*El hecho de que* names a fact, so it presupposes it. The subjunctive treats the fact as the
topic of a comment, which is the usual choice; the indicative re-asserts it as information:

- *El hecho de que el estudio sea pequeño no lo invalida.* — The fact that the study is small
  doesn't invalidate it.
- *El hecho de que el estudio es pequeño lo reconocen los propios autores.* — The fact that the
  study is small is acknowledged by the authors themselves.

### *Aunque* with a fact the listener knows

Lesson 06 showed *Aunque sea tu socio, no tiene razón*. The fact (he is your partner) is
presupposed; the subjunctive grants it and moves on, while *aunque es* informs. Both are
standard.

## Gray zone 2: certainty and its negation

Expressions of certainty assert, so they take the indicative: *Es indudable que el clima ha
cambiado. Es innegable que hubo errores. Tengo la certeza de que vendrá.* Negating them removes
the assertion, so the subjunctive becomes the usual choice: *No es seguro que venga; No tengo la
certeza de que venga.*

The interesting case is *no dudar*. *Dudar que* (to doubt) takes the subjunctive, but *no
dudo que* expresses near-certainty, so both moods are correct:

- *No dudo que tienes razón.* — I'm sure you're right. (indicative: I assert it)
- *No dudo que tengas razón.* — I don't doubt you may be right. (subjunctive: I grant it, often
  before a "but")

*No dudo de que*, with *de*, is equally correct.

### *Lo más probable* and *lo más seguro*

B2 taught *Lo más probable es que llegue mañana*, with the subjunctive, and that remains the
standard choice: probability is not assertion. With *lo más seguro es que*, which leans toward
certainty, the subjunctive is the careful choice (*ya se haya ido*), but the indicative is common
in speech: *Lo más seguro es que ya se fue* (He's most likely already gone). You may also hear *lo más probable es que* + indicative in casual speech;
recognize it, and write the subjunctive.

## Gray zone 3: relatives after superlatives and *el único*

A relative clause after a superlative, *el único* or *el primero* can take either mood:

- *Es la mejor novela que he leído.* — It's the best novel I've read. (my experience, stated)
- *Es la mejor novela que haya leído.* — It's the best novel I've ever read. (of all possible
  cases)
- *Eres el único que me entiende / me entienda.* — You're the only one who understands me.

The indicative reports a fact; the subjunctive widens the claim to every possible case, which
makes it more emphatic and a little more formal. Both are correct, and B2's *el mejor atleta que
haya tenido el país* is the subjunctive version.

Don't confuse this with a real difference of reference: *el primero que llegue* (whoever arrives
first, in the future: subjunctive) vs *el primero que llegó* (the person who did arrive first:
indicative).

## Gray zone 4: *después de que* in the news

After *después de que* referring to the past, the indicative is the expected form: *Después de
que el ministro presentó su renuncia, el peso se recuperó.* In newspapers, though, you'll often read
the *-ra* subjunctive instead: *después de que el ministro presentara su renuncia*. The
*Nueva gramática* describes this journalistic use; the meaning is the same, and the *-ra* form
has a slightly formal, written flavor. (A future event after *después de que* takes the
subjunctive anyway: *Después de que presente su renuncia, habrá elecciones.*)

The press also uses the *-ra* form with the value of a pluperfect in relative clauses: *el
informe que publicara en 2019* = *que había publicado*. It's a stylistic choice of formal
writing, to recognize; in your own texts, *que publicó* or *que había publicado* is the safe
option.

## Gray zone 5: doubt adverbs

From lesson 07: *quizás, tal vez* and *posiblemente* take either mood before the verb (*Quizás
viene / venga*). The subjunctive adds doubt. After the verb, only the indicative.

## A decision chart

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the mood when both may be possible
  accDescr: A chain of four questions about the clause. First, does it express a wish, request or aim? If yes, use the subjunctive. If not, is it new information the speaker asserts? If yes, use the indicative. If not, is it a known fact in the background, or a relative clause after a superlative or el único? If yes, both moods are possible: the subjunctive backgrounds the fact or widens the claim, the indicative re-asserts it or states a fact. If not, is it denied or doubted? If yes, use the subjunctive, though the indicative is also correct when the speaker still vouches for the fact, as after no dudo que or no sabía que. If not, it is a plain statement: use the indicative.
  Q1{"Wish, request or aim?"} -- yes --> S1["subjunctive"]
  Q1 -- no --> Q2{"New information the speaker asserts?"}
  Q2 -- yes --> I1["indicative"]
  Q2 -- no --> Q3{"Known fact in the background, or a relative after a superlative or el único?"}
  Q3 -- yes --> B1["both: subjunctive backgrounds or widens; indicative re-asserts or states a fact"]
  Q3 -- no --> Q4{"Denied or doubted?"}
  Q4 -- yes --> S2["subjunctive; indicative too if the speaker still vouches for it"]
  Q4 -- no --> I2["indicative"]
```

## Worked examples

### Example 1: *el hecho de que* in a test

**Task.** Complete: *El hecho de que el dictamen ___ (ser) favorable no garantiza la
aprobación.*

**Step 1: what does the clause do?** It names a fact (the report is favorable) as the topic of a
comment (it doesn't guarantee approval). That is a known fact in the background.

**Step 2: are both moods possible?** Yes: *sea* (subjunctive) and *es* (indicative) are both
standard after *el hecho de que*.

**Step 3: which fits better here?** The comment is about the fact, not news about it, so *sea* is
the more natural choice. *Es* would stress that the report really is favorable, as if answering
someone who doubts it.

**Answer.** *sea* (best fit); *es* is also correct. In this course, a typed answer accepts both.

### Example 2: *después de que* in a news report

**Task.** A headline reads: *La bolsa sube después de que el banco central ___ (bajar) las
tasas.* Which forms are correct, and what does each say?

**Step 1: time.** The central bank's decision is in the past, before the rise.

**Step 2: the forms.** *bajó* (preterite indicative) is the expected form after *después de que*
for a past event. *bajara* (or *bajase*), the *-ra* subjunctive, is frequent in newspapers and
described by the *Nueva gramática* as a journalistic use. *baje* (present subjunctive) would
mean a future decision: the market rises after the bank lowers rates, as a general rule or a
forecast.

**Step 3: register.** For a headline, either *bajó* or *bajara* works; for your own writing,
*bajó* is the safe choice.

**Answer.** *bajó* or *bajara* (same meaning); *baje* changes the time.

### Example 3: *no dudo que* in a conversation

**Task.** *—El proyecto va a funcionar. —No dudo que ___ (funcionar), pero cuesta mucho.*

**Step 1: what does the speaker do?** They grant the other person's claim before objecting.

**Step 2: the forms.** *funcione* (subjunctive) grants it; *va a funcionar* or *funcionará*
(indicative) asserts it. Both are correct after *no dudo que*.

**Step 3: nuance.** Before a *pero*, the subjunctive is the more natural concession; the
indicative would sound more convinced, as if the doubt were only about the cost.

**Answer.** *funcione* (best fit), *va a funcionar / funcionará* also correct.

## Words for certainty and doubt

- *Es indiscutible que fue un error.* — It's indisputable that it was a mistake.
- *La prueba era irrefutable.* — The evidence was irrefutable.
- *Es cuestionable que el plan funcione.* — It's questionable whether the plan will work.
  (Doubt: subjunctive.)
- *El fiscal aseveró que el acusado mentía.* — The prosecutor asserted that the defendant was
  lying.
- *Vivimos con mucha incertidumbre.* — We live with a lot of uncertainty.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking the subjunctive means "unreal": after *me sorprende que* or *lamento que* the fact is
  true.
- Marking *No dudo que tienes razón* or *Es la mejor novela que he leído* wrong: both are
  standard.
- Reading *después de que el ministro presentara* as hypothetical: in the press it reports a past
  fact.
- Using the subjunctive after an affirmative expression of certainty: *Es indudable que hubo*
  (not ~~haya~~) *errores*.
- Confusing a gray zone with a real difference of meaning: *el primero que llegue* (future,
  unknown) vs *el primero que llegó* (past, known).

## Key points

- A presupposition is what a sentence takes for granted; it survives negation and questions.
- Factive verbs presuppose their clause: those of knowing take the indicative, those of feeling
  or judging the subjunctive.
- A known fact in the background often allows both moods: *el hecho de que*, *aunque* + a known
  fact.
- *No dudo que* + either; certainty (*es indudable, es innegable*) + indicative; its negation +
  subjunctive.
- After a superlative or *el único*, both moods are correct; the subjunctive widens the claim.
- *Después de que* + *-ra* subjunctive for a past fact is a journalistic use; *presentó* is the
  safe choice.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: ¿De qué te ríes? Humor, wordplay and satire
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Understanding a joke is one of the last skills a learner gains, because humor depends on
everything at once: sounds, double meanings, register, culture and timing. The CEFR's C1
descriptors include using language for social purposes, jokes among them, and C1 programs such
as the Universidad de Zaragoza's list humor, jokes and cartoons among their topics. This lesson takes humor apart: how Spanish wordplay works, how the
subjunctive of lesson 07 turns up in jokes, and how Mexican satire and cartooning use language.
Every joke and text here is original.

## How a joke works

Most jokes set up one reading of a situation and then, in the *remate* (punch line), reveal a
second one that also fits. The laugh comes from switching frames quickly. In Spanish, the
switch is often made by a word, which is why wordplay is the heart of everyday humor.

### Puns: one sound, two meanings

A **[[pun]]** (*un juego de palabras*) plays on a word or sound with two meanings. Spanish puns come
from two sources:

1. Homophones: different words that sound the same. Latin American seseo makes *casa*
   (house) and *caza* (hunting) identical, and *b* and *v* sound alike everywhere, so *votar* (to
   vote) and *botar* (to throw away, to bounce) do too.
2. Polysemy: one word with several meanings. In Mexico *el gato* is a cat and a car jack;
   *la pila* is a battery and also energy; *el banco* is a bank and a bench.

An original example of each:

- *—¿Dónde está tu papá? —Se fue de caza. —¿De casa? ¿Ya no vive con ustedes?* — "Where's your
  dad?" "He went hunting (*de caza*)." "He left home (*de casa*)? He doesn't live with you
  anymore?"
- *—Se me ponchó la llanta y no traigo gato. —Llévate el mío; total, nada más duerme.* — "I've got
  a flat tire and no jack (*gato*)." "Take mine (my cat); he just sleeps anyway."

Puns built on seseo don't work in central and northern Spain, where *casa* and *caza* sound
different: humor depends on the variety.

### Double meanings and double entendre

*El doble sentido* is a phrase that can be read two ways. An innocent one, from an imaginary
driving-school ad: *Con nosotros, usted llega lejos* (With us, you'll go far: by car, and in
life). A **[[double entendre]]** is a double meaning where the second reading is risqué. Mexico has a
famous tradition of it, the *albur*: a verbal duel of double meanings, usually sexual, in which
each speaker tries to have the last word (the DLE lists *albur* in this sense for Mexico and the
Dominican Republic). It's a well-known part of popular culture; this course describes it but
gives no examples.

### Irony and exaggeration

Lesson 04's **[[irony]]** says the opposite of what is meant: *¡Qué buen clima!* under a downpour.
Exaggeration is the other basic tool: *Hay tanto tráfico que mi vecino ya cumplió años en el
Periférico* (There's so much traffic that my neighbor has already had a birthday on the ring
road).

## The subjunctive in jokes

Lesson 07's independent subjunctive is a natural joke engine, because *¡Ni que…!* and *¡Quién…!*
set up an exaggeration that the punch line can then turn around:

- *—Oye, ¿me prestas mil pesos? —¡Ni que yo fuera banco! —Bueno, entonces nada más me siento un
  rato.* — "Hey, will you lend me a thousand pesos?" "As if I were a bank!" "OK, then I'll just
  sit down for a bit." (*banco* = bank and bench)
- *¡Quién fuera gato para dormir dieciocho horas!* — If only I were a cat and could sleep eighteen
  hours!

![A comic strip in three panels with empty speech bubbles. Panel 1: two friends sit on a park bench; the one on the left turns to the other, with a speech bubble. Panel 2: the friend on the right crosses his arms and frowns, with a bubble. Panel 3: the friend on the left stands up and points at the bench with a smile, with a bubble, while the other looks puzzled.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The strip above tells the *banco* joke without words: the setup (asking for money), the
rejection (*¡Ni que yo fuera banco!*) and the remate (the bench). In panel 3, the timing matters:
the punch line is the last bubble, and it is short.

## Satire and Mexican cartooning

Satire (*la sátira*) uses humor to criticize: it exaggerates the faults of people in power so
that readers see them clearly. Parody (*la parodia*) imitates a style, often an official one,
to mock it. Mexico has a long tradition of both:

- Nineteenth-century satirical weeklies. Under Porfirio Díaz, papers such as *El Hijo del
  Ahuizote* attacked the government with cartoons and paid for it with closures and jail.
- José Guadalupe Posada (1852–1913), an engraver, drew skeletons (*calaveras*) of every social
  class; his skeleton of a woman in a fancy hat, which he called a *calavera garbancera* and
  which later became known as *la Catrina*, mocked people who copied European fashions.
- Political cartoonists are called *moneros* in Mexico (from *los monos*, cartoon figures),
  and a political cartoon is *un cartón*. One of the best known, Rius (Eduardo del Río,
  1934–2017), created the comic books *Los Supermachos* and *Los agachados* and wrote illustrated
  books explaining politics and history to a wide public.
- The Museo de la Caricatura, opened in 1987 in a Baroque building in Mexico City's historic
  center (the former Colegio de Cristo), shows Mexican caricature and graphic satire from the
  nineteenth century on.

### *Cantinflas* and *cantinflear*

Mario Moreno (1911–1993), known as Cantinflas, was a comic actor whose characters talked and
talked without ever saying anything clear, tying the listener in knots. The language kept his
name: the DLE defines *cantinflear* (colloquial) as speaking or acting in a nonsensical,
incoherent way without saying anything of substance. Today the verb is often used about
politicians: *El diputado cantinfleó durante media hora.* — The congressman talked nonsense for
half an hour.

## Reading: a satirical news item

> **Municipio inaugura bache conmemorativo**
>
> SAN JUAN DEL OLVIDO. — En una ceremonia de lo más solemne, el presidente municipal inauguró
> ayer el bache más antiguo de la avenida Juárez, que este mes cumple diez años sin que nadie lo
> tape. «Hay quien dice que no hacemos nada», declaró el funcionario ante un grupo de vecinos que
> no había sido invitado, pero que pasaba por ahí. «Pues aquí tienen la prueba: hemos conservado
> este patrimonio intacto durante toda una década».
>
> El bache, de metro y medio de diámetro y de profundidad variable según la temporada de
> lluvias, recibió una placa de bronce, un listón tricolor y el nombre oficial de «Bache
> Benemérito de la Paciencia Ciudadana». Con el costo de la placa, según la tesorería, se habría
> podido pavimentar la avenida completa, «pero entonces no habría nada que inaugurar».
>
> Los vecinos reaccionaron con división de opiniones. Doña Rosario Medina, que vive enfrente
> desde hace treinta años, afirmó que el bache ya es parte de la familia: «Mis nietos aprendieron
> a nadar ahí». Un taxista, en cambio, lamentó que el municipio no hubiera elegido otro: «Ese ni
> siquiera es el más grande. El de la calle Morelos ya tiene peces».
>
> Al cierre de esta edición, el ayuntamiento anunció que el próximo año abrirá un concurso para
> elegir, «de manera democrática y transparente», cuál será el siguiente bache conmemorado. Se
> espera que participen todos.

**Summary.** A fictional mayor solemnly "inaugurates" a pothole that has gone unrepaired for ten
years, presenting it as heritage carefully preserved. The pothole gets a bronze plaque, a ribbon
and a pompous official name; the plaque cost as much as paving the whole avenue. One neighbor
says her grandchildren learned to swim in it; a taxi driver complains that a bigger pothole,
which already has fish, was overlooked. The town will hold a "democratic" contest to choose the
next one, and everyone (every pothole) is expected to take part.

**Glosses:** *el bache* = pothole; *tapar* = to fill in, cover; *el listón tricolor* = a ribbon
in the national colors; *benemérito* = worthy, illustrious (an official honorific); *al cierre de
esta edición* = as we went to press.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: why the *gato* joke works

**Setup.** *Se me ponchó la llanta y no traigo gato.* The context (a flat tire) activates the
Mexican meaning "car jack" for *gato*.

**Switch.** *Llévate el mío; total, nada más duerme.* *El mío* only makes sense as "my cat":
nobody's car jack sleeps. The listener has to reread *gato* with its other meaning.

**Why it's funny.** The second speaker pretends to be helpful and gives a useless "solution";
the incongruity comes from polysemy. Language point: *total* (anyway, after all) and *nada
más* (just) give the line its casual Mexican tone. The joke doesn't translate: English *jack*
isn't an animal.

### Example 2: why the satirical article works

**Setup.** The article copies the register of official news: *En una ceremonia de lo más solemne;
declaró el funcionario; según la tesorería; de manera democrática y transparente.* That is
parody of style.

**Switch.** The content inside that register is absurd: inaugurating a pothole, a plaque that cost
as much as the repair, a pothole with fish.

**Why it's funny.** The distance between serious form and ridiculous content is the joke, and the
target is real (public works that never get done), so it is satire. Language points: *sin que
nadie lo tape* (*sin que* + subjunctive); *lamentó que el municipio no hubiera elegido otro*
(a factive verb of feeling + pluperfect subjunctive); the closing *Se espera que participen
todos* is a remate with a double meaning: all the potholes, or all the residents.

## Pronunciation

- *humorista, humorístico*: the *h* is silent: *u-mo-RIS-ta, u-mo-RÍS-ti-co*.
- *sátira, satírico*: *SÁ-ti-ra* (stress on the first syllable) but *sa-TÍ-ri-co*.
- *caricaturista*: six syllables, *ca-ri-ca-tu-RIS-ta*.
- *cantinflear*: four syllables, *can-tin-fle-AR*; *e* and *a* are separate syllables.
- *remate*: *re-MA-te*; the *r* at the start is trilled, as every word-initial *r* is in
  Spanish.

## Common mistakes

- Translating a pun word for word: explain the two meanings instead.
- Assuming a pun works for every speaker: seseo puns fail where *z* and *s* differ.
- Confusing *la sátira* (criticism through humor) with *la parodia* (imitation of a style): many
  texts are both, but they aren't the same thing.
- Using *cantinflear* as praise: it criticizes empty, confusing talk.
- Calling every cartoonist a *monero*: in Mexico it usually means a political cartoonist; the
  general word is *el caricaturista*.

## Key points

- A joke sets up one reading and the remate switches to another.
- Puns come from homophones (*casa / caza* with seseo) and polysemy (*gato, banco, pila*).
- *El doble sentido* is any double reading; a double entendre's second reading is risqué, as in
  Mexico's *albur*.
- *¡Ni que…!* and *¡Quién…!* + imperfect subjunctive are joke openers.
- Satire criticizes through exaggeration; parody imitates a style. Mexico's tradition runs from
  Posada and the satirical weeklies to today's *moneros*.
- *Cantinflear* (DLE, colloquial): to talk without saying anything of substance.
