lessons.title: Ahora bien, con todo: contrast and counterargument
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 2 was about the meaning that mood carries. This module is about what holds a long text
together: the **[[connectors]]** that join ideas, the devices that keep a text cohesive, and the moves
of an argument. It starts with contrast, because contrast is where an argument turns.

You already know a good set of **[[adversative]]** connectors (words that set one idea against
another): A1's *pero*, A2's *sin embargo*, B1's *no obstante, aun así* and *en cambio*, B2's *si
bien*. At C1 the question is no longer "how do I say *but*?" but "which *but*?" Each adversative
has a strength (a mild reservation or a flat contradiction), a **[[register]]** (everyday, formal,
literary) and a place in the sentence. The theme is education: public and private schools,
homeschooling, assessment and inclusion, a debate in which every side has good arguments.

## The adversatives at a glance

![A chart of Spanish adversative connectors. Five rows run from milder at the top to stronger at the bottom: matiza (adds a reservation), concede y contrasta, contrasta, opone dos cosas, and contradice o corrige. Four columns give the register: todos los registros, neutral y formal, formal, and literario (solo para leer). Ahora bien is in the matiza row under neutral y formal, and si bien under formal. Aun así is in the concede row under all registers, con todo under formal. Pero and sin embargo are in the contrasta row under all registers, no obstante under formal, empero under literary. Mientras que and en cambio oppose two things in all registers. Sino and al contrario contradict in all registers, por el contrario under neutral y formal, antes bien under literary.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Down the rows, the contrast gets stronger: *ahora bien* only adds a reservation, while *sino* and
*por el contrario* say the first idea is wrong. Across the columns, the register rises: *pero* fits
a text message, *no obstante* a report, and *empero* a nineteenth-century novel.

## *Ahora bien*: a reservation or a turn

*Ahora bien* (that said, having said that) accepts what came before and adds a "but" that changes
its weight. It opens its sentence, or the clause after a semicolon, and takes a comma:

- *La escuela pública es gratuita. Ahora bien, los útiles y el uniforme cuestan.* — Public school
  is free. That said, supplies and the uniform cost money.
- *El método funciona con grupos pequeños; ahora bien, ¿funcionará con cuarenta alumnos?* — The
  method works with small groups; having said that, will it work with forty students?

It can also just move the argument on, like English "now": *Ahora bien, pasemos a los costos*
(Now, let's turn to the costs).

## *Con todo* and *aun así*: concede, then contrast

Both mean "even so, all the same": the first sentence leads you to expect one thing, and the
second says the opposite happened. B1's *aun así* fits every register; *con todo* is formal.

- *Los grupos son enormes. Con todo, los resultados han mejorado.* — The classes are huge. Even
  so, results have improved.
- *Sabía que era difícil; aun así, lo intentó.* — She knew it was hard; even so, she tried.

*Con todo* can also sit between commas: *El modelo, con todo, tiene ventajas* (The model, even so,
has advantages). Only the context tells it apart from literal "with everything": *Llegó con todo
su material* (She arrived with all her materials).

## *En cambio* or *por el contrario*?

Both are often translated "on the other hand", but they do different jobs.

- B1's *en cambio* opposes two different things: A is like this; B is like that. *Los colegios
  privados cobran colegiatura; las escuelas públicas, en cambio, no.* — Private schools charge
  tuition; public schools, on the other hand, don't.
- *Por el contrario* contradicts: not what was just said, but the opposite. It typically
  follows a negative. *El rendimiento escolar no bajó; por el contrario, subió.* — School
  performance didn't fall; on the contrary, it rose.

*Por el contrario* (and the everyday *al contrario*) can also contrast two things in formal
writing, like *en cambio*; but *en cambio* isn't used to contradict. After *no bajó*, say *por el
contrario* or *al contrario*.

*Mientras que* (whereas) opposes two things inside one sentence: *En la ciudad sobran escuelas,
mientras que en el campo faltan* (In the city there are plenty of schools, whereas in the
countryside there aren't enough). B2's *si bien* (although) concedes first: *Si bien la educación
en casa da autonomía, exige mucho tiempo* (Although homeschooling gives autonomy, it takes a lot
of time).

## *Sino, sino que, si no* and *pero sí*

After a negative, Spanish separates two ideas that English joins with "but":

- *Sino* corrects with a noun, adjective or phrase: *No es un problema económico, sino
  pedagógico.* — It isn't an economic problem but an educational one.
- *Sino que* corrects with a conjugated verb: *No reprobó, sino que dejó la escuela.* — He
  didn't fail; he left school.
- *Pero* after a negative adds instead of correcting: *No es caro, pero sí incómodo.* — It
  isn't expensive, but it is uncomfortable. The *sí* stresses the part that is true.
- *Si no*, two words, is "if not": *Si no hay evaluación, no hay mejora.* — If there's no
  assessment, there's no improvement. Lesson 21 returns to the spelling.

*No… sino* can also mean "only": *No pide sino respeto.* — He asks only for respect.

## Two literary adversatives (for reading)

Recognize these in older or very formal writing; you don't need to use them.

- *Antes bien* (rather, quite the opposite) follows a negative, like *por el contrario*: *No lo
  castigó; antes bien, lo felicitó.* — He didn't punish him; quite the opposite, he congratulated
  him.
- *Empero* (however) is an old equivalent of *sin embargo*, today literary or deliberately
  solemn: *La reforma, empero, nunca se aplicó.* — The reform, however, was never applied.

## Punctuation, position and stacking

- *Sin embargo, no obstante, con todo, ahora bien, por el contrario* and *en cambio* are set off
  by commas: at the start after a period or semicolon (*; sin embargo,*), or between commas inside
  the clause (*Los resultados, sin embargo, mejoraron*).
- A comma normally goes before *pero* (*Es gratuita, pero falta material*); in very short phrases
  it is often left out (*lento pero seguro*).
- One connector per turn. *Pero sin embargo* is heard in speech, but careful writing treats it as
  redundant: choose one.

## Talking about schools

- *El docente / la docente* is the formal word for a teacher (A1's *el maestro* is the everyday
  one); *el profesorado* is the teaching staff, *el alumnado* the student body, and *el pedagogo*
  a specialist in *la pedagogía*, the science or a method of teaching.
- In Mexico *el plantel* is a school campus or branch (*el plantel sur de la prepa*).
- *El rezago educativo* is Mexico's term for being behind in schooling for one's age, or never
  having finished basic education. *La educación en casa* (homeschooling) has a legal status and a
  way of certifying studies that differ by country; this lesson doesn't describe them.

For scale: in the 2024–2025 school year Mexico's in-person school system (*escolarizado*) had
32,516,109 students, and 27,864,633 of them, about 85.7%, were in public schools, according to the
SEP's *Principales cifras del Sistema Educativo Nacional 2024–2025*. The same report gives a
dropout rate of 11.3% in upper secondary (*media superior*) in 2023–2024.

![Two scenes side by side. On the left, a classroom: a teacher at a board and rows of desks with many students; the caption reads en el salón: muchos alumnos, un docente. On the right, a home: a parent and one child at a table with books and a laptop; the caption reads en casa: un alumno, un adulto. Under both, a line reads con todo, los dos modelos necesitan evaluación.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Text: an opinion column and a reply

> *Tres modelos, una misma pregunta*
>
> Cada verano, miles de familias mexicanas se hacen la misma pregunta: ¿a qué escuela mandamos a
> nuestros hijos? Para la gran mayoría la respuesta es la escuela pública; para otras, un plantel
> privado; y para un grupo pequeño pero creciente, la educación en casa. Ninguna opción es
> perfecta. Ahora bien, conviene compararlas con datos y no con prejuicios.
>
> La escuela pública tiene a su favor la equidad: es gratuita y, en principio, recibe a todo el
> alumnado, sin importar de dónde venga. Muchos de sus docentes tienen una formación pedagógica
> sólida y una vocación admirable. Sin embargo, los grupos suelen ser numerosos, los recursos
> escasean y en algunas regiones el rezago educativo sigue siendo enorme. La deserción escolar en
> la preparatoria, además, preocupa a especialistas de todas las corrientes.
>
> Las escuelas privadas, en cambio, ofrecen grupos más pequeños e instalaciones mejor equipadas.
> Con todo, el precio no garantiza la calidad: hay colegios caros con un rendimiento escolar
> mediocre y escuelas públicas excelentes. Tampoco es cierto que su profesorado esté siempre
> mejor preparado; por el contrario, en muchos casos gana menos y cambia de trabajo con más
> frecuencia.
>
> La educación en casa es la opción que más polémica despierta. Quienes la defienden hablan de
> autonomía: el niño aprende a su ritmo, sigue sus intereses y desarrolla el pensamiento crítico
> en lugar de dedicarse a la memorización. Quienes la critican responden que la escuela no solo
> enseña matemáticas, sino que también enseña a convivir con personas distintas. Si bien muchas
> familias organizan actividades con otros niños, no todas pueden hacerlo, ni todas tienen el
> tiempo o la preparación para enseñar.
>
> ¿Qué modelo es mejor, entonces? Creo que la pregunta está mal planteada. No se trata de elegir
> un ganador, sino de exigir que los tres rindan cuentas. Una escuela inclusiva, que use la
> evaluación formativa para detectar a tiempo a quien se queda atrás, puede existir en cualquiera
> de los tres modelos. Lo que no puede existir es una sociedad equitativa con escuelas que solo
> funcionan para algunos.
>
> *Carta de una lectora*
>
> Leí con interés su columna. Ahora bien, me parece injusta con la educación en casa. Mi hija
> estudia en casa desde hace tres años y no vive aislada; por el contrario, toma clases de
> música, juega futbol y tiene amigos de todas las edades. No digo que sea la opción correcta para
> todos, sino que merece el mismo respeto que las otras. Con todo, le doy la razón en algo:
> ningún modelo debería quedar fuera de la evaluación.

Summary of the column: (1) Families choose between public school, private school and, for a
small but growing group, homeschooling; compare them with data, not prejudice. (2) Public school
offers equity and many dedicated teachers, but large classes, scarce resources, regional lag and
high-school dropout. (3) Private schools have smaller classes, but price doesn't guarantee quality
and their teachers often earn less. (4) Homeschooling gives autonomy; critics say school also
teaches living with different people. (5) The question is badly framed: all three models should
be accountable.

The reader's letter, in full: I read your column with interest. That said, I find it unfair to
homeschooling. My daughter has studied at home for three years and doesn't live in isolation; on
the contrary, she takes music lessons, plays soccer and has friends of all ages. I'm not saying it's
the right option for everyone, but that it deserves the same respect as the others. Even so, I
agree with you on one point: no model should be left out of assessment.

(*conviene* — it's advisable; *el colegio* — school, often a private one; *escasear* — to be
scarce; *la corriente* — school of thought; *despertar polémica* — to stir controversy; *mal
planteado* — badly framed; *rendir cuentas* — to be accountable; *quedarse atrás* — to fall behind;
*dar la razón a alguien* — to agree that someone is right.) Find the adversatives: *ahora bien*
(twice), *sin embargo*, *en cambio*, *con todo* (twice), *por el contrario* (twice, each after a
negative idea), *si bien*, and the correction pattern *no… sino (que)*.

## Pronunciation

- *Pedagogía*: five syllables, *pe-da-go-GÍ-a*. The first *g* (before *o*) is hard, as in "go";
  the second (before *í*) is the Spanish *j* sound, a breathy *h*.
- *Escolarización*: six syllables, *es-co-la-ri-za-CIÓN*; *z* is *s* in Latin America.
- *Equidad, equitativo*: *e-qui-DAD, e-qui-ta-TI-vo*; *qu* is a plain *k*, with no *w* sound as in
  English "equity".
- *Empero*: *em-PE-ro*, stress on the middle syllable.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*No es caro, pero barato*~~ → *No es caro, sino barato*. After a negative, a correction takes
  *sino*; *pero* adds (*No es caro, pero sí incómodo*).
- ~~*No reprobó, sino dejó la escuela*~~ → *sino que dejó*: before a conjugated verb, *sino que*.
- ~~*Sino estudias, repruebas*~~ → *Si no estudias…*: "if not" is two words.
- *En cambio* to contradict (*No bajó; en cambio, subió*) sounds odd: use *por el contrario* or
  *al contrario*.
- *Pero sin embargo*: two markers for one turn; in writing, keep one.

## Key points

- Adversatives differ in strength (reservation → contrast → contradiction) and register: *ahora
  bien* adds a reservation; *aun así, con todo* concede then contrast; *pero, sin embargo, no
  obstante* contrast; *en cambio, mientras que* oppose two things; *sino, por el contrario, al
  contrario* contradict. *Antes bien* and *empero* are literary.
- After a negative: *sino* + word or phrase, *sino que* + verb, *pero sí* to add; *si no* is "if
  not".
- Set connectors off with commas; don't stack them.

lessons.title: Toda vez que…: formal cause, consequence and condition
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 09 sorted the adversatives by strength and register. This lesson does the same for the
other big families of connectors: cause, consequence and condition. B1 and B2 gave you the
neutral core (*ya que, puesto que, dado que, por lo tanto, por consiguiente, por ende, así pues, de
ahí que, siempre y cuando, a condición de que*). At C1 you'll read and write reports, regulations
and official letters, and they use a formal layer on top: *toda vez que, habida cuenta de que, en
vista de que, so pena de, en aras de*. You need to understand them, use some, and know when the
plain word is better.

As in B2, a **[[causal clause]]** gives the reason, a **[[consecutive clause]]** gives the result, and a
**[[conditional clause]]** sets the condition. The theme is energy: solar and wind power, oil and gas,
the grid, blackouts and efficiency.

## Cause: the formal range

| Connector | Register | Mood | Plainer word |
|---|---|---|---|
| *porque, como* (first) | all | indicative | — |
| *ya que, puesto que, dado que* | neutral to formal | indicative | *porque* |
| *en vista de que, visto que* | neutral to formal | indicative | *como* |
| *habida cuenta de que* | formal | indicative | *considerando que* |
| *toda vez que* | formal, legal and administrative | indicative | *ya que* |
| *por cuanto* | formal (for reading) | indicative | *porque* |

- *En vista de que no hubo luz en toda la mañana, se suspendieron las clases.* — In view of the
  fact that there was no power all morning, classes were suspended.
- *Visto que el apagón continúa, la tienda cerrará temprano.* — Seeing that the blackout is
  continuing, the store will close early.
- *Habida cuenta de que el consumo se duplica en verano, la red necesita más capacidad.* — Bearing
  in mind that consumption doubles in summer, the grid needs more capacity.
- *Se niega el permiso, toda vez que el proyecto no presentó su estudio de impacto.* — The permit
  is denied, given that the project didn't submit its impact study.

*Toda vez que* is typical of Mexican legal and administrative writing (rulings, official letters,
permits); in conversation it sounds like a judge talking. In *habida cuenta de que*, *habida*
agrees with *cuenta* and never changes; without *que* it takes a noun: *habida cuenta de los
costos* (bearing in mind the costs). *Por cuanto*
appears in legal and philosophical texts (*La medida es injusta, por cuanto afecta solo a los más
pobres*: the measure is unfair, inasmuch as it affects only the poorest); you only need to
recognize it.

## Consequence: from *conque* to *luego*

| Connector | Register | Mood |
|---|---|---|
| *así que, por eso* | all | indicative |
| *conque* | colloquial | indicative |
| *de modo que, de manera que* | neutral | indicative (result) / subjunctive (purpose) |
| *por lo tanto, por consiguiente, en consecuencia* | neutral to formal | indicative |
| *por ende, así pues* | formal | indicative |
| *de ahí que* | written | usually subjunctive |
| *luego* | formal argument (for reading) | indicative |

- *Conque* (so, so then) is colloquial and often draws a conclusion addressed to the listener:
  *Ya se fue la luz dos veces hoy, conque desconecta la computadora.* — The power's gone out twice
  today, so unplug the computer. Spell it as one word; *con que* is "with which" or "provided
  that", and *¿con qué?* "with what?".
- *De modo que* changes meaning with the mood. With the indicative it gives a result: *Se fue
  la luz, de modo que cerramos.* — The power went out, so we closed. With the subjunctive it gives
  a purpose: *Instalaron baterías de modo que la clínica no se quede sin luz.* — They installed
  batteries so that the clinic isn't left without power.
- *Luego* as "therefore" belongs to logic and old-fashioned argument: *Todos los paneles
  necesitan sol; hoy no hay sol; luego, hoy no producen.* — All panels need sun; today there's no
  sun; therefore, today they don't produce. Everywhere else *luego* means "then, later" (and in
  Mexico *luego luego* is "right away").

## Condition, limit and purpose

- *En la medida en que* (insofar as, to the extent that) sets a proportion or a limit. With
  the indicative it states a fact; with the subjunctive, a future or open case: *La transición
  avanza en la medida en que hay inversión.* — The transition advances to the extent that there is
  investment. / *Ahorraremos en la medida en que reduzcamos el consumo.* — We'll save to the extent
  that we reduce consumption.
- *So pena de* (on pain of) + infinitive or noun states a penalty: *Los usuarios deben pagar
  antes del día 15, so pena de suspensión del servicio.* — Users must pay before the 15th, on pain
  of having service suspended.
- *A sabiendas de que* (knowing full well that) + indicative: *Construyeron ahí a sabiendas de
  que la zona se inunda.* — They built there knowing full well that the area floods. *A sabiendas*
  can also stand alone: *Lo hizo a sabiendas.* — He did it knowingly.
- *En aras de* (for the sake of) + noun or infinitive is formal purpose: *En aras de la
  eficiencia, se apagarán las luces a las diez.* — For the sake of efficiency, the lights will be
  turned off at ten.

B2's *siempre y cuando* and *a condición de que* still take the subjunctive: *El proyecto se
aprobará siempre y cuando se garantice el almacenamiento.* — The project will be approved as long
as storage is guaranteed.

![A table of formal connectors and their plainer equivalents in three groups. Causa: toda vez que, habida cuenta de que, en vista de que, visto que, matched with ya que, considerando que, como. Consecuencia: por ende, así pues, de ahí que, matched with por eso, así que. Condición y fin: en la medida en que, so pena de, a sabiendas de que, en aras de, matched with si, si no, sabiendo que, para. A note at the bottom reads: in a message to neighbors, the plain column is usually better.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Commas and overuse

- A connector that opens a sentence takes a comma after it: *Así pues, …; Por ende, …*. Between
  two clauses, *por consiguiente* and *por ende* follow a semicolon or go between commas: *La red es
  vieja; por consiguiente, falla.* / *La red, por ende, falla.* (The grid is old; consequently, it
  fails.)
- Don't string formal connectors together. A paragraph with *toda vez que*, *habida cuenta de que*
  and *en aras de* in three lines reads like a parody of bureaucratic style. One formal connector
  per idea, and the plain one whenever the reader is the general public.

## The grid in words and a picture

![A simple drawing of an electricity system with Spanish labels. On the left, the sun, three wind turbines (el aerogenerador) and, on the ground, a field of solar panels (el panel solar); a house has a panel on its roof. In the center is a gas-fired power plant with a chimney (la central eléctrica). Power lines on two towers (la red eléctrica) run from the plant to a clinic marked with a red cross. Below the clinic is a large battery for storage (la batería).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *La energía solar* comes from *los paneles solares*; *la energía eólica*, from *los
  aerogeneradores* (wind turbines; *eólico* is the adjective). *La central eléctrica* is a power plant; *la red eléctrica* the grid; *el almacenamiento*
  is storage, as in a big battery.
- The fossil fuels (*los combustibles fósiles*): *el petróleo* (crude oil), *el gas natural*.
  *El hidrocarburo* is the chemical and legal word for both. *La matriz energética* is the mix of
  sources a country uses; *la transición energética* is the shift from fossil to clean sources.
- *El apagón* is a blackout (in speech, *se fue la luz*). *La sustentabilidad* is the usual word
  in Mexico; Spain says *la sostenibilidad* (B1's *sostenible* is used everywhere).

For scale: the Secretaría de Energía (SENER) reported that 24.3% of Mexico's electricity
generation in 2023, including distributed generation such as rooftop panels, came from clean
sources, as the IMCO, a Mexican think tank, summarized it in June 2024; the goal set in national
legislation and in Mexico's Paris commitments is 35%.

## Text: a report and its plain version

> *Resumen ejecutivo. Proyecto de energía solar comunitaria de San Isidro del Monte (2024–2026)*
>
> San Isidro del Monte es un municipio rural de unos 6,000 habitantes que, hasta 2024, dependía
> por completo de una sola línea de la red eléctrica. Toda vez que esa línea atraviesa una zona
> de fuertes vientos, los apagones eran frecuentes: en 2023 se registraron 41 interrupciones, la
> más larga de nueve horas. En vista de que la clínica y el pozo de agua quedaban sin servicio en
> cada falla, el ayuntamiento solicitó un estudio de alternativas.
>
> Habida cuenta de que la región recibe una radiación solar elevada durante casi todo el año, el
> estudio recomendó instalar paneles solares en los techos de los edificios públicos y una pequeña
> planta en un terreno municipal, además de un sistema de almacenamiento con baterías. Se descartó
> la energía eólica, visto que los aerogeneradores requerían una inversión inicial tres veces
> mayor.
>
> Los resultados del primer año son alentadores. La clínica y el pozo no han sufrido ningún corte
> prolongado, y el consumo de diésel de los generadores de emergencia bajó un 80 %. Por
> consiguiente, la huella de carbono del municipio se redujo, si bien todavía no es posible
> calcularla con precisión. Los vecinos que instalaron paneles en sus casas reportan, asimismo,
> recibos de luz más bajos.
>
> No obstante, el proyecto enfrenta límites. Las baterías tienen una vida útil de entre diez y
> quince años, de ahí que sea necesario prever desde ahora su reemplazo y su reciclaje. Además, la
> planta solo cubre el consumo de los edificios públicos en la medida en que estos mantengan
> medidas de eficiencia energética; si el consumo crece, la capacidad será insuficiente.
>
> En aras de la sustentabilidad del proyecto, se recomienda: (1) crear un fondo de mantenimiento,
> (2) capacitar a técnicos locales y (3) firmar un convenio con las escuelas para que enseñen el
> uso responsable de la energía. Los responsables de cada instalación deberán entregar un informe
> mensual de consumo, so pena de perder el apoyo del fondo.
>
> *Versión para los vecinos*
>
> ¿Por qué pusimos paneles solares? Porque la luz se iba muy seguido y la clínica y el pozo se
> quedaban sin servicio. Aquí hay mucho sol casi todo el año, así que el sol nos salió más barato
> que el viento. Desde que tenemos paneles y baterías, la clínica no se ha quedado sin luz. Ahora
> bien, las baterías no duran para siempre: en unos diez años habrá que cambiarlas. Por eso vamos
> a juntar un fondo y a capacitar a jóvenes del pueblo. Y si ahorramos luz en las escuelas y
> oficinas, los paneles alcanzan para todos.

Summary of the report: (1) A rural town of about 6,000 depended on one power line through a
windy area: 41 outages in 2023, each leaving the clinic and the well without service. (2) Given
the strong sun, a study recommended solar panels, a small municipal plant and batteries; wind was
ruled out as three times as expensive. (3) First year: no long outages, 80% less diesel, a smaller
carbon footprint, lower household bills. (4) Limits: batteries last ten to fifteen years, and the
plant is enough only if buildings keep saving energy. (5) Recommendations: a maintenance fund,
local technicians, a school agreement, and monthly reports on pain of losing funding.

The residents' version, in full: Why did we put up solar panels? Because the power went out
very often and the clinic and the well were left without service. There's lots of sun here almost
all year, so the sun turned out cheaper than the wind. Since we've had panels and batteries, the
clinic hasn't lost power. That said, batteries don't last forever: in about ten years we'll have
to replace them. That's why we're going to put together a fund and train young people from the
town. And if we save electricity in the schools and offices, the panels are enough for everyone.

(*el ayuntamiento* — the town council; *el pozo* — well; *descartar* — to rule out; *alentador* —
encouraging; *el recibo de luz* — electricity bill; *con precisión* — precisely; *la vida útil* — service life; *prever* — to
plan for; *el convenio* — agreement; *alcanzar* — to be enough.) Compare the two: the formal
causes become *porque* and *así que*, and *so pena de* disappears.

## Pronunciation

- *Aerogenerador*: seven syllables, *a-e-ro-ge-ne-ra-DOR*; *a* and *e* are separate syllables,
  and *ge* has the breathy *j* sound.
- *Eólico*: four syllables, *e-Ó-li-co*.
- *Hidrocarburo*: five syllables, *i-dro-car-BU-ro*; the *h* is silent.
- *Sustentabilidad*: six syllables, *sus-ten-ta-bi-li-DAD*.
- *Habida cuenta*: *a-BI-da CUEN-ta*; the *h* is silent.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*habido cuenta de que*~~ → *habida cuenta de que*: *habida* agrees with *cuenta*.
- *Con que* for "so": write *conque* (*Ya es tarde, conque vámonos*).
- *De modo que* + subjunctive when you mean a result: *Se fue la luz, de modo que cerramos* (result,
  indicative); *de modo que no se quede sin luz* is purpose.
- *Toda vez que* in casual speech or in a note to neighbors: it belongs to rulings and official
  letters. Say *como* or *ya que*.

## Key points

- Formal cause: *en vista de que, visto que* (neutral to formal), *habida cuenta de que, toda vez
  que* (formal; the latter legal and administrative), *por cuanto* (for reading); all with the
  indicative.
- Consequence by register: *conque* (colloquial) → *así que* → *de modo que* → *por consiguiente*
  → *por ende, así pues*; *de ahí que* + subjunctive; *luego* in formal logic.
- *De modo que* + indicative = result, + subjunctive = purpose. *En la medida en que* + indicative
  (fact) or subjunctive (open case). *So pena de, en aras de* + noun or infinitive; *a sabiendas de
  que* + indicative.
- Match the connector to the reader: plain words for the public.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Dicho lo anterior: cohesion and reference in long texts
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 09 and 10 were about connectors, the words that say how two ideas relate. A long text
needs something more: it has to keep track of what it's talking about without repeating the same
noun in every line. That is **[[cohesion]]**, the visible links between sentences. B2's lesson 17
separated it from **[[coherence]]**, whether the ideas make sense together as a whole: a text can be
cohesive (full of *este, dicho, sin embargo*) and still incoherent, if its argument goes nowhere.

This lesson covers **[[anaphoric reference]]** (words that point back to something already
mentioned), synonyms and **[[hypernyms]]**, **[[ellipsis]]**, *lo* for a whole idea, the markers that
organize a text, and the shape of a paragraph. The theme is archives and historical memory: the
Archivo General de la Nación, the Hemeroteca Nacional, codices, and how historians use sources.

## Pointing back: pronouns and demonstratives

The simplest reference is a pronoun or a demonstrative. At C1, the useful ones are:

- *Este, ese, aquel* for what was just named, with *este último* "the latter" and *el
  primero… el segundo* "the former… the latter": *El archivo conserva cartas y mapas; estos
  últimos se restauraron en 2020.* — The archive keeps letters and maps; the latter were restored
  in 2020.
- *Lo* for a whole clause: *Dicen que el códice se perdió en un incendio, pero nadie lo ha
  probado.* — They say the codex was lost in a fire, but nobody has proved it. Neuter *esto, eso*
  do the same: *Eso explica la laguna en la colección.* — That explains the gap in the collection.
- *El primero… el segundo*, *respectivamente*: *La historiadora y el archivista nacieron
  en Puebla y en Mérida, respectivamente.* — The historian and the archivist were born in Puebla
  and Mérida, respectively.

## Formal pointers: *dicho, el citado, tal* and *el susodicho*

Formal and academic writing has its own pointing words, all meaning roughly "the aforementioned":

- *Dicho* + noun, agreeing, with no article: *dicho periódico, dicha colección, dichos
  documentos.* — *Dicho periódico dejó de publicarse en 1911.* — That newspaper stopped publishing
  in 1911.
- *El citado, el mencionado* + noun, with the article: *el citado informe, la mencionada
  hemeroteca.*
- *Tal* + noun, with no article: *Tal decisión sorprendió a los historiadores.* — Such a
  decision surprised historians.
- *El susodicho, la susodicha* is old legal style that today is mostly humorous: *Y el
  susodicho volvió a llegar tarde.* — And the aforesaid arrived late again.

Use them sparingly. *Dicho* every other sentence sounds bureaucratic; one in a paragraph is enough,
and a plain *este* usually does the job.

## Synonyms and hypernyms

To avoid repeating a noun, refer to it with a synonym, a description or a hypernym, a more
general word that includes it:

- *el códice → el manuscrito → el documento*
- *el periódico → el diario → la publicación*
- *Miguel Hidalgo → el cura de Dolores → el insurgente → este*

![A reference chain drawn as six sentence boxes from top to bottom, with lines from every box joining one arrow that points back to the first. 1: Miguel Hidalgo inició la guerra de Independencia en 1810, labeled primera mención. 2: El cura de Dolores llamó a la gente a rebelarse, labeled descripción. 3: El insurgente reunió pronto un gran ejército, labeled sustantivo más general. 4: Pero este perdió en Puente de Calderón, labeled demostrativo. 5: En 1811 lo capturaron en el norte, labeled pronombre. 6: Ø Fue fusilado en Chihuahua ese mismo año, labeled elipsis: sujeto omitido. A caption says all the arrows point to the first mention, Miguel Hidalgo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A chain like this keeps one person in focus, and each description adds information (*el cura de
Dolores* gives his job and parish). The facts are the textbook ones: Hidalgo, parish priest of
Dolores, began the independence uprising in September 1810 and was captured and executed in 1811.

## Ellipsis: leaving words out

Ellipsis omits what the reader can recover. Spanish does it constantly with subjects (the verb
ending says who), and C1 writing also drops repeated verbs, marking the gap with a comma:

- *La biblioteca abre a las nueve; la hemeroteca, a las diez.* — The library opens at nine; the
  newspaper archive, at ten.
- *Unos documentos están en Puebla; otros, en Sevilla.* — Some documents are in Puebla; others, in
  Seville.

The comma stands for the missing verb. Don't confuse this kind of ellipsis with the punctuation
mark of three dots (*los puntos suspensivos*).

## Markers that organize a text

| Marker | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *por su parte* | adds another participant's contribution | *El archivo aportó los documentos; la universidad, por su parte, el equipo.* |
| *a su vez* | "in turn": a chain; also, like *por su parte*, another participant's share | *El acervo creció, y este, a su vez, exigió más espacio.* |
| *del mismo modo, asimismo* (B1) | adds a parallel point | *Del mismo modo, se digitalizaron los mapas.* |
| *respectivamente* | pairs two lists in order | *Nacieron en 1810 y 1821, respectivamente.* |
| *al respecto* | "on the matter", after naming it | *Consultamos a la directora, que no quiso opinar al respecto.* |
| *en este sentido* | "in this respect": develops the last point | *En este sentido, la cronología es clave.* |

## The paragraph

A paragraph in an expository or argumentative text usually has three parts: a topic sentence that
states its idea, development (examples, data, explanation) and, often, a last sentence that closes
or links to the next paragraph. The **[[connectors]]** of lessons 09–10 show the logic between
sentences; the reference devices above keep the topic visible. If you can't say a paragraph's idea
in one sentence, it probably has two ideas, and needs two paragraphs.

## Words for archives and history

- *El acervo* is the holdings of an archive, library or museum (*el acervo de la Hemeroteca*); it
  also means a cultural heritage. *La hemeroteca* is a newspaper and periodicals archive.
- *El códice* is a manuscript book; in Mexico it usually means a pictorial manuscript of the
  Mesoamerican tradition, painted on deerskin, bark paper or cotton, some before the Spanish
  conquest and many after it. *Virreinal* means of the viceroyalty (A2's *el virreinato*, New
  Spain from 1535 to 1821).
- *La fuente primaria* is a document from the time studied; a historian's book about it is a
  secondary source. *Fidedigno* (trustworthy) describes a reliable source or witness.
- *La historiografía* is the writing of history and the study of how it has been written; *la
  periodización* divides it into periods; *la cronología* is a timeline; *el anacronismo* is
  something out of its time (a wristwatch in a film about 1810). *El antecedente* is background
  or a precedent, and *el hilo conductor* the common thread of a story.
- *La efeméride* is the anniversary of an event, or the event itself (*las efemérides del mes*);
  *conmemorar* is to commemorate, and *la conmemoración* the act.

Two real institutions keep much of Mexico's memory. The Archivo General de la Nación (AGN)
traces its origin to 1790, when the viceroy, the second Count of Revillagigedo, proposed a general
archive for New Spain; it took its present name in the late 1910s and since the early 1980s has been housed
in the Palacio de Lecumberri, a prison from 1900 to 1976. The Hemeroteca Nacional de México,
run by the UNAM, was inaugurated on March 28, 1944, and today holds about eight million printed
items on the university's main campus.

## Text: how an archive was saved

> *El Centinela, rescatado del agua*
>
> En octubre de 1999, unas lluvias excepcionales inundaron el centro de Santa Rita, un pequeño
> puerto del Golfo. Entre los edificios afectados estaba la antigua casa de los Ortega, donde se
> guardaba, casi olvidada, la colección completa de *El Centinela*, el periódico que la familia
> publicó entre 1868 y 1911. Para los historiadores de la región, dicha colección era una fuente
> primaria única: el único diario local que había cubierto, número por número, el final del
> siglo XIX.
>
> Cuando el agua bajó, la archivista municipal, Leonor Cházaro, encontró los tomos empapados y
> cubiertos de lodo. Su primera decisión fue también la más difícil: no intentar secarlos al sol,
> como sugerían los vecinos, sino congelarlos. Al respecto, Cházaro explicaría años después que
> el papel mojado se deforma y se llena de hongos en pocos días, mientras que el congelado espera
> sin dañarse. Los pescadores del puerto, por su parte, prestaron sus cámaras de refrigeración, y
> la carnicería del mercado ofreció las suyas.
>
> Durante los dos años siguientes, un pequeño equipo de voluntarios descongeló y secó los tomos
> uno por uno. Del mismo modo, se limpiaron los grabados y se rehicieron las encuadernaciones más
> dañadas. El trabajo avanzaba despacio: cada tomo exigía unas tres semanas. La universidad del
> estado, a su vez, envió a dos restauradoras, quienes formaron a los voluntarios y, con el
> tiempo, a otros archiveros de la región.
>
> Hoy el acervo de *El Centinela* puede consultarse en línea. Su valor no reside solo en las
> grandes efemérides que registró (la llegada del ferrocarril, en 1892, o la epidemia de fiebre
> amarilla de 1903), sino en lo cotidiano: los anuncios, los precios del mercado, las cartas de
> los lectores. En este sentido, el periódico permite reconstruir la vida de un puerto que los
> libros de historia apenas mencionan.
>
> Como ocurre con instituciones mucho mayores, como el Archivo General de la Nación o la
> Hemeroteca Nacional, el rescate de *El Centinela* plantea una pregunta de fondo: ¿quién decide
> qué se conserva? Cházaro lo resume así: un archivo no guarda el pasado, sino lo que alguien
> decidió que valía la pena guardar. Por eso cada año, al conmemorar la inundación, el puerto
> recuerda también a quienes salvaron su memoria.

Summary: (1) In October 1999 floods hit the center of Santa Rita, a small (fictional) Gulf
port, and soaked the complete run of *El Centinela*, a family newspaper published from 1868 to
1911 and a unique primary source on the late nineteenth century. (2) The town archivist froze the
volumes instead of drying them in the sun, because wet paper warps and grows mold while frozen
paper waits undamaged; fishermen and a butcher lent their cold rooms. (3) Over two years volunteers
thawed and dried each volume (about three weeks each), and two restorers from the state university
trained them. (4) The collection is now online; its value lies less in big dates than in daily
life: ads, prices, letters. (5) Like the AGN or the Hemeroteca, the rescue raises the question of
who decides what is kept: an archive holds what someone decided was worth keeping.

(*empapado* — soaked; *el lodo* — mud; *el hongo* — mold; *la cámara de refrigeración* — cold room;
*el tomo* — volume; *el grabado* — engraving; *la encuadernación* — binding; *residir en* — to lie
in; *de fondo* — underlying; *la memoria* — here, collective memory, lesson 05's word.) Find the reference devices: *dicha colección*, *los tomos → uno por
uno*, *las suyas* (= their cold rooms), *quienes* (= the restorers), *el acervo*, *el periódico*,
*lo resume* (= the whole question); and the markers *al respecto, por su parte, del mismo modo, a
su vez, en este sentido*.

## Repair a repetitive text

Here is a paragraph with every link removed. Read it, then compare the repaired version.

> El archivo recibió el códice en 2015. El códice estaba muy dañado. Los restauradores trabajaron
> en el códice durante un año. Los restauradores descubrieron que el códice tenía dos capas de
> pintura. La primera capa de pintura era del siglo XVI. La segunda capa de pintura era del siglo
> XVIII.

> El archivo recibió el códice en 2015. Como el documento estaba muy dañado, los restauradores
> trabajaron en él durante un año, y descubrieron que tenía dos capas de pintura: la primera, del
> siglo XVI; la segunda, del XVIII.

The repaired paragraph uses a hypernym (*el documento*), a pronoun (*en él*), subject ellipsis
(*descubrieron, tenía*), *la primera… la segunda*, and verb ellipsis marked by commas (*la
primera, del siglo XVI*). Translation: The archive received the codex in 2015. Since the document
was badly damaged, the restorers worked on it for a year, and discovered that it had two layers of
paint: the first from the sixteenth century, the second from the eighteenth.

![A drawing of an archive shelf with three levels and a Spanish label under each object. Top shelf: a codex folded like an accordion with colored figures (el códice) and a rolled map tied with a red ribbon (el mapa). Middle shelf: a stack of old newspapers, the top one headed El Centinela (el periódico), and a bound book open to pages of handwriting (el manuscrito). Bottom shelf: two gray archive boxes (la caja) and a paper file folder with a tab and a label (el expediente).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *Hemeroteca*: five syllables, *e-me-ro-TE-ca*; the *h* is silent.
- *Historiografía*: six syllables, *is-to-rio-gra-FÍ-a*; *rio* is one syllable, and the accent
  on *í* splits *ía*.
- *Efeméride*: five syllables, *e-fe-MÉ-ri-de*.
- *Códice*: three syllables, *CÓ-di-se*: *ce* is *se* in Latin America.
- *Fidedigno*: four syllables, *fi-de-DIG-no*; the *g* is hard and *gn* is two separate sounds, not
  the English "gn" of "sign".

## Common mistakes

- ~~*el dicho periódico*~~ → *dicho periódico*: *dicho* and *tal* take no article; *el citado* and
  *el mencionado* do.
- ~~*Dicha colección… dicha colección… dicha colección*~~: one *dicha* per paragraph is plenty;
  alternate with *este*, a synonym or ellipsis.
- *El susodicho* in a serious report: today it sounds humorous.
- *Por su parte* for a chain (A causes B, which in turn causes C): that's *a su vez*.
- Leaving out a verb without the comma that marks it: *la segunda, del XVIII*.

## Key points

- Cohesion links sentences; coherence makes the whole make sense.
- Point back with pronouns and demonstratives (*este último, el primero… el segundo, lo*), formal
  pointers (*dicho, tal* without an article; *el citado, el mencionado* with one), synonyms and
  hypernyms. *El susodicho* is humorous.
- Ellipsis drops what the reader can recover; a comma marks a missing verb.
- *Por su parte* (another participant), *a su vez* (in turn), *del mismo modo, asimismo*
  (parallel), *respectivamente*, *al respecto*, *en este sentido* organize a text.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Es cierto que…, pero: argumentation and fallacies
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 09–11 gave you the parts: connectors of contrast, cause and condition, and the devices
that keep a long text together. This lesson puts them to work in the genre that needs all of them,
the argumentative text: an opinion column, a debate contribution, an essay, a letter to the
editor. You'll learn its structure, the formulas for conceding and refuting, the kinds of argument,
and the commonest **[[fallacies]]**, arguments that look valid but aren't. At the end you write one
yourself.

The theme is animal welfare: zoos, captivity, animal testing and bullfighting. These are real
debates in Mexico and elsewhere, with serious people on every side. The lesson presents the
arguments, not a verdict, and doesn't describe any law, because the rules change often and differ
from place to place.

## The shape of an argumentative text

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The map of an argumentative text
  accDescr: Seven boxes from top to bottom. Introduction, which presents the topic and why it matters. Thesis, the position defended. Argument 1, with data. Argument 2, with an example, an authority or an analogy. Counterargument, where the writer concedes the strongest opposing point with es cierto que or si bien. Refutation, where the writer answers it with sin embargo or no es menos cierto que. Conclusion, which restates the thesis and looks ahead.
  A["Introducción: el tema y por qué importa"] --> B["Tesis: la postura que se defiende"]
  B --> C["Argumento 1: datos"]
  C --> D["Argumento 2: ejemplo, autoridad o analogía"]
  D --> E["Contraargumento: Es cierto que… / Si bien…"]
  E --> F["Refutación: Sin embargo… / No es menos cierto que…"]
  F --> G["Conclusión: la tesis, reforzada"]
```

- The **[[thesis]]** (B2's *la tesis*) is the position the text defends, stated early and clearly:
  *Sostengo que…; A mi juicio, …; Lo que defiendo es que…*
- The arguments support it. A **[[counterargument]]** is the strongest point against it; a good writer
  states it fairly and then answers it. Ignoring the other side is weaker than conceding and
  refuting.
- The conclusion restates the thesis in new words and often says what should happen next: *En
  definitiva, …; Por todo lo anterior, …*

## Conceding and refuting

Concession admits part of the other side; refutation (*la refutación*) shows why it doesn't change
the conclusion. Spanish has a set of formulas, mostly from lessons 09–10 and B2:

| Move | Formula | Mood |
|---|---|---|
| concede | *Es cierto que…; Es verdad que…; No cabe duda de que…* | indicative |
| concede | *Si bien…* (B2) | indicative |
| concede (hypothetical) | *Podría pensarse que…; Cabe pensar que…* | indicative |
| refute | *…; sin embargo, …; …, pero no es menos cierto que…; Ahora bien, …* | indicative |
| object | *Cabe objetar que…; Cabría preguntarse si…* | indicative |
| deny | *No es cierto que…; No es verdad que…* | subjunctive |

- *Es cierto que los zoológicos educan; sin embargo, eso no justifica cualquier zoológico.* — It's
  true that zoos educate; however, that doesn't justify any zoo whatsoever.
- *Si bien la experimentación con animales ha salvado vidas, no es menos cierto que hoy existen
  alternativas.* — Although animal testing has saved lives, it is no less true that alternatives
  exist today.
- *Podría pensarse que prohibir resuelve el problema, pero el abandono de animales no ha
  disminuido.* — One might think that banning solves the problem, but animal abandonment hasn't
  gone down.
- *Cabe objetar que no todos los animales sufren igual en cautiverio.* — One could object that not
  all animals suffer equally in captivity.

Note the mood: *es cierto que* states a fact (indicative), but *no es cierto que* denies one
(normally subjunctive): *No es cierto que los zoológicos sean solo negocios* (It isn't true that zoos
are only businesses). B1's *la objeción* gives the
noun; the verb is *objetar* (*objeto, objetas…*: a regular *-ar* verb).

## Strong and weak claims

How sure you sound is a choice. Strong modality closes the debate; weak modality leaves room.

- Strong: *Es evidente que…; No cabe duda de que…; Es indiscutible que…* (*indiscutible* =
  indisputable). All take the indicative.
- Middle: *Todo indica que…; Los datos sugieren que…* (indicative).
- Weak: *Cabe pensar que…; Podría pensarse que…* (indicative), *Es posible que…; Puede que…*
  (subjunctive).

A *contundente* argument (compelling, forceful) is one the other side can't easily answer; a
*convincente* one (convincing) persuades. Strong modality without strong evidence isn't
*contundente*; it's only loud. Academic writing in module 5 will use the weak end more often.

## Kinds of argument

- Data: *Según la encuesta, siete de cada diez visitantes…* — According to the survey, seven
  out of ten visitors…
- Authority (*el argumento de autoridad*): an expert's view. It's valid when the expert works
  in the field and others agree; it becomes a fallacy when the authority isn't relevant (a
  famous actor on veterinary medicine) or stands against the evidence.
- Example: one well-chosen case. It illustrates; it doesn't prove a rule.
- Analogy (*la analogía*): *Encerrar a un animal que recorre kilómetros al día es como encerrar
  a una persona en un baño.* — Locking up an animal that roams for kilometers a day is like
  locking a person in a bathroom. An analogy persuades; it's only as good as the similarity behind it.
- Consequences: *Si se cierran los zoológicos, ¿qué pasará con los animales que no pueden
  volver a la naturaleza?* — If zoos close, what will happen to the animals that can't go back
  to the wild?

## Fallacies

A fallacy (*la falacia*; the adjective is *falaz*, fallacious) is a flaw in reasoning that can
still persuade. *El sofisma* is an older word for a deliberately clever false argument, and *la
demagogia* is arguing by flattering people's fears and prejudices rather than by reasons. Here are
six to spot, with original examples:

![Six cards, each with an example of a fallacy and its name below. Card 1: No le hagas caso: él come carne, ¿qué va a saber de bienestar animal? Name: el ataque personal. Card 2: Los que critican los zoológicos quieren que todos los animales vivan sueltos por la ciudad. Name: el hombre de paja. Card 3: Mi vecino tiene un perro y lo maltrata; la gente que tiene perros no los cuida. Name: la generalización apresurada. Card 4: O tenemos zoológicos o las especies se extinguen. Name: el falso dilema. Card 5: Si hoy prohíben las corridas, mañana prohibirán comer carne y después tener mascotas. Name: la pendiente resbaladiza. Card 6: Siempre se ha hecho así; por algo será. Name: la apelación a la tradición.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

1. *El ataque personal* (*ad hominem*): attacking the person instead of the argument.
2. *El hombre de paja* (the straw man): attacking a weaker version of the other side's view.
3. *La generalización apresurada* (hasty generalization; B2's *la generalización*): a rule
   drawn from one or two cases.
4. *El falso dilema*: only two options presented when there are more.
5. *La pendiente resbaladiza* (the slippery slope): one step is said to lead, without
   evidence, to a chain of disasters.
6. *La apelación a la tradición*: something is right because it has always been done.

Naming a fallacy isn't a refutation in itself. Say what's wrong: *Eso es un falso dilema: también
existen los santuarios.* (That's a false dilemma: sanctuaries exist too.)

## Words for animal welfare

- *El bienestar animal* (B1's *el bienestar*), *el maltrato* (mistreatment) and *maltratar*,
  *la crueldad* and *cruel* (plural *crueles*), *el abandono* (abandonment, neglect: *el abandono
  de mascotas*).
- *El zoológico* (often *el zoo* in speech) and *el cautiverio* (captivity: *en cautiverio*);
  *la extinción* (B1's *en peligro de extinción*, endangered).
- *La experimentación con animales* is animal testing; *vegano* (also a noun, *el vegano, la
  vegana*) and *el vegetarianismo*.
- *La tauromaquia* is bullfighting as an art or tradition; *la corrida de toros* is one bullfight.

## Text: two sides of a debate

> *¿Deben existir los zoológicos? Dos opiniones*
>
> *Sí, pero mejores.* Es cierto que el zoológico del siglo XX, con jaulas de cemento y animales
> aburridos, tenía poco que ver con el bienestar animal. Sin embargo, juzgar los zoológicos de hoy
> por los de ayer es injusto. Los mejores trabajan con universidades, financian proyectos de
> conservación y crían en cautiverio especies que ya casi no existen en libertad. El lobo
> mexicano, que llegó a desaparecer del medio silvestre, ha vuelto a algunas zonas gracias a
> ejemplares criados en cautiverio. Muchos zoológicos, además, reciben animales heridos o
> decomisados al tráfico ilegal que ya no podrían sobrevivir solos; cerrarlos de golpe no los
> liberaría, sino que los dejaría sin hogar. Asimismo, millones de niños ven por primera vez un animal
> salvaje en un zoológico, y muchos biólogos cuentan que su vocación empezó ahí. Podría pensarse
> que basta con los documentales, pero una pantalla no despierta el mismo respeto que un animal
> real. Si bien hay zoológicos que deberían cerrar, la solución no es eliminarlos todos, sino
> exigir normas estrictas, inspecciones y espacios adecuados para cada especie. Al fin y al cabo,
> o tenemos zoológicos o aceptamos que muchas especies desaparezcan.
>
> *No: el cautiverio no es conservación.* Nadie duda de las buenas intenciones de muchos
> zoológicos. Ahora bien, las intenciones no cambian un hecho: un elefante que en libertad
> recorre muchos kilómetros al día pasa su vida en unos cuantos miles de metros cuadrados. Los
> veterinarios describen en muchos animales en cautiverio movimientos repetitivos, señal de
> estrés. Es verdad que algunos programas de cría han tenido éxito; no es menos cierto que la
> mayoría de los animales exhibidos no pertenece a especies en peligro, sino a las que más
> público atraen. Además, la cría en cautiverio solo tiene sentido si existe un hábitat al que
> devolver a los animales; sin él, se crían ejemplares destinados a vivir siempre detrás de un
> vidrio. Se dice que el zoológico educa, pero ¿qué aprende un niño al ver a un oso
> caminar en círculos? Cabe objetar que sin zoológicos se perdería dinero para la conservación;
> por el contrario, ese dinero podría ir directamente a proteger hábitats y a santuarios que no
> exhiben a los animales. Por cierto, quienes defienden los zoológicos suelen ser los mismos que
> viven de ellos.

Summary: *Yes, but better:* The cement-cage zoo of the twentieth century had little to do with
welfare, but today's best zoos work with universities, fund conservation and breed species nearly
gone from the wild; the Mexican wolf, once gone from the wild, has returned to some areas from
captive-bred animals. Zoos inspire children and future biologists, and screens don't create the
same respect. Many also take in injured or confiscated animals that couldn't survive alone. Some zoos should
close; the answer is strict rules and inspections, not closing all.
*No:* Good intentions don't change the fact that an elephant that walks many kilometers a day
lives in a small space; vets describe repetitive movements, a sign of stress. Some breeding
programs work, but most animals shown are crowd-pleasers, not endangered species, and breeding makes sense only
if there's a habitat to return them to. The money could
go to habitats and sanctuaries that don't exhibit animals.

(*tener poco que ver con* — to have little to do with; *la conservación* — conservation; *criar* — to breed, raise; *el medio
silvestre* — the wild; *el ejemplar* — specimen; *al fin y al cabo* — after all; *exhibir* — to
display; *decomisado* — confiscated; *de golpe* — all at once; *por cierto* — by the way.) Each piece follows the map: thesis, arguments, a conceded
counterargument (*Es cierto que…; Es verdad que…*), refutation (*Sin embargo…; no es menos cierto
que…*). And each ends with a fallacy. The first closes with a false dilemma (zoos or extinction,
as if protecting habitats weren't an option); the second with a personal attack (defenders of
zoos make a living from them, which says nothing about their arguments). Spotting both is part of
reading fairly.

## Pronunciation

- *Tauromaquia*: four syllables, *tau-ro-MA-quia*; *au* and *ia* are each one syllable, and *qu*
  is *k*.
- *Demagogia*: four syllables, *de-ma-GO-gia*; the second *g*, before *i*, is the breathy *j*.
- *Falaz, falaces*: *fa-LAS, fa-LA-ses*: in Latin America *z* and *ce* sound like *s*.
- *Contundente*: four syllables, *con-tun-DEN-te*.

## Common mistakes

- *No es cierto que los zoológicos son negocios*: the indicative is heard, but careful writing
  uses *No es cierto que sean*: a denied claim normally takes the subjunctive.
- Conceding without refuting: *Es cierto que…* must be followed by your answer (*sin embargo, …*),
  or you've argued the other side.
- Calling every argument from authority a fallacy: it's a fallacy only when the authority is
  irrelevant or contradicted by the evidence.
- *Argumento* for a quarrel: B1's *el argumento* is a reason (or a plot); a quarrel is *una
  discusión* or *un pleito*.
- Naming a fallacy instead of answering it: explain what's missing.

## Key points

- An argumentative text: introduction, thesis, arguments (data, authority, example, analogy,
  consequences), the strongest counterargument conceded and refuted, and a conclusion.
- Concede: *Es cierto que…, Si bien…, Podría pensarse que…*; refute: *sin embargo, no es menos
  cierto que, ahora bien*; object: *Cabe objetar que…*. *No es cierto que* + subjunctive.
- Strong (*Es evidente que, Es indiscutible que*, "it is indisputable that") vs weak modality (*Cabe pensar que, Es posible
  que* + subjunctive): match it to your evidence.
- Six fallacies: the personal attack, the straw man, hasty generalization, the false dilemma, the
  slippery slope, the appeal to tradition.

## Your turn: write an argumentative text

Use the two pieces above as models of structure, not of opinion. The task below is graded by your
teacher or parent with a rubric; you can rate your own draft against it first. Choose one topic,
take the side you find stronger, and before handing it in check your text against this list: a
thesis in the first paragraph; at least two kinds of argument; the strongest counterargument
conceded and refuted; at least three connectors from lessons 09–10, set off by commas; reference
devices from lesson 11 instead of repeated nouns; no fallacy.

```assignment
writing: es5-m3-argumentative
```

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Retórica: the figures of a good speech
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 12 was about argument: a thesis, reasons, a counterargument answered. A speech needs all
that and something more, because listeners can't reread. They need patterns they can hear, images
they can picture and moments that move them. The art of building those is *la retórica*
(rhetoric), and its tools are the **[[figures of speech]]** (*las figuras retóricas*): ways of
arranging or bending words to make them stick.

This honors lesson covers the classical parts of a speech, the three kinds of appeal the Greeks
named, and the figures you'll hear most in Spanish speeches: **[[anaphora]]**, **[[antithesis]]**,
enumeration and climax, **[[hyperbole]]**, the **[[rhetorical question]]**, the simile beside B1's *la
metáfora*, and **[[irony]]**, which module 1 introduced. Then you'll analyze an original graduation
speech figure by figure and rewrite a flat speech into a better one.

## Three appeals and four parts

In the fourth century BC, Aristotle's *Rhetoric* described three ways a speaker persuades. In
plain terms:

- *ethos*: the speaker's credibility (why should we listen to you?);
- *pathos*: the listeners' emotions (why should we care?);
- *logos*: the reasons and evidence (why is it true?).

A good speech uses all three; a personal story is often *ethos* and *pathos* at once.

Roman teachers of rhetoric, from Cicero in the first century BC to Quintilian in the first century
AD, divided a speech into parts. Spanish textbooks still use their Latin-based names:

![A speech's structure drawn as four stacked blocks. Exordio, at the top: greet, win the audience's goodwill, announce the topic. Narración: tell the facts or the story. Argumentación: prove your thesis and refute the objections. Peroración, at the bottom: sum up and move the audience. A side bar shows where each appeal weighs most: ethos at the start, logos in the middle, pathos at the end.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

1. *El exordio* (opening): greet, earn goodwill, announce the topic.
2. *La narración*: the facts or the story.
3. *La argumentación*: the proof and the answers to objections (lesson 12's structure).
4. *La peroración* (closing): a summary and an emotional appeal.

## The figures

- Anaphora (*la anáfora*): repeating a word or phrase at the start of successive sentences or
  clauses. *Aprendimos a dudar. Aprendimos a preguntar. Aprendimos a equivocarnos.* (We learned to
  doubt. We learned to ask. We learned to be wrong.) It creates a rhythm the ear can follow, which
  is why it's the speech figure par excellence. Martin Luther King Jr.'s speech at the March on
  Washington (August 28, 1963) is the best-known modern example in English.
- Antithesis (*la antítesis*, plural *las antítesis*): opposed ideas in parallel form. *No
  vinimos a recibir respuestas, sino a aprender a buscarlas.* (We didn't come to receive answers,
  but to learn to look for them.) Lesson 09's *no… sino* is its natural engine.
- Enumeration and climax: a list that grows in force, ending on the strongest item: *Nos dieron un salón, una biblioteca, un laboratorio… y una segunda oportunidad* (They gave us a
  classroom, a library, a lab… and a second chance).
- Hyperbole (*la hipérbole*): deliberate exaggeration that no one takes literally: *Subimos esa escalera un millón de veces* (We climbed
  those stairs a million times).
- Rhetorical question (*la pregunta retórica*): a question asked for effect, with an obvious
  answer: *¿Quién de nosotros no llegó tarde alguna vez?* (Which of us never arrived late?) Cicero's speeches against Catiline (63
  BC) are a classic case: the first of them opens with a string of them.
- Simile (*el símil*) and B1's *la metáfora*: a simile compares with *como* (*La escuela fue
  como un puerto*), a metaphor identifies (*La escuela fue nuestro puerto*).
- Irony: saying the opposite of what you mean, so the audience smiles: *Gracias, cafetería, por enseñarnos a sobrevivir* (Thank you,
  cafeteria, for teaching us to survive).

A speaker with *elocuencia* (eloquence) uses figures so naturally that the audience notices the
effect, not the technique. An *elocuente* speech isn't one stuffed with figures; it's one where
each figure does a job. *Retórico* means "of rhetoric" (*un recurso retórico*), but in everyday
speech it can also mean "empty, just words": *Eso es pura retórica* (That's just talk).

Spanish-language speeches you can look up and listen for these figures include Lázaro Cárdenas's
radio message announcing the oil expropriation (March 18, 1938) and the Nobel lectures of the
Literature laureates, published on the Nobel Prize website (Gabriel García Márquez, 1982;
Octavio Paz, 1990). Read or listen to them, and name the figures yourself.

## The speech

> *Discurso de graduación, preparatoria Benito Juárez, generación 2023–2026*
>
> Maestras, maestros, familias, compañeras y compañeros: buenas noches.
>
> Hace tres años, el primer día de clases, me perdí buscando el salón 14. Di tres vueltas al
> edificio, subí y bajé la misma escalera y, cuando por fin llegué, la maestra Rosales ya había
> pasado lista. Esa noche le dije a mi mamá que no iba a durar ni una semana. Hoy estoy aquí, con
> toga y birrete, y todavía no sé muy bien dónde está el salón 14. Pero sí sé otras cosas.
>
> Aprendimos a dudar. Aprendimos a preguntar. Aprendimos a equivocarnos sin que el mundo se
> acabara. Y aprendimos, sobre todo, que nadie llega solo a ningún lado.
>
> ¿Quién de nosotros no llegó tarde alguna vez? ¿Quién no se desveló estudiando para un examen que
> luego resultó más fácil de lo que temía? ¿Quién no pensó, al menos un lunes, en dejarlo todo?
> Y, sin embargo, aquí estamos.
>
> No vinimos a esta escuela a recibir respuestas, sino a aprender a buscarlas. Llegamos como
> desconocidos y nos vamos como amigos; llegamos con miedo y nos vamos con planes. Algunos
> estudiarán medicina, otros diseño, otros se irán a trabajar con su familia. Ningún camino es
> pequeño si se recorre con ganas.
>
> Esta escuela fue como un puerto: un lugar donde reparar las velas antes de salir al mar. Nos dio
> un salón, una biblioteca, un laboratorio, unos maestros que se quedaban después de la hora… y,
> a muchos, una segunda oportunidad. Gracias, maestra Rosales, por no rendirse con el grupo C,
> aunque el grupo C hizo todo lo posible para que se rindiera. Gracias, señor Tomás, por abrir la
> puerta a las siete en punto, llueva o truene, durante treinta años. Y gracias, cafetería, por
> enseñarnos a sobrevivir.
>
> Dicen que los números no mienten, así que les doy algunos. En tres años leímos cuarenta y dos
> libros, entregamos más de doscientas tareas y presentamos doce proyectos ante el público; uno de
> ellos, sobre el agua de la colonia, hoy lo usa el ayuntamiento. Perdimos, eso sí, todos los
> partidos de futbol contra los maestros. Los números, como ven, tampoco lo dicen todo.
>
> A nuestras familias les debemos más de lo que cabe en un discurso. Ustedes madrugaron con
> nosotros, nos esperaron en la puerta, nos repitieron un millón de veces que hiciéramos la tarea.
> Algunos de ustedes no pudieron terminar la escuela; por eso este papel que hoy recibimos también
> es suyo.
>
> Compañeros: el mundo que nos espera no es fácil. Hay quien dice que nuestra generación no sabe
> esforzarse, que solo vive pegada al celular. Ahora bien, yo vi a esta generación organizar una
> colecta cuando se inundó la colonia del Río, dar clases a niños de primaria en vacaciones y
> estudiar de noche después de trabajar todo el día. No somos la generación que se rinde; somos la
> generación que pregunta.
>
> Así que esta noche no les deseo que todo les salga bien. Les deseo algo mejor: que cuando algo
> les salga mal, recuerden la escalera, recuerden el salón 14, recuerden que una vez llegaron
> tarde y aun así llegaron.
>
> Muchas gracias.

Summary: (1–2) The speaker greets teachers, families and classmates, and recalls getting lost
on the first day, three years ago, looking for room 14; she still doesn't know where it is, but
she knows other things. (3) They learned to doubt, ask, be wrong, and that nobody gets anywhere
alone. (4) Who never arrived late, stayed up for an easy exam, or thought of quitting? Yet here
they are. (5) They came to learn to look for answers; they arrived as strangers and leave as
friends, with different paths ahead, none small. (6) The school was like a port; she thanks a
teacher who never gave up on group C, the janitor who opened the door for thirty years, and the
cafeteria. (7) Numbers: forty-two books, over two hundred assignments, twelve public projects (one
now used by the town council), and every soccer game lost to the teachers. (8) Families deserve
more than a speech can hold; the diploma is theirs too. (9) People
say this generation doesn't try hard; she has seen it raise money after a flood, tutor children
and study after work. (10) She wishes them not that all goes well, but that when it doesn't, they
remember they once arrived late and still arrived.

(*pasar lista* — to take attendance; *la toga y el birrete* — gown and mortarboard; *desvelarse* —
to stay up late; *las velas* — sails; *llueva o truene* — come rain or shine; *madrugar* — to get
up early; *la colecta* — fund-raiser.)

## Worked examples

### Example 1: analyzing the speech figure by figure

Go part by part and name what each passage does.

- *Exordio* (paragraphs 1–2). The greeting lists the audience in rising closeness. The anecdote
  of room 14 builds *ethos* through self-deprecating humor: the speaker is one of them, not above
  them. The last line (*Pero sí sé otras cosas*) is lesson 09's *pero sí*, turning the joke into
  the theme.
- *Narración* (paragraphs 3–4). Anaphora: *Aprendimos a…* three times, then a fourth with
  *sobre todo* that breaks the pattern for emphasis. Then three rhetorical questions with
  *¿Quién…?*, a second anaphora, answered by *Y, sin embargo, aquí estamos*.
- *Argumentación* (paragraphs 5–9). Antithesis with *no… sino* and with parallel pairs
  (*como desconocidos / como amigos; con miedo / con planes*). A simile (*como un puerto*)
  extended into a metaphor (*reparar las velas*). Enumeration and climax: *un salón, una
  biblioteca, un laboratorio… y una segunda oportunidad*, the strongest item last after a pause.
  Irony: *gracias, cafetería, por enseñarnos a sobrevivir*. Paragraph 7 offers *logos* in numbers
  and then undercuts it with a joke. Hyperbole: *un millón de veces*. In paragraph 9 she states a counterargument (*Hay quien dice que…*), refutes it with
  *ahora bien* and three examples (*logos*), and closes with another antithesis.
- *Peroración* (paragraph 10). A surprise (*no les deseo que todo les salga bien*), a triple
  anaphora (*recuerden…*), and a return to the opening anecdote, which ties the speech into a
  circle. This is *pathos*: the audience leaves with an image, not a statistic.

### Example 2: rewriting a flat speech

Here is a flat closing for the same event, and a rewrite.

> *Bueno, ya terminamos la prepa. Fue difícil, pero lo logramos. Gracias a los maestros y a los
> papás. Espero que nos vaya bien a todos en el futuro. Gracias.*

> *Terminamos la prepa. No fue fácil; por eso vale tanto. Gracias a los maestros, que nos
> enseñaron a pensar; gracias a nuestras familias, que nos enseñaron a no rendirnos. No sé qué
> nos espera, pero sé con quién aprendí a enfrentarlo.*

Translation of the flat version: Well, we've finished high school. It was hard, but we made it.
Thanks to the teachers and parents. I hope things go well for all of us in the future. Thanks.
Translation of the rewrite: We've finished high school. It wasn't easy; that's why it means so
much. Thanks to the teachers, who taught us to think; thanks to our families, who taught us not to
give up. I don't know what lies ahead, but I know who I learned to face it with.

What changed: the filler *bueno* is gone (module 1); the plain contrast became an argument (*No
fue fácil; por eso vale tanto*); the thanks became an anaphora (*gracias a…*) with a parallel
relative clause for each group; and the vague wish became an antithesis (*No sé qué… pero sé
con quién*). It is barely longer, but every sentence does a job.

## Pronunciation

- *Hipérbole*: four syllables, *i-PÉR-bo-le*, stressed on the second; the *h* is silent.
- *Anáfora*: four syllables, *a-NÁ-fo-ra*.
- *Antítesis*: four syllables, *an-TÍ-te-sis*; the plural is the same.
- *Elocuencia*: four syllables, *e-lo-CUEN-cia*; *cuen* and *cia* are one syllable each.
- *Símil*: two syllables, *SÍ-mil*.

## Common mistakes

- *La hipérbola* for hyperbole: *la hipérbola* is the curve in geometry; the figure is *la
  hipérbole*.
- Overloading: a figure in every sentence sounds like a parody. Save anaphora for a key moment.
- A rhetorical question that the audience might answer the wrong way: *¿Alguien aquí cree que fue fácil?* (Does anyone here think it was easy?) can get a laugh and a "yes".
- Quoting a famous speech instead of writing your own lines: name it, date it, and say what the
  speaker did.
- *Retórica* as only a compliment: in everyday speech *pura retórica* means empty words.

## Key points

- Classical parts: *exordio, narración, argumentación, peroración*. Three appeals: *ethos*
  (credibility), *pathos* (emotion), *logos* (reasons).
- Figures: anaphora (*la anáfora*), antithesis (*la antítesis*), enumeration and climax, hyperbole
  (*la hipérbole*), the rhetorical question (*la pregunta retórica*), simile (*el símil*) and
  metaphor, irony.
- *Elocuencia* is figures that serve the message; *pura retórica* is words without one.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Entre dos lenguas: false friends, calques and mediating
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 09–12 were about building a text in Spanish. This honors lesson is about the moment when a
text crosses from English into Spanish, or back: when you translate a sign for a visitor, answer an
e-mail for a colleague, or adapt a web page for Mexican customers. At C1 that's a real skill,
and the DELE C1 tests it under the name of mediation: passing on what a text means, for a given
reader, rather than what each word says.

Three dangers wait at that crossing. **[[False friends]]** are words that look alike in both languages
but mean different things. The **[[calque]]**, from lesson 03 (*el calco*), copies an English pattern
word for word. And literal translation in general (*literal, literalmente*) keeps the words and
loses the sense. This lesson covers all three, explains the difference between translating and
**[[interpreting]]**, introduces **[[localization]]**, and works through two real-world tasks.

## Classic false friends

You met most of these Spanish words years ago; the trap is the English word they resemble.

| Spanish | Means | The English look-alike is… |
|---|---|---|
| *actual* (A1) | current, present-day | actual → *real, verdadero*; actually → *en realidad* |
| *eventual* | possible, contingent; temporary (*un trabajo eventual*) | eventual → *final*; eventually → *con el tiempo, al final* |
| *sensible* (B1) | sensitive | sensible → *sensato* |
| *la librería* (A1) | bookstore | library → *la biblioteca* |
| *el éxito* (A1) | success | exit → *la salida* |
| *embarazada* (A1) | pregnant | embarrassed → *avergonzado*; in Mexico *me da pena* |
| *constipado* (Spain) | having a cold | constipated → *estreñido* |

A few notes. *Eventualmente* means "possibly" or "now and then" in careful usage; its use for
"eventually, in the end" spreads under English influence, but careful writing still avoids it.
*Estar constipado* is the usual Spanish of Spain for a cold; in Mexico people usually say *tener
gripa* or *estar resfriado*, and *constipado* is less common there and understood in different
ways (a cold, a stuffy nose), so avoid it. And *me da pena* means "I'm embarrassed" in Mexico
and much of Latin America; *dar pena* also means "to make someone sad or sorry" (*Me da pena
verlo así*, It makes me sad to see him like that), and in Spain that is its usual sense.

## Partial false friends

The harder cases are words whose meanings overlap with English in part.

- A2's *asistir* usually means to attend: *Asistí a la conferencia* (I attended the lecture). It
  can also mean to help, in fixed contexts: *asistir a un herido* (to aid an injured person), *la
  asistencia técnica* (technical support). To assist someone with a task is usually *ayudar*.
- B2's *soportar* is to put up with (*No soporto el ruido*) or to bear a load (*Las columnas
  soportan el techo*). To support a cause, a team or a person is B1's *apoyar*.
- A1's *realizar* is to carry out (*realizar un estudio*); *realizarse* is to fulfill oneself. To
  realize, in the sense of becoming aware, is A1's *darse cuenta*: using *realizar* for it is a
  calque that careful usage avoids.

When in doubt, check the word in a monolingual dictionary such as the DLE (dle.rae.es): if none of
its senses fits, it's a false friend.

![A chart of six false-friend pairs. Each row shows an English word on the left, the tempting Spanish look-alike crossed out in the middle, and the right Spanish word on the right. Library: librería crossed out, biblioteca. Exit: éxito crossed out, salida. Embarrassed: embarazada crossed out, avergonzado or me da pena. Sensible: sensible crossed out, sensato. Actually: actualmente crossed out, en realidad. Eventually: eventualmente crossed out, al final or con el tiempo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Calques

A calque copies an English structure into Spanish words. Some are now standard; others still
sound translated:

- *tomar lugar* (take place) → *tener lugar*: *La reunión tendrá lugar el lunes* (The meeting will take
  place on Monday).
- *hacer sentido* (make sense) → *tener sentido*: *Eso no tiene sentido* (That makes no sense). *Hacer sentido* is heard,
  especially from speakers in daily contact with English, but careful writing prefers *tener sentido*.
- *Estar supuesto a* (be supposed to) → *deber, tener que* or *se supone que*: *Se supone que llegan a las ocho* (They're supposed to arrive at
  eight).

## Translating, interpreting, localizing

Interpreting (*la interpretación*) is oral: *el intérprete* or *la intérprete* renders speech,
either while the speaker talks (*interpretación simultánea*, at conferences, in booths) or after
each segment (*interpretación consecutiva*, in courts, hospitals and meetings). Translating (*la
traducción*) is written. *El intérprete* also means a performer, a singer or an actor, which goes
with B1's *interpretar* (to play a role).

Localization (*la localización*) adapts a product, a website or a game to a market: not just
the language but the currency, units, date format, examples, images, legal notices and register.
A US site localized for Mexico uses pesos, centimeters and kilos, day-month-year dates, Mexican
words (*el celular, la computadora*) and, often, *usted* or a friendly *tú* depending on the brand.
*La localización* also has its everyday sense, location (*la localización del celular*).

Both depend on equivalence (*la equivalencia*): finding the expression with the same effect,
which may share no words with the original. An idiom has a literal sense and a figurative sense
(*el sentido figurado*); you translate the figurative one. "It's a piece of cake" is B1's *es pan
comido*; "It's not my cup of tea" is *no es lo mío*. A translator keeps a glossary (*el glosario*)
of agreed equivalents, so that one English term is always rendered the same way in a project.

Signs show the same principle in a few words. Spanish signs use their own fixed formulas, often an
infinitive or a noun, rather than a translation of the English: "Wet floor" is *Piso mojado* (in
Spain *Suelo mojado*); "No trespassing" is *Prohibido el paso* or *Propiedad privada*; "Please do
not feed the animals" is *Prohibido alimentar a los animales* or *No alimente a los animales*.
Look at what a Mexican sign says in the same situation and use that.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: localizing a product page for Mexico

The English page of an online store:

> *Trail backpack, 30 L. Weighs just 2.1 lb. Free shipping on orders over 50 dollars. Order by
> 11/20 for delivery before the holidays. Pay in 4 interest-free installments.*

A word-for-word version would keep pounds, dollars and the US date, and would read as foreign.
The localized version:

> *Mochila para senderismo, 30 litros. Pesa solo 950 gramos. Envío gratis en compras de más de
> 900 pesos. Haz tu pedido antes del 20 de noviembre y recíbela antes de las fiestas. Paga a
> meses sin intereses.*

Decisions: pounds became grams (2.1 lb is about 950 g); the free-shipping threshold became a
round figure in pesos chosen by the store, not a converted 50 dollars; 11/20 became *20 de
noviembre*, since 11/20 would be read as day 11 of month 20; "the holidays" became *las fiestas*;
and the installment offer became *meses sin intereses*, the usual form of that offer in Mexico.
*Haz tu pedido* uses the friendly *tú* many Mexican stores use online. Translation of the localized
version: Hiking backpack, 30 liters. Weighs only 950 grams. Free shipping on purchases over 900
pesos. Order before November 20 and get it before the holidays. Pay in interest-free monthly
installments.

### Example 2: mediating an English e-mail into a Spanish summary

Your Mexican colleague Daniela doesn't read English and asks what a US partner wrote:

> *Hi team, quick heads-up: the shipment's been pushed back a week because of the port strike.
> We're still on track for the launch, but it's going to be tight. Could you double-check that
> the Spanish labels are final by Friday? Thanks a ton, Mark.*

A literal translation (*Hola equipo, rápido aviso por adelantado: el envío ha sido empujado
atrás una semana…*) is unreadable. Daniela needs the content, in her register:

> *Daniela: Mark escribe que el envío se retrasó una semana por la huelga en el puerto. Dice que
> el lanzamiento sigue en pie, aunque con el tiempo justo, y pide que confirmemos a más tardar el
> viernes que las etiquetas en español ya están listas.*
