What changed: the greeting, the thanks and the colloquial "heads-up" were dropped, because the
summary reports, not translates; "pushed back" became *se retrasó*, "still on track" *sigue en
pie*, and "tight" *con el tiempo justo*; *el lanzamiento* (the launch, lesson 22's word) stayed; the request became reported speech with *pide que* +
subjunctive (B2); and the deadline was kept exactly, because it's the one fact Daniela must act on.
Translation of the summary: Daniela: Mark writes that the shipment was delayed a week because of
the port strike. He says the launch is still on, although tight on time, and asks us to confirm by
Friday at the latest that the Spanish labels are ready.

## Pronunciation

- *Intérprete*: four syllables, *in-TÉR-pre-te*, stressed on the second.
- *Equivalencia*: five syllables, *e-qui-va-LEN-cia*; *qui* is *ki*.
- *Literalmente*: five syllables, *li-te-ral-MEN-te*; the *l* of *ral* closes its syllable.
- *Localización*: five syllables, *lo-ca-li-za-CIÓN*; *z* is *s* in Latin America.

## Common mistakes

- *Estoy muy embarazada* for "I'm very embarrassed": say *Me da mucha pena* (Mexico) or *Estoy
  muy avergonzada*.
- *Realicé que…* for "I realized that…": say *Me di cuenta de que…*.
- *Una persona muy sensible* for "a very sensible person": that's *sensata*; *sensible* is
  sensitive.
- Translating every word of an e-mail: mediation keeps what the reader needs and drops the rest.
- *Interpretación* for a written translation: *la interpretación* is oral (or an interpretation of
  meaning); the written one is *la traducción*.
- Converting a price instead of localizing it: a store sets prices for each market.

## Key points

- False friends: *actual, eventual, sensible, librería, éxito, embarazada, constipado*; partial
  ones: *asistir, soportar, realizar*. Check the DLE when in doubt.
- Calques copy an English pattern: *tener lugar*, not *tomar lugar*; *tener sentido* in careful
  writing.
- Interpreting is oral (simultaneous or consecutive), translating written; localization adapts a
  product to a market.
- Translate the figurative sense, keep a glossary, and in mediation give the reader what they need.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Hablar hasta por los codos: idioms for people and behavior
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In B1 lesson 21 you met your first **[[idioms]]**: *meter la pata, tomar el pelo, echar la mano,
ponerse las pilas, echarle ganas*. At C1 the question changes: not only what an idiom means, but
how it behaves in a sentence, where it's said (Mexico, Spain or everywhere), how formal it is, and
when it's one too many. This module (13 to 16) is about the fixed parts of Spanish: idioms,
sayings, verbs with their own preposition, and words that like to go together.

This lesson's idioms describe people: those who talk too much, keep secrets badly, lose their
temper or play dumb. The theme is gossip and reputation in an apartment building, so B1's *el
chisme* (a piece of gossip), *chismear* and *el rumor* come back often.

## How an idiom behaves in a sentence

An idiom is fixed, but not frozen: the verb conjugates and pronouns attach as usual, in any tense
or mood (*Ojalá demos en el clavo* — I hope we get it exactly right). Four patterns need care:

1. Some take a person as an object: *Le echó en cara que nunca la visitaba* (She threw it in his
   face that he never visited her); *A mi papá lo saca de quicio el tráfico* (Traffic drives my
   dad up the wall).
2. In some the thing is the subject, like B2's accidental *se*: *Se me fue la lengua* (I let it
   slip), *Se le fue la lengua a Rosa*. The dictionary form *írsele* shows this.
3. A possessive agrees with the person: *No doy mi brazo a torcer* (I won't give in).
4. An adjective agrees too: *No te hagas la tonta* (Don't play dumb, to a woman).

| Idiom | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *dar la cara* | ordinary verb | *Fer vino a dar la cara.* — Fer came to face the music. |
| *morderse la lengua* | reflexive | *Me mordí la lengua.* — I bit my tongue. |
| *sacar de quicio* | direct object | *Me saca de quicio.* — It drives me up the wall. |
| *echar en cara* | indirect object | *Le echó en cara su indiscreción.* — She threw his indiscretion in his face. |
| *írsele la lengua* | thing as subject | *Se me fue la lengua.* — I let it slip. |
| *hacerse el tonto* | agreeing adjective | *Se hicieron los tontos.* — They played dumb. |
| *no dar su brazo a torcer* | agreeing possessive | *No dimos nuestro brazo a torcer.* — We didn't budge. |

## Mexico, Spain or everywhere?

Most of these idioms are general Spanish, but a few belong to one side of the Atlantic, and
dictionaries don't always record what people say.

- Inseparable friends: in Mexico two friends who are always together *son uña y mugre* ("nail and
  dirt"). The DLE and the *Diccionario del español de México* (DEM) record only *ser uña y carne*
  ("nail and flesh"), the general form, usual in Spain and also used in Mexico. In a 2019 study by Carmen
  Fajardo Rojas (El Colegio de México), most of 800 Mexican speakers completed the phrase with
  *mugre*. Both are correct, and both are understood in Mexico.
- Turning a blind eye: the DLE gives *hacer la vista gorda*; in Mexico you'll often hear *hacerse
  de la vista gorda*: *El policía se hizo de la vista gorda*. Both are correct.
- Talking nonstop: the dictionary form is *hablar por los codos*; Mexicans usually add *hasta*.
- Fed up: *estar hasta el gorro* has no country mark in the DLE (only "colloquial"), but it's one
  of the most common ways to say it in Mexico. You'll also hear *estar hasta la coronilla* and,
  especially in Spain, *estar hasta las narices*.
- Gossip: Spain also says *el cotilleo* and *cotillear*, colloquially; in Mexico the words are *el
  chisme* and *chismear*, which are understood everywhere.

## Idioms that work as adverbs

Some idioms describe how something happens. They're often neutral enough for writing.

| Idiom | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *a regañadientes* | grudgingly | *Aceptó a regañadientes.* — He grudgingly accepted. |
| *de mala gana* | unwillingly | *Nos atendió de mala gana.* — She served us reluctantly. |
| *de buenas a primeras* | out of the blue | *De buenas a primeras, renunció.* — Out of the blue, he quit. |
| *en un abrir y cerrar de ojos* | in the blink of an eye | *Se acabó en un abrir y cerrar de ojos.* — It was over in the blink of an eye. |
| *al pie de la letra* | to the letter | *Siga las instrucciones al pie de la letra.* — Follow the instructions to the letter. |
| *a ciegas* | blindly | *No compres a ciegas.* — Don't buy blind. |
| *en carne propia* | firsthand | *Lo viví en carne propia.* — I experienced it firsthand. |

*A regañadientes* ("scolding with your teeth") and *de mala gana* both describe doing something you
don't want to do; the first adds grumbling resistance, the second the bad mood you do it in.

## Literal and figurative

Many idioms are easier to remember once you see the picture inside them. *Hablar hasta por los
codos* imagines someone talking so much that the words come out of their elbows. *Estar hasta el
gorro* imagines being filled up to your cap.

![A two-by-two grid. Top row, hablar hasta por los codos: on the left, the literal picture, a woman with speech bubbles coming out of her elbows; on the right, the figurative meaning, a woman talking nonstop while a man beside her looks bored and half asleep. Bottom row, estar hasta el gorro: on the left, a man standing in a tank filled with water up to his cap, marked full; on the right, a frowning man at a desk beside a tall pile of papers, saying ¡Ya basta! (That's enough!).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Others hide a picture you need to be told about. *El quicio* is the part of a door frame the door
turns on, so *sacar de quicio* is to force someone off their hinges. *Tener cara de pocos amigos*
is to have "a face of few friends": a look that keeps people away.

## Register: can it go in a formal e-mail?

Most idioms are informal, but not all. Some are neutral and appear in newspapers and even in
reports: *dar la cara, dar en el clavo, al pie de la letra, a ciegas, en carne propia, de buenas a
primeras, en un abrir y cerrar de ojos*. *Poner el grito en el cielo* (to hit the roof) is common
in the press: *Los comerciantes pusieron el grito en el cielo*. The rest of this lesson's idioms
(*hablar hasta por los codos, estar hasta el gorro, sacar de quicio, írsele la lengua, hacerse el
tonto, ser uña y mugre, tener cara de pocos amigos*) belong to conversation and informal writing.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Should I use this idiom?
  accDescr: A decision chart. First question: is the text formal, such as a report or an e-mail to a client? If no, informal idioms are fine, but use at most one or two per paragraph. If yes, second question: is the idiom neutral, such as dar la cara or al pie de la letra? If yes, it can stay. If no, replace it with its plain meaning, for example estoy hasta el gorro becomes la situación ya no es sostenible.
  A["Is the text formal? (a report, an e-mail to a client)"] -->|no| B["Informal idioms are fine: at most one or two per paragraph"]
  A -->|yes| C["Is the idiom neutral? (dar la cara, al pie de la letra)"]
  C -->|yes| D[It can stay]
  C -->|no| E["Use the plain meaning: la situación ya no es sostenible"]
```

Don't stack idioms: *Estoy hasta el gorro, me saca de quicio y se le va la lengua* sounds like a
phrasebook, not a person. Use them like salt, one in the right place. In a formal e-mail, instead
of *Estoy hasta el gorro de los retrasos*, write *Los retrasos ya no son aceptables* (The delays
are no longer acceptable).

## Recognizing an idiom you've never heard

At C1 you'll meet idioms you don't know, in conversation and on the exam: the Instituto Cervantes
describes the last listening task of the DELE C1 as a set of short everyday dialogues, each
testing what an idiomatic or colloquial expression means and why the speaker uses it. Three clues
help:

1. The literal meaning is absurd: nobody's elbows talk, so look for a figurative one.
2. The reaction tells you the tone: if the other speaker laughs, apologizes or protests, the
   idiom was a joke, an accusation or a complaint.
3. What follows often explains it: *Me quedé con la boca abierta: no lo podía creer.* The
   second half (I couldn't believe it) tells you the first half means "I was speechless".

## Reading: a radio soap

*Edificio Jacarandas* is a fictional radio soap set in a Mexico City apartment building. *El
inquilino* is the tenant, *el administrador* the building manager, *atrasarse con la renta* to fall
behind on the rent, and *mija* (from *mi hija*) an affectionate "dear".

```dialogue
# Edificio Jacarandas, episodio 14
Narrador: Son las ocho de la mañana en el Edificio Jacarandas. Como cada lunes, doña Rosa ya está en el pasillo con su escoba, aunque todos saben que barre poco y platica mucho.
Doña Rosa: ¡Buenos días, Marisol! ¿Ya supiste lo del 302? Dicen que el nuevo inquilino no ha pagado la renta en tres meses. Y no lo digo yo, ¿eh? Lo dice todo el edificio.
Marisol: Ay, doña Rosa, usted sí habla hasta por los codos. ¿Quién le contó eso?
Doña Rosa: Bueno… se me fue la lengua. Me lo dijo don Chema, el administrador, pero me pidió que no dijera nada.
Narrador: Marisol se muerde la lengua. Ella y Fer, la del 205, son uña y mugre desde la secundaria, y sabe muy bien que el inquilino nuevo es el hermano de Fer. El señor Íñigo, el madrileño del 101, diría que en este edificio no hay chismes, sino «cotilleo».
Marisol: Mire, yo no sé nada. Pero no repita esos chismes: una reputación se pierde en un abrir y cerrar de ojos.
Narrador: En ese momento baja don Chema, con cara de pocos amigos.
Don Chema: Doña Rosa, ¿usted anda diciendo que el del 302 no paga? ¡Ya estoy hasta el gorro de los rumores en este edificio! Me saca de quicio que alguien sea tan indiscreto.
Doña Rosa: ¿Yo? Ay, don Chema, no se haga el tonto. Usted mismo me lo contó el viernes.
Don Chema: Yo le dije que había un problema con un recibo, nada más. Usted siempre toma las cosas al pie de la letra… o, peor, las inventa.
Narrador: Doña Rosa pone el grito en el cielo.
Doña Rosa: ¡Qué falta de respeto! Treinta años viviendo aquí y nadie me había echado en cara una indiscreción.
Narrador: Marisol no dice nada, pero piensa que don Chema dio en el clavo. Esa tarde, de buenas a primeras, Fer toca a la puerta de doña Rosa.
Fer: Doña Rosa, vengo a dar la cara. El del 302 es mi hermano Toño. Se quedó sin trabajo y por eso se atrasó con la renta. Ya lo arreglamos con don Chema.
Doña Rosa: ¿Tu hermano? Me quedé con la boca abierta. Perdóname, mija. Hablé a ciegas, sin saber nada.
Fer: Está bien. Usted también vivió en carne propia lo difícil que es cuando falta el dinero, ¿se acuerda? Cuando murió don Pepe, todo el edificio la ayudó.
Narrador: Doña Rosa, que nunca da su brazo a torcer, acepta a regañadientes que se equivocó. Al día siguiente le lleva a Toño un plato de tamales, y don Chema decide hacerse de la vista gorda con el recibo atrasado un mes más.
Doña Rosa: Y ahora, ¿de qué voy a platicar en el pasillo?
Narrador: Doña Rosa barre, de mala gana, un pasillo muy silencioso. No se pierdan el próximo episodio de *Edificio Jacarandas*.
```

Summary. Doña Rosa, who talks nonstop, tells Marisol that the new tenant in 302 hasn't paid
his rent; the manager, don Chema, told her in confidence. Marisol bites her tongue: the tenant is
her best friend Fer's brother. Don Chema, furious at the gossip, says Rosa takes everything
literally or invents it, and Rosa protests loudly. Fer comes to explain: her brother lost his job,
and it's settled. Rosa apologizes and grudgingly admits her mistake, and the hallway falls silent.

Glosses. *¿Ya supiste lo del 302?* — Have you heard about 302? (*saber* in the preterite:
to find out). *Me pidió que no
dijera nada* — he asked me not to say anything (B2's sequence of tenses). *Toca a la puerta* —
knocks at the door (Mexico also *toca la puerta*). *Lo difícil que es* — how hard it is.

## Pronunciation

- *regañadientes* has five syllables: *re-ga-ña-dien-tes*, stress on *dien*. The *ñ* is the
  sound in English "canyon".
- *quicio* has two syllables, *qui-cio*, with the stress on the first: "KEE-syoh" (*qu* is a
  plain *k*; *ci* is *s* in Mexico).
- *indiscreción* has four syllables, *in-dis-cre-ción*, stress on the last.
- *gorro* has a trilled double *r*; don't let it slide into *gordo* (fat). *Hasta el gorro*
  links into *has-tael-go-rro*.
- *abrir y cerrar*: the *y* sounds like Spanish *i*, and the *r* of *abrir* links to it: *a-bri-ri
  ce-rrar*. The *rr* is trilled.

## Common mistakes

- Translating the English idiom word for word. "To bite the bullet" isn't ~~*morder la
  bala*~~; the Spanish picture is *dar la cara* or *aguantarse*. "Turn a blind eye" is *hacerse de
  la vista gorda* (or *hacer la vista gorda*), not ~~*voltear un ojo ciego*~~.
- Forgetting the pronoun. ~~*Fue la lengua*~~ → *Se me fue la lengua* (I let it slip).
- Freezing the possessive. ~~*No doy su brazo a torcer*~~ → *No doy mi brazo a torcer*.
- Using an informal idiom in a formal text. *Estoy hasta el gorro* doesn't belong in a
  complaint to a company; *La situación ya no es aceptable* does.

## Key points

- Idioms conjugate and take pronouns like any verb: *se me fue la lengua, me saca de quicio, le
  echó en cara*. Possessives and adjectives agree: *no doy mi brazo a torcer, se hizo la tonta*.
- Mexico says *ser uña y mugre* (dictionaries give the general *uña y carne*), *hacerse de la vista
  gorda* (also *hacer la vista gorda*) and *hablar hasta por los codos*; Spain also says *el
  cotilleo* for *el chisme*. Every one of these forms is correct.
- Adverbial idioms (*a regañadientes, de buenas a primeras, al pie de la letra, a ciegas, en carne
  propia*) are often neutral enough for writing.
- Most people idioms are informal: use one at a time, and in formal texts give the plain meaning.
- For a new idiom: notice an absurd literal meaning, watch the reaction, read what follows.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete

lessons.title: Dar gato por liebre: idioms with animals and food, and sayings
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 taught idioms for people. This one turns to two of the richest sources of idioms in any
language: animals and food. You'll also see how one meaning gets a different idiom in each
country, how fixed comparisons work, how a saying differs from an idiom (a preview of the honors
lesson on proverbs), and which Spanish idioms look like English ones but aren't.

The theme is the market: the weekly *tianguis* (A1), regular customers, haggling (A1's
*regatear*), buying wholesale and selling retail, and the countryside the food comes from. B1's
*ser pan comido* (to be a piece of cake) and B2's *por si acaso* (just in case) are used freely.

## Animals in idioms

| Idiom | Literally | Means | Where, register |
|---|---|---|---|
| *dar gato por liebre* | to give cat for hare | to rip someone off | general, informal |
| *buscarle tres pies al gato* | to look for three feet on the cat | to overcomplicate things | general, informal |
| *estar como pez en el agua* | to be like a fish in water | to be in one's element | general, neutral |
| *llevarse como perro y gato* | to get along like dog and cat | to fight like cats and dogs | general, informal |
| *la oveja negra* | the black sheep | the black sheep | general, neutral |
| *matar dos pájaros de un tiro* | to kill two birds with one shot | to kill two birds with one stone | general, neutral |
| *por si las moscas* | in case the flies | just to be safe | general, informal |

*Dar gato por liebre* remembers an old trick: selling cooked cat as hare. Today it's any fraud
that passes off something worse as something better: *En ese puesto te dan gato por liebre* (At
that stall they rip you off). In *buscarle tres pies al gato* the *le* is fixed and doesn't change:
*No le busques tres pies al gato* (Don't overcomplicate it). Some speakers say *cinco pies*, which
makes the logic clearer: a cat has four, so the fifth doesn't exist.

*Por si las moscas* is the informal twin of *por si acaso*: *Llévate un suéter, por si las moscas*
(Take a sweater, just to be safe). In writing, use *por si acaso* or *en caso de que*.

## Food in idioms

| Idiom | Literally | Means | Where, register |
|---|---|---|---|
| *importar un comino* | to matter a cumin seed | not to care at all | general, informal |
| *ser harina de otro costal* | to be flour from another sack | to be another story | general, neutral to informal |
| *hacérsele agua la boca* | for one's mouth to turn to water | to make one's mouth water | see below |
| *dar atole con el dedo* | to give atole with one's finger | to string someone along | Mexico, informal |
| *echar toda la carne al asador* | to put all the meat on the grill | to go all out | general, neutral to informal |
| *pagar los platos rotos* | to pay for the broken plates | to take the blame | general, neutral to informal |
| *ahogarse en un vaso de agua* | to drown in a glass of water | to make a mountain out of a molehill | general, informal |

*Importar un comino* works like *gustar*: the thing that doesn't matter is the subject, the person
is the indirect object. *Me importa un comino* (I couldn't care less); *A mis hijos les importan un
comino las noticias* (My kids couldn't care less about the news). *El atole* is a hot, thick corn
drink: *dar atole con el dedo* is giving someone a taste on your finger instead of a cup, that is,
fooling them with promises: *El casero nos da atole con el dedo* (The landlord is stringing us
along). It's Mexican; elsewhere you'd say *dar largas*.

## One meaning, many countries

Idioms are where Spanish varies most. Word order can shift: in Mexico food *hace agua la boca* (*Se
me hace agua la boca*), while in Spain it usually *hace la boca agua* (*Se me hace la boca agua*).
Sometimes each country has its own picture. In a 1986 study of Mexican phraseology, Károly Morvay
collected the ways to say "to skip school" and noted that no single figurative expression covers
the whole Spanish-speaking world. A few from his list, several with animals:

| Country | Idiom | Literally |
|---|---|---|
| Mexico | *irse de pinta*, *hacer pinta* | *la pinta*: a spot or mark (origin unclear) |
| Spain | *hacer novillos* | to do young bulls |
| Argentina, Uruguay | *hacerse la rabona* | from *el rabo*, the tail |
| Chile | *hacer la cimarra* | related to *cimarrón*, runaway |
| Colombia | *hacer conejo* | to do rabbit |
| Peru | *hacerse la vaca* | to make oneself the cow |

Usage changes, so treat a forty-year-old list as a starting point, but the lesson holds: when you
read a Spanish text from another country, an unknown idiom may simply be that country's version of
one you know. The dictionaries help: the DLE marks words and phrases with a country (*Méx.*,
*Arg.*), and the Asociación de Academias' *Diccionario de americanismos* records Latin American
usage country by country.

## Fixed comparisons

Spanish also has comparisons that come as a set, usually exaggerated: *ir como sardinas en lata*
(to be packed like sardines), *ser más terco que una mula* (to be as stubborn as a mule), *dormir
como un tronco* (to sleep like a log), *ser más lento que una tortuga* (to be slower than a
tortoise). Change the animal and the effect is lost: nobody is packed like tuna.

- *En el metro íbamos como sardinas en lata.* — On the metro we were packed like sardines.
- *Mi abuelo es más terco que una mula.* — My grandfather is as stubborn as a mule.

## An idiom or a saying?

An idiom is a piece of a sentence: you conjugate it and build around it (*Me dieron gato por
liebre*). A saying, *el refrán* (B1), is a complete sentence with a lesson, quoted as it is:

- *Más vale pájaro en mano que cien volando.* — A bird in the hand is worth a hundred flying (better
  something sure than more that's uncertain).

It has two balanced halves, a general truth with no particular person, and a rhythm that makes it
easy to remember. The honors lesson on proverbs looks at these in detail.

## False friends among idioms

Many animal idioms match English: *la oveja negra* (the black sheep), *matar dos pájaros de un
tiro*, *llevarse como perro y gato*. That makes the ones that don't match dangerous.

- "It's raining cats and dogs" isn't about animals in Spanish: *Está lloviendo a cántaros* ("by the
  jugful").
- "To spill the beans" isn't ~~*tirar los frijoles*~~; in Mexico you'll hear *soltar la sopa* (to
  let the soup go), and anywhere *irse de la lengua* or lesson 13's *írsele la lengua*.
- "A storm in a teacup" is *ahogarse en un vaso de agua* for a person; you'll
  also read *una tormenta en un vaso de agua* for an event.

## At the market

![A Sunday street market under pink and blue awnings. On the left, a fruit stall with crates of oranges and bananas and a hanging scale; a woman vendor stands behind it. Beside the stall, a woman with a shopping bag is waiting to buy. In the middle of the aisle, a man pushes a cart with a sign reading Elotes. On the right, a second stall with hats.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the picture: *el puesto* (A1: the stall), *la báscula* (B2: the scale), *la marchanta* (the
regular customer) and *el vendedor ambulante* (the street vendor). To bargain politely: *¿Cuánto
es lo menos?* (What's your best price?); *¿Me lo deja en cincuenta?* (Will you let me have it for
fifty?); *Si me llevo dos kilos, ¿me hace precio?* (If I take two kilos, will you give me a deal?).
Vendors call out *¡Pásele, marchanta!* (Come on in!) and *¿Qué le damos?* (What can we get you?).

## Reading: Sunday at the tianguis

A fruit vendor tells her own story, *crónica*-style. She buys at the Central de Abasto, Mexico
City's huge wholesale market. *Las garnachas* are fried snacks (*tlacoyos, quesadillas, sopes*),
*la banqueta* is the sidewalk, and *la alcaldía* is the borough government.

> Me llamo Lucha y llevo veintidós años poniendo mi puesto de fruta en el tianguis de los domingos. Me levanto a las cuatro, porque a las cinco compro al mayoreo en la Central de Abasto, y a las siete ya tengo que estar vendiendo al menudeo. En el tianguis estoy como pez en el agua: aquí crecí, aquí aprendí a hacer cuentas y aquí conocí a mi marido, que vendía jitomates en el puesto de enfrente.
>
> Los domingos la calle se llena tanto que a mediodía vamos como sardinas en lata. Entre los puestos pasan los vendedores ambulantes con sus carritos de elotes, y con ese olor a garnachas a cualquiera se le hace agua la boca.
>
> Mis marchantes son lo más importante. La señora Pili viene desde hace quince años; le aparto los mangos más dulces y ella nunca me regatea. Otros, en cambio, le buscan tres pies al gato: que si el plátano está muy verde, que si en la tienda de abarrotes de la esquina está más barato. El regateo es parte del juego, pero yo no doy gato por liebre: si una fruta está golpeada, lo digo y la vendo más barata.
>
> Con don Fermín, el de los sombreros, me llevo como perro y gato desde que me quitó medio metro de banqueta. Mi hija dice que me ahogo en un vaso de agua, pero a mí me importa un comino lo que digan: medio metro son dos cajas de naranjas.
>
> Hace unos años la alcaldía prometió techar el tianguis. Nos dio atole con el dedo: vinieron, tomaron fotos y del techo nunca más supimos. Cuando llueve, los comerciantes pagamos los platos rotos.
>
> Mi hijo menor, Beto, es la oveja negra de la familia: estudió Administración y trabaja en una oficina. Pero cuando hay que echar toda la carne al asador, como en diciembre, se pone la camiseta y viene a ayudar. Así mata dos pájaros de un tiro: me echa la mano y, de paso, ve a sus amigos de la infancia.
>
> Mi papá era de un rancho de Tlaxcala donde la familia vivía de la ganadería: unas cuantas cabezas de ganado y mucho trabajo. Me contaba que de niño cambiaba huevos por maíz con los vecinos, porque en su pueblo el trueque todavía era normal. Hoy todo se paga, a veces con transferencia, pero yo siempre traigo cambio, por si las moscas.
>
> ¿Que si me voy a retirar algún día? Eso ya es harina de otro costal. Mientras pueda cargar una caja, aquí me van a encontrar cada domingo, gritando: «¡Pásele, marchanta! ¿Qué le damos?».

Summary. Lucha has sold fruit at a Sunday market for 22 years: she buys wholesale at dawn and
sells retail from seven, and feels completely at home there. At midday the market is packed, and
the street food smells delicious. Her regulars matter most; some customers nitpick and haggle,
but she never cheats anyone. She fights with the hat seller over half a meter of sidewalk. The
borough promised a roof and never delivered, so the vendors suffer when it rains. Her son, who
works in an office, still comes to help in December. Her father grew up among cattle, where
people bartered. Retire? That's another story.

Glosses. *Llevo veintidós años poniendo* — I've been setting up for 22 years (*llevar* +
gerund). *Le aparto* — I set aside for her. *Que si…, que si…* — the complaints she hears, one
after another ("it's this, it's that"). *Golpeada* — bruised. *Techar* — to put a roof over. *Me
echa la mano* — B1's "gives me a hand". *Se pone la camiseta* — he shows his commitment (literally
"puts on the team shirt"; common in Mexico and much of Latin America). *Cabezas de ganado* — head of
cattle.

## Pronunciation

- *trueque* has two syllables, *true-que* ("TRWEH-keh"): *ue* is one syllable, and *qu* is a plain
  *k*.
- *mayoreo* has four syllables, *ma-yo-re-o*, stress on *re*; in Mexico *y* sounds like the *y* in
  "yes". *menudeo* also has four: *me-nu-de-o*.
- *comino* stresses the middle syllable: *co-MI-no*.
- *abarrotes*: four syllables, *a-ba-rro-tes*, with a trilled *rr*.
- In *marchante* the *ch* is the sound in "church": *mar-CHAN-te*.

## Common mistakes

- Swapping the animal or food: ~~*dar perro por liebre*~~, ~~*como atunes en lata*~~. The words are
  fixed even when they seem arbitrary.
- Agreement with *importar*: ~~*Me importa un comino las noticias*~~ → *Me importan un comino las
  noticias* (the news is plural).
- Using *dar atole con el dedo* outside Mexico and expecting everyone to understand. It's Mexican;
  *dar largas* is understood everywhere.
- Translating English animal idioms: there are no cats or dogs in *Está lloviendo a cántaros*.
- *Por si las moscas* in a formal letter: write *por si acaso* or *en caso de que* + subjunctive.

## Key points

- Animal and food idioms are mostly general Spanish and informal; *dar atole con el dedo* and
  *ponerse la camiseta* are especially common in Mexico.
- The words of an idiom are fixed, but grammar works inside it: *me importan un comino las
  noticias; no le busques tres pies al gato*.
- One meaning can have a different idiom in each country ("to skip school": *irse de pinta,
  hacer novillos, hacerse la rabona*); word order can change too (*se me hace agua la boca / se me
  hace la boca agua*).
- Fixed comparisons (*como sardinas en lata, más terco que una mula*) don't allow substitutions.
- A saying is a complete sentence you quote; an idiom is a piece you build into your own sentence.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Hacerse cargo: pronominal verbs and verbs with prepositions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 13 and 14 were about idioms, fixed groups of words. This lesson is about a smaller kind of
fixed group: a verb and the preposition it always takes. In B1 lesson 22 you learned *atreverse a,
fijarse en, contar con, tratarse de, burlarse de, olvidarse de*. At C1 the list grows, and the verbs
get more formal: *carecer de, constar de, incurrir en, atenerse a, optar por, velar por*. You'll
also see verbs whose meaning changes when they take *se*, and two values of *se* that B2 left for
C1.

The theme is care work: looking after children, older relatives and people with disabilities, and
who does it.

## Verbs with a fixed preposition

A **[[prepositional verb]]** comes with its own preposition, and the preposition stays whatever
follows it: a noun, an infinitive or a whole clause. English has the same thing (to rely on, to
consist of), but the prepositions rarely match, so learn each verb with its preposition.

![A chart of verbs grouped by the preposition they take. Under a: atenerse a, negarse a, dirigirse a. Under de: carecer de, constar de, abstenerse de, jactarse de, desentenderse de. Under en: incurrir en, empeñarse en. Under por: optar por, velar por. Each column has one example sentence: Me atengo a las reglas; El curso consta de seis módulos; Se empeña en ayudar; Optamos por la segunda opción.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Verb | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *atenerse a* | to abide by, to go by | *Me atengo a lo que dice el contrato.* — I'm going by what the contract says. |
| *negarse a* | to refuse to | *Se negó a firmar.* — She refused to sign. |
| *dirigirse a* | to address (lesson 01) | *Se dirigió a los vecinos.* — He addressed the neighbors. |
| *carecer de* | to lack | *La clínica carece de rampas.* — The clinic lacks ramps. |
| *constar de* | to consist of | *El programa consta de tres partes.* — The program consists of three parts. |
| *abstenerse de* | to refrain from | *Me abstuve de opinar.* — I refrained from giving an opinion. |
| *jactarse de* | to boast about | *Se jacta de su puntualidad.* — He boasts about his punctuality. |
| *desentenderse de* | to wash one's hands of | *No te desentiendas de tu abuela.* — Don't wash your hands of your grandmother. |
| *incurrir en* | to incur, to fall into | *Incurrió en un error grave.* — He made a serious error. |
| *empeñarse en* | to insist on | *Se empeña en cocinar ella.* — She insists on cooking herself. |
| *optar por* | to opt for | *Optamos por la segunda opción.* — We opted for the second option. |
| *velar por* | to look after, to safeguard | *La ley vela por los derechos de los menores.* — The law safeguards children's rights. |

Most of these are formal or written. In conversation you'll more often hear the everyday
equivalent: *le falta* for *carece de*, *escogimos* for *optamos por*, *presume de* (B1) for *se
jacta de*, *no quiso* for *se negó a*. Knowing both lets you move up and down the scale.

Three of them have a second preposition worth knowing. *Constar en* means "to be on record": *Consta
en el acta* (It's in the minutes), and *Me consta que…* means "I know for a fact that…". *Optar a*
means "to be eligible for, to compete for" (*optar a una beca*). *Velar* alone means to keep vigil,
or to hold a wake (B2's *el velorio*).

## The preposition before an infinitive or a clause

The preposition doesn't disappear when a verb or a clause follows:

- *Se negó a pagar.* — He refused to pay. (*a* + infinitive)
- *Se negó a que pagáramos nosotros.* — He refused to let us pay. (*a que* + subjunctive)
- *Mi mamá se empeña en que vayamos todos los domingos.* — My mom insists that we all go every
  Sunday.
- *Se jacta de que nunca ha faltado.* — He boasts that he has never missed a day.

The mood after *que* follows the meaning, as in lesson 05: *negarse a que* and *empeñarse en que*
try to influence what others do, so they take the subjunctive; *jactarse de que* states a fact, so it
takes the indicative. Leaving out the preposition (*Se empeña que vayamos*) is the queísmo of lesson
03: frequent in speech, avoided in careful writing.

## Pronominal verbs that change meaning

A **[[pronominal verb]]** is a verb used with *me, te, se, nos*. Some are just reflexive (*lavarse*),
but in others the pronoun changes the meaning, and often brings a preposition with it:

| Without *se* | With *se* |
|---|---|
| *negar* — to deny: *Negó los hechos.* (He denied the facts.) | *negarse a* — to refuse: *Se negó a declarar.* (He refused to testify.) |
| *ocurrir* (A2) — to happen: *¿Qué ocurrió?* (What happened?) | *ocurrírsele a alguien* — to occur to someone: *Se me ocurrió una idea.* (I had an idea.) |
| *valer* — to be worth: *Vale mil pesos.* (It's worth a thousand pesos.) | *valerse de* — to make use of: *Se valió de un amigo.* (He used a friend.) *Valerse por sí mismo* — to manage alone. |
| *hacer* — to do: *Hizo la cena.* (She made dinner.) | *hacerse cargo de* — to take charge of: *Me hago cargo.* (I'll take care of it.) |
| *acordar* — to agree on: *Acordamos un horario.* (We agreed on a schedule.) | *acordarse de* (A2) — to remember: *¿Te acuerdas de él?* (Do you remember him?) |

*Ocurrírsele* works like *gustar*: the idea is the subject and agrees with the verb, and the person
is an indirect object. *Se me ocurrió una idea; se nos ocurrieron dos soluciones*. In *valerse por sí
mismo* the last words agree with the person: *Mi abuela ya no se vale por sí misma* (My grandmother
can't manage on her own anymore).

## Two more values of *se*

B2 lesson 15 put the values of *se* on one map: reflexive, reciprocal, *se* for *le*, pronominal,
accidental, passive and impersonal, and the *se* of involvement with eating and reading. C1 names that
last one and adds a relative of it. Learn to recognize both; use them where they sound natural.

The **[[aspectual se]]** marks an action as complete, often with a sense of enjoyment or effort. With a
verb that takes an object, it needs a definite, limited one:

- *Se comió todo el pastel.* — He ate up the whole cake.
- *Me leí el libro en un día.* — I read the whole book in a day.
- *Mi hija ya se sabe la tabla del siete.* — My daughter already knows the seven times table by
  heart.

Without the pronoun the facts are the same (*Comió todo el pastel*); with it, the action is felt as
finished and personal. With an open-ended object it doesn't fit: *Comió pastel* (He ate some cake)
has no *se*.

The **[[dative of interest]]** is an extra *me, te, le, nos* for a person who is affected by the
action without taking part in it. Mexican speech uses it constantly, often warmly:

- *No se me enfermen, ¿eh?* — Don't you go getting sick on me, OK? (a mother to her children)
- *Se me fue el camión.* — The bus left without me (and I'm the one who suffers).
- *Cuídamela mucho.* — Take good care of her for me.

Grammars split these datives into several kinds; for a learner the test is simple: drop the
pronoun and the sentence still works, but you lose the speaker's involvement.

## Care work in Mexico

*Los cuidados* (care work, in the plural) is the daily work of looking after people who can't
manage on their own: children, *los adultos mayores* (the respectful Mexican term for older adults)
and people with *discapacidad*. In Mexico much of it is unpaid and done by women. INEGI's National
Time Use Survey (ENUT 2024, press release of August 28, 2025) found that women aged 12 and over
spent on average 39.7 hours a week on unpaid domestic work, care and volunteering, against 18.2
for men: more than twice as much. Counting paid work as well, women worked 61.1 hours a week and men
58.0. On unpaid care for members of their own household alone, women spent 13.6 hours a week and
men 8.7.

That is *la doble jornada*: a paid job, then a second shift at home. Two words name the answers
under discussion: *la corresponsabilidad* (sharing care among families, the state and employers)
and *la conciliación* (work-life balance). Paid care has its own law too: on July 2, 2019, the
*Diario Oficial de la Federación* published a decree reforming the Ley Federal del Trabajo and the
Ley del Seguro Social "en materia de las personas trabajadoras del hogar". For the
details of workers' rights, read the official text, not a summary.

![A weekly care schedule for grandma Carmen, a table with seven columns from Monday to Sunday. Monday to Friday, 9 to 5: Marta, the domestic worker. Saturday: Gaby, the granddaughter. Sunday: Lety, the daughter. Below, a row for Paquito, daycare until 4, with Gaby on Tuesday and Thursday. At the bottom, a note: Raúl pays half of the costs.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: a family meeting

Lety, her brother Raúl (on a video call from Monterrey), Lety's daughter Gaby and grandma Carmen
meet after Carmen broke her hip. Paquito is Lety's youngest son. *Cargar con todo* is to carry the
whole load; *va* is Mexican "OK, deal".

```dialogue
# La junta del domingo
Lety: Bueno, ya estamos todos. Gracias por conectarte, Raúl. La junta consta de un solo punto: quién se va a hacer cargo de mamá ahora que salió del hospital.
Raúl: Ya sé, Lety. Y antes de que empieces: no me estoy desentendiendo. Es que desde Monterrey no puedo hacer mucho.
Lety: Nadie te está acusando. Pero desde la caída mamá ya no se vale por sí misma, y yo llevo tres semanas con doble jornada: salgo del hospital y me voy directo a su casa.
Gaby: Mi mamá tiene razón, tío. Entre su trabajo remunerado, el trabajo doméstico de las dos casas y los cuidados de la abuela, es una sobrecarga.
Raúl: Lo entiendo. ¿Y si contratamos a una cuidadora? Yo pago la mitad.
Lety: Ya lo pensé. Pero mamá se niega a que una desconocida la bañe. Se empeña en que lo hagamos nosotras.
Abuela Carmen: Porque así es. Yo cuidé a mi suegra once años y nunca me quejé.
Gaby: Abuela, usted siempre se jacta de eso, pero también nos contó que terminó agotada.
Abuela Carmen: Bueno… sí. Pero en mis tiempos no había de otra.
Raúl: Ahora sí hay. A ver, se me ocurre algo. La señora Marta, la trabajadora del hogar que va los martes, conoce a mamá desde hace años. ¿Por qué no le proponemos más días, con contrato por escrito y con seguro social?
Lety: Me parece bien, siempre que se respeten sus derechos. No quiero que incurramos en lo que hace tanta gente: pagar poco y exigir mucho.
Gaby: Y yo puedo ir los sábados. Además, el baño de la abuela carece de barras de apoyo: hay que instalarlas.
Lety: Gracias, mija. Pero tú también tienes tu vida. Aquí se trata de corresponsabilidad, no de que una sola persona cargue con todo.
Raúl: Entonces yo opto por lo de la señora Marta. Ma, ¿usted qué dice?
Abuela Carmen: Que me atengo a lo que decidan… siempre que nadie me trate como si tuviera una discapacidad. Soy una adulta mayor, no una niña.
Lety: Nadie dice eso, ma. Velamos por usted porque la queremos.
Raúl: ¿Y tu jefa, Lety? ¿No te da permisos?
Lety: Habla mucho de conciliación, pero cuando pido salir temprano, pone cara de pocos amigos.
Gaby: Y no se olviden de Paquito. La estancia infantil cierra a las cuatro, y alguien tiene que recogerlo.
Raúl: Yo me abstengo de opinar sobre eso, porque no estoy ahí, pero pago el transporte si hace falta.
Lety: Va. Que conste en el chat de la familia: Marta, de lunes a viernes; Gaby, los sábados, y por Paquito los martes y jueves; yo, los domingos; Raúl, la mitad de los gastos.
```

Summary. The family meets to decide who will take charge of grandma Carmen, who can no longer
manage alone. Lety, who works at a hospital, is working a double shift; her brother Raúl lives far away but
offers to pay half for a caregiver. Carmen refuses to be bathed by a stranger and boasts of having
cared for her mother-in-law for eleven years, though she admits it exhausted her. Raúl suggests
giving more days to Marta, the domestic worker who already knows Carmen, with a written contract
and social security. Everyone agrees on a weekly plan.

Glosses. *Gracias por conectarte* — thanks for joining (the call). *No había de otra* — there was
no other way (informal Mexican). *Que conste* — let it be on record (*constar en*). *Pone cara de
pocos amigos* — lesson 13's "looks grumpy". *Siempre que se respeten* — as long as they're
respected (*siempre que* + subjunctive for a condition).

## Pronunciation

- *corresponsabilidad* has seven syllables: *co-rres-pon-sa-bi-li-dad*, stress on the last. Say it
  slowly once, then at speed.
- *desentiendo*: *de-sen-tien-do*, four syllables; the *ie* is one syllable.
- *carezco*: *ca-res-co* in Mexico, where *z* sounds like *s*.
- *ocurrírsele* is stressed on *rrír*: *o-cu-RRÍR-se-le*, five syllables, written accent on the *í*.
- *remunerado*: five syllables, *re-mu-ne-ra-do*. Don't swap the consonants into
  ~~*renumerado*~~, a common slip even among native speakers.

## Common mistakes

- Guessing the preposition: *constar* takes *de* (*consta de seis módulos*), though its synonym
  *consistir* takes *en*; ~~*optar para*~~ → *optar por*.
- Dropping the preposition before *que*: *Se empeña en que vayamos* in careful writing.
- Forgetting agreement with *ocurrírsele*: ~~*Se me ocurrió dos ideas*~~ → *Se me ocurrieron dos
  ideas*.
- Confusing *negar* and *negarse a*: *Negó haberlo dicho* (He denied having said it) vs *Se negó a
  decirlo* (He refused to say it).
- Overusing the dative of interest in formal writing: it belongs to speech.

## Key points

- Prepositional verbs keep their preposition before a noun, an infinitive or a clause: *Me atengo
  a…; Se negó a firmar; Se empeña en que vayamos*.
- The mood after *que* follows the meaning: influence → subjunctive (*negarse a que, empeñarse en
  que*); a fact → indicative (*jactarse de que*).
- Some verbs change meaning with *se*: *negar / negarse a, ocurrir / ocurrírsele, valer /
  valerse de, hacer / hacerse cargo de, acordar / acordarse de*.
- The aspectual *se* marks a complete action with a definite object (*Se comió todo el pastel*); the
  dative of interest adds a person who is affected (*No se me enfermen*).
- Many of these verbs are formal; know their everyday equivalents (*carecer de / faltar*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Cometer un error garrafal: collocations and lexical precision
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last lesson of this module is about a kind of fixed language that's easy to miss because each
word in it is ordinary. Nobody needs a dictionary for *cometer* or *error*, but you do need to know
that Spanish says *cometer un error*, not ~~*hacer un error*~~. At C1, this is often what separates
a correct text from one that sounds native: the right verb for the noun, the right adjective for
the right intensity, and precise verbs where a beginner would put *hacer, tener* or *decir*.

The theme is business: boards, shareholders, mergers, suppliers and market share. A2's *la
factura* (invoice) and B1's *el gerente* (manager) and *el presupuesto* (budget) are used freely.
All the companies are fictional.

## What a collocation is

A **[[collocation]]** is a combination of words that speakers use together by habit. The meaning is
transparent, unlike an idiom's, but the choice of word isn't logical, so it has to be learned. In
English you *make* a mistake and *take* a decision; in Spanish you *cometes un error* and *tomas
una decisión*. A learner who says ~~*hacer un error*~~ is understood, but the phrase marks them as
a learner.

Three common shapes:

- verb + noun: *desempeñar un cargo, entablar una conversación*;
- adjective + noun: *un éxito rotundo, un craso error*;
- noun + *de* + noun: *una ola de despidos, un sinfín de trámites*.

## Verb + noun

| Verb | Typical nouns | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *cometer* | *un error, un delito, una falta* | *Cometimos un error de cálculo.* — We made a miscalculation. |
| *desempeñar* | *un cargo, un papel, una función* | *Desempeñó el cargo de tesorera.* — She served as treasurer. |
| *entablar* | *una conversación, negociaciones, una relación* | *Entablaron negociaciones con el sindicato.* — They opened talks with the union. |
| *contraer* | *matrimonio, una deuda, una obligación, una enfermedad* | *Contrajeron matrimonio en mayo.* — They were married in May. |
| *saldar* | *una deuda, una cuenta* | *Ya saldé la tarjeta.* — I've paid off the card. |
| *zanjar* | *una discusión, una polémica, un asunto* | *La votación zanjó el asunto.* — The vote settled the matter. |
| *conciliar* | *el sueño* | *No pude conciliar el sueño.* — I couldn't get to sleep. |
| *cursar* | *estudios, una carrera, una materia* | *Cursa la maestría en línea.* — She's doing her master's online. |
| *acatar* | *una orden, una norma, una decisión* | *El equipo acató la decisión.* — The team accepted the decision. |
| *ejercer* | *una profesión, un derecho, presión* | *Ejerce como abogada desde 2015.* — She has practiced law since 2015. |
| *formular* | *una pregunta, una propuesta, una queja* | *Formuló una queja formal.* — He filed a formal complaint. |

Most of these are formal. In conversation a Mexican would say *se casaron* rather than *contrajeron
matrimonio*, *no me podía dormir* rather than *no podía conciliar el sueño*, *estudia* rather than
*cursa*. The formal version belongs in reports, news and official letters, which is exactly where
the DELE C1 asks you to write.

Notice how narrow some are. *Conciliar* in this sense goes only with *el sueño*. *Zanjar* takes
disputes and matters, not debts. *Saldar* is the verb for debts and accounts (and figuratively
*saldar cuentas con alguien*, to settle scores); it can also close an event in news style (*El
enfrentamiento se saldó con dos heridos*: the clash ended with two injured), but to end an argument,
use *zanjar*. *Ejercer* is a false friend: you *ejercer* a profession or a
right, but you exercise your body with *hacer ejercicio*.

## Adjective + noun

Intensifying adjectives are especially picky:

- *rotundo* (resounding, flat) goes after *éxito, fracaso, negativa, no*: *un éxito rotundo, una
  negativa rotunda* (a flat refusal).
- *craso* (gross) goes almost only before *error* and *ignorancia*: *un craso error*.
- *garrafal* (monumental) goes after *error, falta, equivocación*: *un error garrafal*. Same form
  for both genders: *una falta garrafal*.
- *abrumador* (overwhelming) goes with *mayoría, victoria, evidencia*: *una mayoría abrumadora*.

Word order matters: *un craso error*, but ~~*un garrafal error*~~ sounds odd; *un error garrafal*.

## Noun + *de* + noun

Some nouns measure or describe a quantity in a fixed way: *una ola de* (a wave of: *despidos,
calor, protestas*), *un sinfín de* (an endless number of: *trámites, problemas*), *una lluvia de*
(a shower of: *críticas, preguntas*). For example: *Una ola de despidos sacudió el sector* (A wave of layoffs hit the sector); *Tuvimos
que hacer un sinfín de trámites* (We had to go through endless paperwork).

## Catch-all verbs

A **[[catch-all verb]]** (*el verbo comodín*, from the joker in a deck of cards) is one that fits
anywhere and says little: *hacer, tener, poner, haber, decir, dar*. They're not wrong, and speech is
full of them, but in a formal text each one is a missed chance to be precise.

| Vague | Precise |
|---|---|
| *hacer una pregunta* | *formular / plantear una pregunta* |
| *hacer un informe* | *elaborar / redactar un informe* |
| *tener una reunión* | *celebrar una reunión* |
| *decir que* | *afirmar, señalar, sostener, advertir que* |
| *poner atención* | *prestar atención* |
| *hay un problema* | *surge / se plantea un problema* |
| *dar una opinión* | *expresar / emitir una opinión* |
| *hacer la carrera de Derecho* | *cursar la carrera de Derecho* |

![A grid of collocations: five verbs down the side (cometer, contraer, saldar, zanjar, desempeñar) and five nouns across the top (un error, una deuda, matrimonio, una discusión, un cargo). A check mark shows each typical combination: cometer un error; contraer una deuda and contraer matrimonio; saldar una deuda; zanjar una discusión; desempeñar un cargo. The other cells are empty.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## How to find collocations

You can't guess a collocation, but you can look it up:

1. The DLE's examples and its "locuciones" often show the usual partner of a word.
2. A combinatorial dictionary lists the words that go with each word; for Spanish the best known
   is *Redes*, directed by Ignacio Bosque (2004).
3. The RAE's corpora (large searchable collections of real texts) show how often a combination
   appears and in which countries.
4. A search engine with quotation marks ("contraer una deuda" vs "hacer una deuda") gives a rough
   idea, but check that the results come from good sources.

## Inside a company

![An organization chart of a company. At the top, the shareholders' meeting (Asamblea de accionistas); below it, the board of directors (Junta directiva); below the board, the CEO (Directora general); below the CEO, three managers: sales, marketing and finance.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Los accionistas* (shareholders) own the company and meet in *la asamblea de accionistas*. They
elect *la junta directiva* (board of directors), which appoints *el director general* or *la
directora general* (CEO). Under the CEO are *los gerentes* (B1: managers). A large company may
*cotizar en la bolsa de valores* (be listed on the stock exchange); in Mexico that's the Bolsa
Mexicana de Valores. Its health shows in *la facturación* (revenue) and *la cuota de mercado* (market
share), which a *fusión* (merger) can raise overnight. Mexican business writing also says *la
participación de mercado*, and *la mercadotecnia* where Spain more often says *el marketing*.

## Reading: two versions of a report

The fictional Grupo Bajío, a food company, writes a short report to its shareholders. The first
version is a draft full of catch-all verbs; the second is the final text. *El ejercicio* is the
fiscal year.

> Borrador. Este año la empresa hizo muchas cosas importantes. En marzo tuvimos una reunión con la junta directiva y se dijo que había que hacer cambios. Pusimos más dinero en mercadotecnia y eso hizo que la facturación subiera. También hicimos un trato con Lácteos del Norte para juntarnos, y ahora tenemos más mercado. Hubo problemas con dos proveedores que no hacían las entregas a tiempo, pero ya se arreglaron. Tenemos una deuda que ya casi pagamos. Algunos accionistas hicieron preguntas sobre las acciones y la directora dijo que todo va bien. Fue un año con un éxito muy grande.

> Estimados accionistas:
>
> El ejercicio 2026 fue un año de transformación para Grupo Bajío. En marzo, la junta directiva celebró una sesión extraordinaria en la que se planteó la necesidad de reorganizar la empresa. Como resultado, se destinó un 15 % más de recursos a mercadotecnia, lo que contribuyó a que la facturación creciera un 12 %, hasta 3400 millones de pesos.
>
> En julio concluyó la fusión con Lácteos del Norte, que la asamblea había aprobado por una mayoría abrumadora y que elevó nuestra cuota de mercado del 9 al 14 %. Para financiarla, la empresa contrajo una deuda de 600 millones de pesos, de la cual ya se ha saldado el 80 %.
>
> Durante el primer semestre surgieron retrasos en las entregas de dos proveedores. La dirección entabló negociaciones con ambos y logró zanjar el conflicto sin recurrir a los tribunales. Agradecemos al personal, que desempeñó sus funciones con gran profesionalismo y acató las nuevas normas de seguridad sin un solo accidente grave.
>
> En la asamblea de septiembre, varios accionistas formularon preguntas sobre las acciones, que cotizan en la Bolsa Mexicana de Valores desde 2019. La directora general señaló que la empresa no hace pronósticos sobre su precio.
>
> También cometimos errores: el lanzamiento de una línea de bebidas en el sureste fue un fracaso rotundo, y retiraremos el producto en enero. Entrar a un mercado sin estudiarlo fue un craso error que no repetiremos.
>
> Atentamente,
>
> La Junta Directiva

Summary. Both versions report the same year. The draft says, vaguely, that the company "did many
things", "had a meeting", "put more money" into marketing and "did a deal" to merge. The final
version names each action precisely: an extraordinary board session, a 15% increase in marketing
spending, 12% revenue growth, a merger approved by an overwhelming majority that raised market share
from 9% to 14%, a debt of 600 million pesos 80% repaid, a supplier dispute settled through
negotiation, and a failed product launch admitted openly.

Glosses. *Se destinó* — was allocated. *Contribuyó a que la facturación creciera* — helped revenue
grow (subjunctive after *contribuir a que*). *Sin recurrir a los tribunales* — without going to
court. *El sureste* — Mexico's southeast.

Compare the pairs: *tuvimos una reunión → celebró una sesión; se dijo → se planteó; pusimos más
dinero → se destinó un 15 % más; hicimos un trato para juntarnos → la fusión; hubo problemas →
surgieron retrasos; ya casi pagamos → ya se ha saldado el 80 %; un éxito muy grande → (an honest
account, with a fracaso rotundo)*. The final version is longer, but every sentence says something
a shareholder can check.

## Pronunciation

- *garrafal*: three syllables, *ga-rra-fal*, stress on the last; trill the *rr*.
- *desempeñar*: four syllables, *de-sem-pe-ñar*.
- *abrumador*: four syllables, *a-bru-ma-dor*; *br* is one sound cluster, as in "brush".
- *mercadotecnia*: five syllables, *mer-ca-do-tec-nia* (*nia* is one syllable), stress on *tec*.
- *accionista*: the *cc* is two sounds, *k* + *s*: *ak-sio-nis-ta*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*Hacer un error*~~ → *cometer un error* (a calque of English "make a mistake").
- ~~*Ejercer en el gimnasio*~~ → *hacer ejercicio*. *Ejercer* is for professions, rights and pressure.
- Mixing up *saldar* and *zanjar*: debts are *saldadas*; arguments are usually *zanjadas*.
- Moving the adjective: *un error garrafal*, *un craso error*; *un éxito rotundo*.
- Replacing every catch-all verb in conversation: *¿Tuvieron junta?* is perfectly natural at work.
  Precision is for formal texts.

## Key points

- A collocation is a habitual combination: *cometer un error, contraer una deuda, saldar una cuenta,
  zanjar una discusión, conciliar el sueño, un éxito rotundo, una mayoría abrumadora*.
- Many C1 collocations are formal; know the everyday equivalent (*contraer matrimonio / casarse*).
- Catch-all verbs (*hacer, tener, poner, decir, haber*) are fine in speech; in formal writing replace
  them with precise verbs (*formular, celebrar, afirmar, surgir*).
- Look collocations up: dictionary examples, a combinatorial dictionary, a corpus.

the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: El refranero: proverbs and how people use them
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 14 drew the line between an idiom, a piece you build into your own sentence, and a saying,
a complete sentence you quote. This honors lesson is about the second kind. B1 taught *el refrán*
(a traditional saying with a lesson) and *el dicho* (any popular saying). Here you'll see how
proverbs are built, why they're so easy to remember, how speakers cut them short, how Mexico's
versions differ from Spain's, and how to choose the right one, which is harder than it looks. The
traditional sayings in this lesson are quoted as sayings; all the explanations, dialogues and
headlines are original.

## What a proverb is

A **[[proverb]]** is a short, traditional, anonymous sentence that sums up a piece of practical
wisdom: *Perro que ladra no muerde* (A barking dog doesn't bite). Spanish has several words in this
area, and they're not quite synonyms:

| Word | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *el refrán* (B1) | a traditional saying, usually anonymous, often rhymed | *Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho.* |
| *el proverbio* | the same, in a more formal or literary register; also sayings from other cultures or books | *un proverbio chino* |
| *el dicho* (B1) | any popular saying, including set phrases that aren't proverbs | *¡Ni modo!* |
| *la máxima* | a rule of conduct, often a person's own | *Su máxima era no endeudarse.* |
| *el aforismo* | a short, witty statement with a known author | *los aforismos de un escritor* |

*El refranero* is a collection of proverbs, or the whole stock of them in a language or a person's
head: *Mi abuela tiene un refranero para todo*. What it holds is *la sabiduría popular*, folk
wisdom: knowledge nobody signed, passed from mouth to mouth.

Collections exist for every variety of Spanish. For Mexico, Herón Pérez Martínez's *Refranero
mexicano* (Fondo de Cultura Económica, 2004) is a standard reference; the Instituto Cervantes
publishes an online *Refranero multilingüe* that matches Spanish proverbs with equivalents in other
languages.

## How a proverb is built

Proverbs survive because they're easy to remember, and they're easy to remember because of their
shape.

1. Two halves. Most proverbs split into two balanced parts, often separated by a comma in
   writing: *En casa de herrero, / cuchillo de palo*.
2. Rhythm. The halves often have the same number of syllables. Counted the way B1 lesson 90
   counted verse (vowels between words join into one syllable, silent *h* doesn't count):
   *Del-di-choal-he-cho* (5) / *hay-mu-cho-tre-cho* (5); *En-ca-sa-de he-rre-ro* (6, with *de he*
   said as one syllable) / *cu-chi-llo-de-pa-lo* (6).
3. Rhyme. Full rhyme (*hecho / trecho*) or assonance, where only the vowels match from the stressed
   one on: *se duerme / la corriente* both end in *e…e*.
4. Missing verbs. *En casa de herrero, cuchillo de palo* has no verb at all; the listener supplies
   "there is".
5. Timeless subjects. Proverbs talk about types, not people: *camarón que se duerme* (a shrimp that
   falls asleep), *perro que ladra* (a dog that barks), *el que madruga* (whoever gets up early), all
   in the present tense.

![A matching layout with two columns of proverb halves. Left column, first halves: Camarón que se duerme; En casa de herrero; Del dicho al hecho; A caballo regalado; Perro que ladra. Right column, second halves, in a different order: no muerde; hay mucho trecho; se lo lleva la corriente; no se le ve el colmillo; cuchillo de palo. Dotted lines join each first half to its second half.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Cutting a proverb short

Because everyone knows how a proverb ends, speakers often say only the first half and let the
listener finish it in their head:

- *Ya vendieron el departamento que te gustaba. Camarón que se duerme…* — They've already sold the
  apartment you liked. You snooze…
- *Prometió que este año sí iba a ahorrar. Del dicho al hecho…* — He promised that this year he'd
  really save. Easier said…

The cut version is friendlier and less preachy than the full proverb: you're reminding, not
lecturing. For a learner it's also a trap: you need to know the whole proverb to understand the
half. When you hear a sentence trail off after something that sounds like a saying, that's what's
happening.

Speakers also play with proverbs, extending or twisting them for a laugh: *Perro que ladra no
muerde… pero por si las moscas, no le des la mano* (A barking dog doesn't bite… but just to be safe,
don't hold out your hand).

## Mexico and Spain

Most proverbs are shared across the Spanish-speaking world, but many have local versions, and the
version you choose tells people where you learned your Spanish:

| Mexico | Spain | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *A caballo regalado no se le ve el colmillo.* | *A caballo regalado no le mires el diente.* | Don't look a gift horse in the mouth. |
| *Al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda.* | *A quien madruga, Dios le ayuda.* | The early bird catches the worm. |

The Mexican horse shows its *colmillo* (canine tooth); in Spain it's *el diente*. In the second
pair the pronoun differs: Mexico usually says *lo ayuda*, Spain often *le ayuda*. Many other variants
exist; these are the usual forms.

## Proverbs in conversation and headlines

In conversation, proverbs do four jobs: they advise (*No le busques más: a caballo regalado…*),
console (*No hay mal que por bien no venga* — Every cloud has a silver lining), comment on
someone's behavior (*En casa de herrero, cuchillo de palo*), and close a topic, because there's
little left to say after a proverb. They sound wise from an older person and slightly ironic from a
young one. In a formal text, one well-chosen proverb can open or close a column, but not more.

Headlines love them, usually twisted. These are invented examples of the pattern:

- *Del dicho al hecho: el puente prometido cumple cinco años en maqueta.* — From word to deed: the
  promised bridge marks five years as a model.
- *En casa de herrero, wifi de palo: la oficina de innovación, sin internet.* — The innovation
  office has no internet.

The joke works only if the reader knows the original, which is why headlines use the best-known
proverbs.

## False friends among proverbs

Some Spanish proverbs match English ones closely: *Perro que ladra no muerde* and "Barking dogs
seldom bite"; *Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho* and "Easier said than done". Others share a
meaning but use a different picture: "The shoemaker's children go barefoot" is the blacksmith's
wooden knife; "Speak of the devil" is *Hablando del rey de Roma* (speaking of the king of Rome). And
some look like a match but aren't: "The early bird catches the worm" encourages getting up early,
but Spanish also has the opposite warning, *No por mucho madrugar amanece más temprano* (Getting up
early won't make the sun rise sooner): rushing doesn't speed things up. Translate the meaning, never
the words.

## Reading: Grandma has a proverb for everything

Diego, 24, visits his grandmother Chelo in Puebla after a bad week. *La chamba* (B1) is a job.

```dialogue
# Con la abuela Chelo
Diego: Abuela, estoy de malas. Me ofrecieron una chamba en una agencia de diseño, pero les dije que lo iba a pensar, y cuando les hablé ya habían contratado a otra persona.
Abuela Chelo: Ay, mijo. Camarón que se duerme…
Diego: …se lo lleva la corriente, ya sé. Y luego mi jefe actual me prometió un aumento en enero.
Abuela Chelo: Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho. Yo que tú, seguía buscando.
Diego: Pues sí. Y mi tío Toño me regaló su computadora vieja. Es lentísima.
Abuela Chelo: A caballo regalado no se le ve el colmillo. Úsala mientras juntas para una nueva.
Diego: Lo peor es que mi jefa grita todo el día. Me tiene con los nervios de punta.
Abuela Chelo: ¿Te ha hecho algo, aparte de gritar?
Diego: No, la verdad no. Grita y al rato se le pasa.
Abuela Chelo: Entonces perro que ladra no muerde.
Diego: Abuela, tú tienes un refranero en la cabeza. ¿Y para ti no hay refrán? Llevas diez años diciendo que vas a arreglar esa ventana.
Abuela Chelo: Ah, pues para eso también hay uno: en casa de herrero, cuchillo de palo. Tu abuelo era carpintero, ¿te acuerdas?
Diego: Eso no es sabiduría popular, abuela. Eso es pretexto.
```

Summary. Diego lost a job offer because he took too long to answer; his grandmother reminds him
that those who hesitate lose out. His boss promised a raise, and she warns that promises aren't
facts. He complains about an old computer his uncle gave him, and she tells him not to criticize a
gift. His boss shouts but does nothing worse, so her bark is worse than her bite. Finally Diego
teases her about a window she never fixes, and she answers with the proverb of the blacksmith's
wooden knife (his grandfather was a carpenter); he calls it an excuse.

Glosses. *Estoy de malas* — I'm in a bad mood (the opposite of B1's *estar de buenas*). *Cuando les
hablé* — when I called them (Mexico: *hablarle a alguien*, to phone someone). *Yo que tú, seguía buscando* — If I were you,
I'd keep looking (the imperfect in place of the conditional is common in speech). *Juntas* — you
save up. *Me tiene con los nervios de punta* — she has me on edge. *Al rato se le pasa* — it passes
after a while.

## Choosing the right proverb

Knowing what a proverb means isn't enough; it has to fit the situation exactly.

### Example 1: a gift with flaws

Situation: your friend Ana got a free secondhand bike from a neighbor, and she's complaining that
the seat is old. Which proverb fits: *Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente*, *A caballo
regalado no se le ve el colmillo* or *Perro que ladra no muerde*?

1. Name the situation in plain words: someone is criticizing something they got for free.
2. Find the proverb whose lesson matches: *a caballo regalado* is exactly "don't criticize a gift".
   Its picture even matches: you don't check the teeth of a horse you didn't pay for.
3. Check the others. *Camarón que se duerme* is about missing a chance by being slow; nobody missed
   anything here. *Perro que ladra* is about threats that come to nothing; there's no threat.
4. Decide on full or cut form. Among friends, the cut form is warmer: *Ay, Ana, a caballo
   regalado…*

### Example 2: a promise or a threat?

Situation: a city council member announces that she'll close down every noisy bar on your street
"this month". Your neighbor is worried. You doubt anything will happen. Do you say *Del dicho al
hecho hay mucho trecho* or *Perro que ladra no muerde*?

1. Ask what kind of statement it is. To the bar owners it's a threat; to your neighbor, who
   wants quiet, it's a promise.
2. *Perro que ladra no muerde* fits a threat from someone who makes noise but doesn't act: it would
   reassure the bar owners.
3. *Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho* fits any announcement that may never be carried out, and
   it's the natural thing to say to your neighbor: don't expect too much.
4. So the answer depends on who you're talking to. With your neighbor: *Pues del dicho al hecho hay
   mucho trecho.* With a bar owner: *Tranquilo, perro que ladra no muerde.*

## Common mistakes

- Mixing the halves of two proverbs: ~~*Camarón que se duerme no muerde*~~. Learn each proverb as
  one unit.
- Changing the words: ~~*No le mires la boca a un caballo regalado*~~, built on the English, will be
  understood, but it sounds like a translation. Use one of the established forms in the table above.
- Translating English proverbs word for word: ~~*El pájaro temprano agarra el gusano*~~ → *Al que
  madruga, Dios lo ayuda*.
- Using a proverb in the wrong situation: *Camarón que se duerme* to someone who has just lost a
  relative would be cruel, not wise.
- Piling them up. One proverb is wisdom; three in a row is a parody.

## Key points

- A proverb (*refrán, proverbio*) is a short, anonymous sentence of practical wisdom; an *aforismo*
  has an author, and a *máxima* is a rule of conduct.
- Proverbs are built to be remembered: two balanced halves, rhythm, rhyme or assonance, missing verbs
  and timeless subjects.
- Speakers often say only the first half (*Camarón que se duerme…*), so learn every proverb whole.
- Mexico and Spain sometimes differ: *no se le ve el colmillo / no le mires el diente*.
- To choose a proverb, name the situation plainly, match its lesson, and think about who's
  listening.
