## What this lesson is for

The Boom generation read lesson 92's Rulfo as a master. In the 1960s a handful of
Latin American novelists became world famous almost at once, and the label **[[the Boom]]** (*el
Boom*, from the English word) stuck. This lesson treats it as two things at once, a literary
movement and a publishing phenomenon, and asks who was left out. It ends with an original opening
of a family saga and an analysis of its techniques.

## A movement and a market

The Boom is usually dated to the 1960s, though critics argue about where it begins and ends.
Writers who had been publishing for years suddenly found readers across Latin America, in Spain
and in translation. Several forces came together:

- Publishers: in Barcelona, Seix Barral, whose editor Carlos Barral ran the Premio Biblioteca
  Breve; in Buenos Aires, Editorial Sudamericana; in Mexico, the Fondo de Cultura Económica and
  Joaquín Mortiz.
- An agent: Carmen Balcells (1930–2015), the Barcelona *agente literaria* who handled García
  Márquez's rights from the early 1960s and represented Vargas Llosa, Fuentes and José Donoso,
  among many others. Writers called her the "Mamá Grande" of the Boom; she pushed for contracts
  limited by territory and time, at a time when a book was often sold to one publisher for good.
- Politics: the Cuban Revolution (1959) turned the world's eyes to Latin America, and its later
  turns, especially the jailing of the poet Heberto Padilla in 1971, divided the group.

Most Boom novels are *experimentales*: they take from the European and American *vanguardia*
(avant-garde) a freedom with time, voice and structure that Rulfo had already shown.

## Four names

- Gabriel García Márquez (Aracataca, Colombia, 1927 – Mexico City, 2014): *Cien años de soledad*
  (Buenos Aires, 1967), written in Mexico City. Nobel Prize in Literature, 1982. In brief: the
  Buendía family founds the isolated town of Macondo, and over seven generations its members
  repeat the same names, passions and solitudes, through civil wars, a banana boom and a
  massacre, until the last adult of the line deciphers a prophecy about the family and the town
  disappears.
- Mario Vargas Llosa (Arequipa, Peru, 1936 – Lima, 2025): *La ciudad y los perros* (1963), about
  the cadets of a military school in Lima, winner of the Premio Biblioteca Breve; the book's
  success was his *consagración*. Nobel Prize, 2010.
- Carlos Fuentes (Panama City, 1928 – Mexico City, 2012; Mexican): *La muerte de Artemio Cruz*
  (1962). A dying magnate who fought in the Revolution and grew rich betraying it remembers his
  life in three voices: *yo* for his present agony, *tú*, in the future tense, for something like
  his conscience, and *él* for his past.
- Julio Cortázar (Brussels, 1914 – Paris, 1984; Argentine): *Rayuela* (1963), set in Paris and
  Buenos Aires, which its first page invites you to read in more than one order, like the
  hopscotch game of its title.

## Magical realism, the total novel, the dictator

**[[Magical realism]]** (B1 taught *el realismo mágico*) is a label with a history: a German critic,
Franz Roh, used it for painting in 1925, and in 1949 the Cuban Alejo Carpentier proposed *lo real
maravilloso*, the marvelous that he said was part of American reality. Applied to García
Márquez, it came to mean the impossible narrated as normal. Use it with care: Vargas Llosa is a
realist, Cortázar writes the fantastic, and critics warn that the label became a marketing
formula.

*La novela total* is a term associated above all with Vargas Llosa: a novel that tries to contain
a whole world, its history, myths, classes and voices. *Cien años* and *Artemio Cruz* are its
usual examples.

Several writers took on *el dictador*: Miguel Ángel Asturias, *El Señor Presidente* (1946); Augusto
Roa Bastos, *Yo el Supremo* (1974); Carpentier, *El recurso del método* (1974); García Márquez, *El
otoño del patriarca* (1975); and later Vargas Llosa, *La fiesta del Chivo* (2000).

## Who was left out

The famous list is all men. Elena Garro and Rosario Castellanos (lesson 92) were writing major
novels in the same years, and critics today discuss why they were rarely counted. After the Boom
(the "post-Boom" of the 1970s and 1980s) came writers such as Isabel Allende, whose *La casa de
los espíritus* (1982) is a family saga, and Elena Poniatowska (Paris, 1932), whose *Hasta no verte
Jesús mío* (1969) and *La noche de Tlatelolco* (1971) mix testimony and fiction; she won the
Premio Cervantes, often called the highest prize for literature in
Spanish, in 2013. A *consagrado* writer like her is an established one.

## The text: the opening of a saga

The text is original. A *saga* follows a family, its *estirpe* (lineage), over generations.

![A family tree in three generations, titled La familia Villaseñor. At the top, Eusebio Villaseñor, the patriarch (1891), married to Altagracia Luna. Below them, their three children: Joaquín, the eldest; Consuelo, who moves to the capital; and Benigno, who plays the violin. Joaquín is married to Mercedes Ortiz; below them, their two children, Eusebio and Altagracia, named after their grandparents. An equals sign marks each marriage.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> #### La casa de los Villaseñor
>
> Eusebio Villaseñor llegó a Santa Rita de los Vientos en 1891 con una mula, un baúl de libros que
> no sabía leer y la escritura de unas tierras que había ganado en una partida de dominó a un
> coronel borracho. Nadie en el puerto creyó que aquel papel valiera nada, porque las tierras
> estaban del otro lado del río, donde el monte era tan espeso que de día había que encender
> faroles. Pero Eusebio no era hombre de dudas. En seis meses desmontó el terreno, en un año
> sembró el primer café, y en diez construyó una casa con tantos cuartos que nunca supo contarlos.
>
> Se casó con Altagracia Luna, la hija del farmacéutico, una muchacha seria que tenía la costumbre
> de contestar las preguntas antes de que se las hicieran. Al principio aquello asustaba a las
> visitas; con el tiempo, todo el pueblo se acostumbró, y cuando alguien iba a la casa con una
> pregunta difícil, se quedaba callado en la puerta para ahorrarse la molestia de formularla.
> Altagracia le dio a su marido tres hijos, una biblioteca ordenada y la única regla que la familia
> respetaría durante cien años: en la casa de los Villaseñor nadie podía irse a dormir enojado.
>
> Joaquín, el mayor, heredó la terquedad de su padre y la hacienda entera. Consuelo heredó los
> silencios de su madre y se fue a vivir a la capital, de donde mandaba cartas tan largas que había
> que leerlas en tres días. Benigno, el menor, no heredó nada que se pudiera medir: tocaba el violín
> de oído y aseguraba que los cafetos crecían mejor si les cantaba. Por más que su padre se burlara
> de él, la parte del cafetal donde Benigno tocaba daba siempre los granos más grandes, y nadie
> se atrevió nunca a explicar por qué.
>
> Cuando llegó la Revolución, llegó también a Santa Rita, con retraso y en forma de un coronel
> sudado que venía a llevarse los caballos. Altagracia lo recibió en la puerta, le dijo que los
> caballos estaban en el potrero de atrás, que su hijo Joaquín no iba a irse con la tropa y que
> el café recién hecho estaba en la mesa. El coronel, que todavía no había abierto la boca, se
> tomó el café, se llevó dos caballos en lugar de diez y se fue con la incómoda sensación de que
> alguien había hablado por él. Años después contaba, en cantinas lejanas, que en una casa junto
> al río una mujer le había ganado una discusión que él no había empezado.
>
> Fue Joaquín quien se casó con Mercedes Ortiz y quien, para disgusto de su madre, insistió en
> ponerles a sus hijos los nombres de los abuelos. Altagracia, que ya sabía lo que iba a pasar,
> le advirtió que los nombres repetidos acaban repitiendo las vidas. Joaquín se rio. Nació un
> segundo Eusebio, que desde la cuna miraba el río como si quisiera cruzarlo, y una segunda
> Altagracia, que a los cuatro años empezó a terminar las frases de los demás.
>
> El patriarca envejeció sin enfermarse, como envejecen los árboles. Cuando cumplió noventa años,
> mandó sacar su sillón al corredor y anunció que no volvería a levantarse hasta que alguien de la
> familia le leyera en voz alta todos los libros del baúl, que seguían intactos. Su nieta, la
> segunda Altagracia, que tenía entonces doce años, se sentó a su lado con el primer libro. Tardó
> tres años en terminar el baúl. La tarde en que cerró el último volumen, Eusebio Villaseñor le
> dio las gracias, cerró los ojos y se quedó dormido para siempre, con una sonrisa de quien por fin
> ha entendido algo.
>
> Esa misma noche, el río, que llevaba un siglo en su lugar, cambió de curso sin hacer ruido, y a la
> mañana siguiente la casa amaneció del otro lado, junto al puerto, como si hubiera querido
> acercarse al mundo. Nadie en Santa Rita lo comentó demasiado. Estaban acostumbrados a los
> Villaseñor.

Glosses: *la escritura* (title deed), *la partida de dominó* (game of dominoes), *el monte* (here:
dense forest), *desmontar* (to clear land), *la terquedad* (stubbornness), *el cafeto* (coffee
plant), *de oído* (by ear), *el corredor* (veranda).

In brief: in 1891 Eusebio Villaseñor reaches the port of Santa Rita de los Vientos with a mule, a
trunk of books he can't read and the deed to jungle land he won at dominoes. He clears it, plants
coffee and builds a house with uncountable rooms. His wife Altagracia answers questions before
they're asked and sets one rule: nobody goes to bed angry. Of their children, Joaquín inherits
the land, Consuelo moves to the capital, and Benigno plays the violin to the coffee plants, which
grow bigger beans. When a revolutionary colonel comes for the horses, Altagracia answers him
before he speaks, and he leaves with two instead of ten. Joaquín names his children after their grandparents, despite his
mother's warning that repeated names repeat lives, and the new Eusebio and Altagracia resemble them. At
ninety the patriarch waits for someone to read him every book in the trunk; his granddaughter
takes three years, and he dies smiling. That night the river changes course and the house wakes
up on the other side. Nobody is surprised.

### Example 1: what makes it "magical"

The impossible (answers before questions, the singing that grows coffee, the river that moves a
house) is told in the same calm voice as the coffee harvest, and the town *se acostumbró*: that
calm is what critics call magical realism. Note the narrator's distance: an omniscient,
third-person voice that summarizes decades in a sentence (*En seis meses… en un año… en diez*).

### Example 2: the techniques of a saga

- Repetition across the *estirpe*: names that return (*Eusebio, Altagracia*) and a warning that
  lives will return too. Picture the tree: the third generation mirrors the first.
- Hyperbole and exact numbers side by side (*tantos cuartos que nunca supo contarlos; tres años*).
- A founding story: the *patriarca* wins the land by chance and tames it by will.
- C1 grammar at work: a cleft (*Fue Joaquín quien…*), a concessive (*Por más que su padre se
  burlara*), *como si* + pluperfect subjunctive (*como si hubiera querido acercarse*).

## Pronunciation

*Boom* is said as in English, roughly *bum*. *Estirpe* is *es-tir-pe*, stress on *tir*.
*Patriarca* has three syllables: *pa-triar-ca*, stress on *triar*.

## Common mistakes

- Treating every Boom novel as magical realism: *La ciudad y los perros* is realist, *Rayuela*
  experimental.
- Using *la estirpe* for a social class: it is a lineage (*la estirpe de los Buendía*); a class is
  *la clase social*.
- *Consagrado* (acclaimed, established) is not "sacred" in this sense: *un autor consagrado*.

## Key points

- The Boom (1960s): García Márquez, Vargas Llosa, Fuentes, Cortázar; publishers, prizes and the
  agent Carmen Balcells.
- Magical realism (Roh 1925, Carpentier 1949), the total novel, the dictator novel.
- Garro, Castellanos, Allende and Poniatowska (Premio Cervantes 2013) complete the picture.
- A saga: lineage, repeated names, a founding patriarch, the impossible told calmly.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

sections.name: Los matices del subjuntivo (nuance in the subjunctive)
Conectar con precisión (connectors, cohesion and argument)
La lengua idiomática (idioms, collocations and verbs with prepositions)
Lengua académica y textos largos (academic language and longer texts)
La lengua en uso y el DELE C1 (language in use and the C1 exam)
Honors: Clásicos de la literatura en español (classics of literature in Spanish)

questions.stem: When were the two parts of Cervantes's Don Quijote published?
questions.explanation: Part I came out in 1605 and Part II in 1615. Cervantes was born in 1547 and died in 1616; 1571 is Lepanto and 1575–1580 his captivity in Algiers; 1614 is the year of Avellaneda's false sequel.

questions.stem: What did a chivalric romance (una novela de caballerías) usually tell?
choices: The life of a poor boy who serves one master after another
The letters of two lovers separated by war
The adventures of a knight-errant who fights giants and enchanters for a lady
The history of a real Spanish king, year by year
questions.explanation: The genre followed a caballero andante through endless fights and enchantments, for the love of a lady; Amadís de Gaula is the best-known Spanish example. A boy serving several masters is the picaresque Lazarillo de Tormes, a different genre.

questions.stem: After the windmill throws him to the ground, how does don Quijote explain what happened?
choices: Sancho had tricked him for a joke.
An enchanter turned the giants into windmills to rob him of the victory.
The wind was stronger than any giant.
questions.explanation: He never admits that they were windmills all along: an enchanter, he says, changed the giants into mills. That is how his madness protects itself throughout Part I.

questions.stem: Which of these is one reason critics give for calling Don Quijote "the first modern novel"?
choices: It was the first long prose fiction ever written.
It has no humor, unlike the romances it replaced.
It is set in an imaginary kingdom far from Spain.
Its narrator plays with the fiction, claiming to follow an Arabic manuscript by an invented historian.
questions.explanation: The game with Cide Hamete Benengeli's "manuscript" is one of the reasons, with characters who change through conversation and adventures on real Spanish roads. It wasn't the first long prose fiction (the lesson names earlier works), it is very funny, and it is set in real La Mancha.

questions.stem: Match each form from the Spanish of 1605 to its modern equivalent.
questions.explanation: Vuestra merced (your grace) shrank into usted; agora and mesmo are old forms of ahora and mismo; the old x of dixo became the j sound, spelled j; ínsula is the bookish word don Quijote uses for Sancho's island. Vosotros is Spain's plural "you", not a modern form of any of these.

questions.stem: The imitation "Si alguno viniere, avísame" uses the future subjunctive. Complete the modern version with the right form of venir: "Si alguien ___, avísame."
questions.explanation: In a modern "if" clause about the future, Spanish uses the present indicative: Si alguien viene, avísame (If anyone comes, let me know). The future subjunctive (viniere) survives only in legal texts and set phrases; the present subjunctive (venga) is not used after si.

questions.stem: Name the numbered places on this simplified map of don Quijote's world.

image.alt: A simplified, unlabeled map of La Mancha with six numbered places: 1 a cluster of houses in the middle, 2 a single house with a sign to the west, 3 three windmills to the east, 4 a small church to the northeast, 5 mountains to the south, and 6 an arrow leaving the map toward the northeast.

questions.explanation: The village (never named in the novel) is in the middle; the inn (la venta), where he is dubbed a knight, is a single house with a sign; the windmills are the giants; El Toboso is Dulcinea's town; Sierra Morena is the mountain range to the south; Barcelona, where he is defeated, lies far to the northeast. Alcalá de Henares is Cervantes's birthplace, and Lepanto a naval battle, not places on this map.

questions.stem: Who was "Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda"?
choices: The innkeeper who dubs don Quijote a knight
The neighbor who defeats him as the Knight of the White Moon
The pen name of the unknown author of a false Part II, published in 1614
questions.explanation: Avellaneda published an unauthorized sequel in 1614, and his identity is still debated; Cervantes answered him inside his own Part II (1615). Don Quijote dies as Alonso Quijano, and the Knight of the White Moon is a neighbor in disguise.

questions.stem: In the lesson's "lost chapter", why does Sancho refuse to govern the "island" of Mexico City?
choices: Governing Barataria cost him sleep, the city's troubles look endless, and a taco with a friend is island enough.
Lupita tells him that only Mexicans may govern the city.
He is afraid that don Quijote will be jealous.
He wants to go back to Guanajuato to see the museum.
questions.explanation: He looks at the traffic, thinks of the quarrels and complaints of twenty million neighbors, recalls that ten days in Barataria cost him more sleep than his whole life as a farmer, and decides that a taco and a friend are enough. Nothing in the text supports the other three.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish (a reduplicated concessive, as Sancho says it).
questions.prompt: However they offer it to me, I don't want it.
questions.explanation: The reduplicated concessive repeats the subjunctive around como: me la ofrezcan como me la ofrezcan (however they offer it to me). It can open the sentence or follow the main clause. The indicative ofrecen would state a fact, not "whatever way they might".

questions.stem: "Abrir una librería en ese pueblo de cien habitantes fue un proyecto quijotesco." What does quijotesco mean here?
questions.explanation: Quijotesco (quixotic) describes a generous ideal pursued with little regard for reality, like don Quijote's. It isn't simply comic, outdated or risky. Note the lowercase q.

questions.stem: Complete: "Al final de la novela, don Quijote recupera la ___ y muere como Alonso Quijano."
questions.explanation: La cordura is sanity: he recovers it on his deathbed. La quimera is a pipe dream, una andanza an adventure, and la locura (madness) is what he loses at the start, not what he recovers.

questions.stem: In the lesson's model commentary on the inn episode, which sentence gives the reasoned judgment?
choices: El episodio de la venta pertenece a los primeros capítulos de la primera parte (1605).
En él, don Quijote confunde una venta con un castillo.
A mi juicio, el episodio es más que una broma, porque muestra que todos necesitamos historias.
Lo que llama la atención es el doble juego del narrador.
questions.explanation: A mi juicio… porque… gives a personal assessment with its reason: that is the judgment. The first sentence situates the episode, the second summarizes it, and Lo que llama la atención introduces the interpretation.

questions.stem: Put these episodes in the order in which they happen in the novel.
choices: The innkeeper dubs him a knight in a mock ceremony.
He charges the windmills, thinking they are giants.
He is defeated on a beach in Barcelona.
He recovers his sanity and dies as Alonso Quijano.
questions.explanation: The inn and the windmills belong to Part I (1605); Barataria, the defeat by the Knight of the White Moon in Barcelona and the death at home to Part II (1615), in that order.

questions.stem: What can you say accurately about Sor Juana's year of birth?
choices: She was born in 1651; no other year has ever been proposed.
She was born in 1695, the year of the epidemic.
Sources give 1651 (her first biographer) or 1648 (a baptism record many scholars accept).
She was born in Mexico City in 1669.
questions.explanation: The year is disputed, so the honest answer names both: 1651 comes from her first biographer, 1648 from a baptism record. She was born in San Miguel Nepantla; 1669 is the year she took her vows, and 1695 the year she died.

questions.stem: In which convent did Sor Juana take her vows in 1669 and spend the rest of her life?
choices: The Discalced Carmelites, in Mexico City
questions.explanation: She took her vows at San Jerónimo in 1669; the building now houses the Universidad del Claustro de Sor Juana. She had spent a few months with the Discalced Carmelites in 1667 and left. She never lived in Puebla or Spain.

questions.stem: Put these events of Sor Juana's life in chronological order.
choices: She serves at the viceregal court.
She spends a few months with the Discalced Carmelites.
She takes her vows at San Jerónimo.
Inundación castálida is printed in Madrid.
The bishop of Puebla prints her Carta atenagórica.
She writes the Respuesta a sor Filotea.
questions.explanation: Court (about 1664–1667), the Carmelites (1667), San Jerónimo (1669), Inundación castálida (1689), the Carta atenagórica (1690), the Respuesta (dated 1691) and her death (1695).

questions.stem: Who was "Sor Filotea de la Cruz"?
choices: Sor Juana's sister in the convent
A nun from Spain who published her poems
The pen name of the bishop of Puebla, who printed her critique and advised her to leave secular study
questions.explanation: The bishop of Puebla signed his letter "Sor Filotea de la Cruz". Sor Juana's Respuesta answers him. The vicereine who helped publish her poems was María Luisa Manrique de Lara.

questions.stem: Match each name or term to its description.
choices: wit of ideas: puns and paradoxes
ornament of form: Latinate words, reordered syntax, mythology
the poet behind the name gongorismo
questions.explanation: Conceptismo works through ideas, culteranismo through form. Francisco de Quevedo is the great conceptista, and culteranismo is also called gongorismo after Luis de Góngora. Amadís de Gaula is a chivalric romance in Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo's version, unrelated to either.

questions.stem: The lesson's original line "Tanto me alejo de mí por buscarte, que cuando al fin te encuentro, ya no me encuentro" is in the spirit of which current, and why?
choices: Culteranismo, because it uses words from Latin
Conceptismo, because its wit lies in an idea: the verb encontrar turns against itself
Culteranismo, because the word order is reversed
Conceptismo, because it alludes to mythology
questions.explanation: The sentence has plain words and normal order; its cleverness is a paradox built on encontrar (finding you means losing myself). That is conceptismo. Latinate words, reordered syntax and mythology belong to culteranismo.

questions.stem: In the lesson's culterano example "Del alba el oro, que en cristal desata la fuente, al monte da su luz primera", what is the subject of desata?
questions.explanation: Rebuilt in normal order: El oro del alba, que la fuente desata en cristal, da al monte su primera luz. Inside the relative clause, la fuente (the spring) sets loose the gold (que); the gold of dawn is the subject of the main verb da, and el monte receives the light. Finding the verbs first and asking who does each one is the strategy.

questions.stem: Complete with the adjective meaning "self-taught": "De niña, sor Juana leyó la biblioteca de su abuelo; fue en gran parte ___."
questions.explanation: Autodidacta is the usual form for both genders (él es autodidacta, ella es autodidacta). The DLE also has a masculine autodidacto, much less common.

questions.stem: Which banknote has shown Sor Juana since November 12, 2020?
choices: The vertical 100-peso note, with the monarch butterfly reserve on the back
The 200-peso note, with Hidalgo and Morelos
questions.explanation: Banxico put the vertical 100-peso note with Sor Juana into circulation on November 12, 2020; its back shows the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve. She was on the 1,000-peso note from 1978 and the 200-peso note from 1994 until a new design with Hidalgo and Morelos replaced her in 2019.

questions.stem: Build Isabel's wish in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I wish I had had someone to explain it to me.
questions.explanation: A regret about the past takes ojalá + pluperfect subjunctive (hubiera tenido; hubiese tenido is also correct). The relative clause describes someone who didn't exist, so it takes the subjunctive too, in the past: que me lo explicara. The indicative explica would describe a real, known person.

questions.stem: In the letter, what is Isabel's dilemma?
choices: Whether to leave Puebla and work in Mexico City
Whether to marry a merchant's son or enter a convent, when she fears both may close the door to books
Whether to publish a book of poems
Whether to sell her father's printing shop
questions.explanation: Her father wants her to marry a kind but unbookish merchant's son; her confessor suggests a convent; she doesn't know whether she has a vocation as a nun or only as a reader, and fears that either road will end her reading.

questions.stem: Isabel writes "¡Quién tuviera esa pluma!" after imagining Sor Juana's answer to the friar. What does she mean?
choices: Someone should lend her a pen.
She asks who wrote the friar's joke.
I wish I could write like that!
questions.explanation: ¡Quién + imperfect subjunctive! expresses a wish the speaker thinks unlikely, here about herself: if only I had that pen (that skill as a writer). It isn't a question about who has the pen.

questions.stem: According to the lesson, which ideas does Sor Juana defend in the Respuesta? Select all that apply.
choices: Women should be able to teach girls.
Even a kitchen is a place for observing the world.
Only nuns should be allowed to read.
Women should stay away from all learning except prayer.
questions.explanation: She tells her own story of study and argues, with examples of learned women, that women may study and teach girls, and that the whole world, even a kitchen, can be observed. The last two are the opposite of her argument.

questions.stem: In New Spain, who was la virreina?
choices: A woman who governed New Spain for the king
questions.explanation: El virrey governed for the king; la virreina was usually his wife and had no office of her own, though vicereines such as Leonor Carreto and María Luisa Manrique de Lara mattered greatly to Sor Juana. An abbess is la abadesa.

questions.stem: How did Mariano Azuela's Los de abajo first appear?
choices: As a film script in Mexico City, 1940
In installments in a Spanish-language newspaper in El Paso, Texas, in 1915
In a magazine in Buenos Aires, 1955
questions.explanation: Los de abajo was serialized in El Paso in 1915, while the Revolution was still being fought. Madrid, 1929 is Guzmán's La sombra del caudillo, and 1955 is the year of Pedro Páramo.

questions.stem: What gives Nellie Campobello's Cartucho (1931) its special point of view?
choices: It is told by a general who later became president.
It is narrated by the town itself.
It is a long novel told by a landowner.
Its very short scenes of the war are seen through the eyes of a girl.
questions.explanation: Cartucho collects very short scenes of the Revolution in the north, seen by a girl, in a plain voice that makes the violence hard to forget. The town as narrator is Garro's Los recuerdos del porvenir.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: a strongman who leads by force and loyalty
a farmhand who works the land
questions.explanation: A caudillo leads an army or a nation; a cacique controls a town or region; the hacendado owns the estate and the peón works it; the ejido was the land reform's main form of land grant. The viceroy's wife is la virreina (lesson 91).

questions.stem: How does Pedro Páramo begin, in the lesson's summary?
choices: Juan Preciado goes to Comala to find his father, as he promised his dying mother.
Pedro Páramo returns to Comala after the Revolution to find his son.
Susana San Juan writes letters to Juan Preciado from Mexico City.
A teacher arrives in an abandoned town to reopen the school.
questions.explanation: Juan Preciado's promise to his mother takes him to Comala, where he slowly understands that everyone, and then he himself, is dead. The teacher in an abandoned town belongs to the lesson's original story, not to Rulfo.

questions.stem: What is an interior monologue?
choices: A speech a character gives to an audience
A letter written by a character
A character's thoughts given directly, as they flow, without "he thought"
A narrator's summary of what everyone thinks
questions.explanation: An interior monologue lets us into the flow of a mind without a narrator in between. A public speech or a letter is addressed to others, and a narrator who reports everyone's thoughts is an omniscient narrator.

questions.stem: Which techniques does the lesson attribute to Pedro Páramo? Select all that apply.
choices: Short fragments with no chapter titles
Two lines of time cut together
A single narrator who explains everything at the end
Strict chronological order from birth to death
questions.explanation: The novel is made of about seventy fragments, gives voice to the dead and cuts Juan Preciado's journey together with Pedro Páramo's past. That is why it is polyphonic: no single narrator explains everything, and time doesn't run in order.

questions.stem: Who narrates Elena Garro's Los recuerdos del porvenir (1963)?
choices: A general who occupies the town
A dead man speaking from his grave
questions.explanation: Garro's narrator is the town of Ixtepec, remembering the Cristero years. The girl in Chiapas narrates much of Castellanos's Balún Canán, and the voices of the dead belong to Pedro Páramo.

questions.stem: Where and when is Rosario Castellanos's Balún Canán (1957) set?
choices: In Mexico City during the Cristero conflict
In Comitán, Chiapas, in the 1930s, during the land reform
questions.explanation: A landowning family in Comitán faces the land reform of the 1930s, and a girl slowly sees the injustice done to the Tseltal workers. Comala is Rulfo's town; the Cristero years are Garro's setting.

questions.stem: "Agua Escondida" is told out of order. Put these events in the order in which they happened.
choices: The ejido assembly divides don Celso's pasture (1938).
Rosa writes from Chicago, begging the family not to sell (1991).
The narrator's mother makes him promise not to sign without seeing the town.
He arrives in the empty village on a Thursday.
At dawn he tears up the sale contract.
questions.explanation: Fragment 2 (1938) comes first, then the letter of fragment 6 (1991), the mother's request in hospital (7), the arrival (1) and the ending (8). Placing each fragment on a timeline is the second reading question: when?

questions.stem: Who most likely speaks in fragment 4 of "Agua Escondida", the one in italics?
choices: The old landowner whose pasture was taken
questions.explanation: Nobody names him, but the speaker lost his pasture "con un papel", kept the big house and used to count his cows: the landowner don Celso of fragment 2. The italics and the flow of thought without a listener mark it as an interior monologue.

questions.stem: Which motif links fragments 1, 4 and 8 of "Agua Escondida"?
questions.explanation: The bell moves by itself in 1, the old man hears it alone in 4, and it rings once in 8. The blackboard links fragments 3 and 8; the letter and the stream appear only once.

questions.stem: Complete with the adjective meaning "fragmentary", in the right form: "Pedro Páramo tiene una estructura ___."
questions.explanation: Estructura is feminine, so fragmentario becomes fragmentaria.

questions.stem: Build the sentence from Rosa's letter in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Tell Mom not to sell the land.
questions.explanation: Decir que + subjunctive passes on a request (lesson 05): Dile que no venda. With the indicative, Dile que no vende would report a fact (tell her she isn't selling).

questions.stem: Why does the lesson say that the name Pedro Páramo is suggestive?
choices: Páramo is the name of a real town in Jalisco.
Páramo means a rich, green valley.
Páramo is an old word for a priest.
Un páramo is a barren plain, and the cacique leaves wasteland behind him.
questions.explanation: Un páramo is a wasteland, a barren plain (in the Andes, a cold high grassland). The man who lets Comala die carries the image of desolation in his surname.

questions.stem: Where and when was Cien años de soledad first published?
questions.explanation: Editorial Sudamericana published it in Buenos Aires in 1967; García Márquez wrote it in Mexico City. 1982 is the year of his Nobel Prize; 1962 and 1963 are the years of Artemio Cruz and of La ciudad y los perros and Rayuela.

questions.stem: Who was Carmen Balcells?
choices: A Barcelona literary agent who represented García Márquez, Vargas Llosa, Fuentes and many others
A Mexican novelist left out of the Boom
The editor of the Premio Biblioteca Breve
questions.explanation: Balcells (1930–2015) was the Boom's great literary agent, handling García Márquez's rights from the early 1960s; writers called her the Mamá Grande. Carlos Barral, at Seix Barral, ran the Premio Biblioteca Breve.

questions.stem: Match each writer to his novel.
questions.explanation: Cien años de soledad (1967), La ciudad y los perros (1963), La muerte de Artemio Cruz (1962) and Rayuela (1963). Pedro Páramo (1955) is Juan Rulfo's, before the Boom.

questions.stem: How does Carlos Fuentes tell Artemio Cruz's life?
choices: Through the voices of the dead in a town
As a play in three acts
In three voices: yo for his present agony, tú in the future tense, él for his past
questions.explanation: The three grammatical persons divide the novel: yo, the dying man now; tú, a voice like his conscience, in the future tense; él, the past he betrayed. The voices of the dead are Pedro Páramo's.

questions.stem: What did Alejo Carpentier propose in 1949?
choices: The term "magical realism", for German painting
Lo real maravilloso: the marvelous as part of American reality
questions.explanation: Carpentier's lo real maravilloso (1949) claimed that the marvelous belongs to American reality itself. Franz Roh used "magical realism" for painting in 1925; "total novel" is associated with Vargas Llosa; Asturias's El Señor Presidente (1946) came earlier.

questions.stem: Which of these are dictator novels? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Asturias (1946), Roa Bastos (1974) and García Márquez (1975) all built novels around a dictator. Rayuela is an experimental novel set in Paris and Buenos Aires, and Balún Canán is about a family in Chiapas during the land reform.

questions.stem: Which writer won the Premio Cervantes in 2013?
questions.explanation: Elena Poniatowska, author of Hasta no verte Jesús mío (1969) and La noche de Tlatelolco (1971), won the 2013 Premio Cervantes. Castellanos died in 1974 and Garro in 1998; Allende is known for La casa de los espíritus (1982).

questions.stem: Name the people in the empty boxes of the Villaseñor family tree.

image.alt: A family tree in three generations with four empty, numbered boxes: 1 the spouse of Eusebio Villaseñor at the top; 2 the third child, beside Joaquín and Consuelo; 3 the spouse of Joaquín; 4 the second child of Joaquín, beside the grandson Eusebio.

questions.explanation: Eusebio married Altagracia Luna (1); their children were Joaquín, Consuelo and Benigno (2), the violinist; Joaquín married Mercedes Ortiz (3), and their children were the second Eusebio and the second Altagracia (4). Celso Aranda and Rosa belong to lesson 92's story.

questions.stem: In "La casa de los Villaseñor", the house wakes up on the other side of the river and "Nadie en Santa Rita lo comentó demasiado." What does this calm reaction show?
choices: The impossible is told as normal, which is what critics call magical realism.
The narrator doesn't believe the story.
The townspeople are afraid of the family.
The event was only a dream.
questions.explanation: The narrator tells the impossible in the same voice as the coffee harvest, and the town accepts it. That calm is the mark of magical realism. Nothing suggests fear, a dream or a doubting narrator.

questions.stem: Complete with the noun meaning "patriarch": "Eusebio Villaseñor es el ___ de la familia: llegó en 1891 y fundó la hacienda."
questions.explanation: El patriarca ends in -a but is masculine (el patriarca, los patriarcas), like el poeta. A woman who heads a family is la matriarca.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish, giving Joaquín the focus.
questions.prompt: It was Joaquín who married Mercedes Ortiz.
questions.explanation: A cleft sentence puts the focus on Joaquín: Fue Joaquín quien se casó con Mercedes Ortiz. The pseudo-cleft order, Quien se casó con Mercedes Ortiz fue Joaquín, is also correct. La que would need a feminine antecedent (el que is also correct here, but it isn't among the tiles).

questions.stem: "Era el último de una estirpe de cafetaleros." What does estirpe mean?
choices: a lineage, a line of descent
questions.explanation: La estirpe is a lineage: the last of a line of coffee growers. A social class is la clase social; a plantation is la plantación or el cafetal.

questions.stem: What does the lesson say about women writers and the Boom?
choices: There were no women novelists in Latin America in the 1960s.
The Boom was led by Carmen Balcells as a novelist.
Women were excluded from publishing until the 1990s.
Elena Garro and Rosario Castellanos wrote major novels in the same years but were rarely counted in the famous list.
questions.explanation: The famous list is all men, yet Garro (1963) and Castellanos (1957) published major novels in the same years; critics today discuss why they were left out. Balcells was an agent, not a novelist, and the post-Boom brought Allende and Poniatowska to wide fame.

questions.stem: "El premio Biblioteca Breve y el éxito de La ciudad y los perros fueron la consagración de Vargas Llosa." What does consagración mean here?
choices: his breakthrough, the moment he was recognized
questions.explanation: In literature, la consagración is the acclaim that establishes a writer: his breakthrough. The religious sense (consecration) exists but doesn't fit here. Un autor consagrado is an established, acclaimed author.

questions.stem: Laura needs the director to confirm the guests by June 8. Which request fits an oficio to him?
choices: Mucho le agradecería que nos confirmara la asistencia a más tardar el 8 de junio.
questions.explanation: An oficio uses usted, the conditional of courtesy and an exact deadline: Mucho le agradecería que nos confirmara… a más tardar el 8 de junio. The others use tú or slang (porfa, ¿sale?) or a bare command (Confírmenos rápido), which sounds abrupt to a superior.

questions.stem: Complete the notice on a Mexican parking lot gate: "___ no estacionarse frente a la puerta."
questions.explanation: Mexican notices use Favor de + infinitive: Favor de no estacionarse. Se ruega is also used, but without de (Se ruega no estacionarse). Por favor and Le pedimos don't take de before an infinitive (Le pedimos no estacionarse).

questions.stem: A wedding invitation says "Cena de etiqueta". What does it tell the guests?
choices: Name tags will be handed out at the door.
The dinner follows a strict seating plan.
Guests should bring a labeled gift.
questions.explanation: De etiqueta means formal dress. La etiqueta is formal manners (and also a label or tag, B2's etiquetar), but on an invitation the phrase refers to clothes.

questions.stem: You are writing a formal e-mail to an engineer, Laura Robles, whom you have never met. Which greeting is right?
questions.explanation: Estimada agrees with a woman, the title ingeniera is used as in Mexican offices, and a Spanish greeting ends with a colon. A comma is the English habit; Estimado doesn't agree with ingeniera; Querida is for people you know well.

questions.stem: Which of these are typical of the formal register? Select all that apply.
choices: Le agradecería que me enviara el programa.
La entrega de diplomas se realizará a las once.
Se informa a los asistentes que la sede cambió.
questions.explanation: Le agradecería que + imperfect subjunctive, the nominal style (la entrega de diplomas) and impersonal se (Se informa a los asistentes) are marks of formal Spanish. O sea is a filler and nomás a colloquial Mexican word: both belong to the voice note, not the oficio.

questions.stem: Complete the opening of a formal letter with the verb dirigirse: "Me ___ a usted para solicitar información sobre la ceremonia."
questions.explanation: Me dirijo a usted para… (I am writing to you to…). Dirigirse changes g to j before o and a: me dirijo, me dirija.

questions.stem: Complete the written request with enviar: "Le agradecería que me ___ la lista de invitados."
questions.explanation: After the conditional agradecería, the usual formal choice is the imperfect subjunctive: enviara (enviase is also correct). Many Latin Americans say and write envíe; it isn't a mistake, but enviara is the safest choice in a formal letter.

questions.stem: Match each everyday verb to its formal equivalent.
questions.explanation: Formal Spanish prefers longer, Latin-based verbs: solicitar for pedir, iniciar for empezar, apoyar for ayudar, comunicar for decir. Evolucionar (to evolve) is the formal equivalent of none of them.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this oficio.

image.alt: The oficio from the lesson with six numbered markers: 1 by the university letterhead at the top, 2 by the subject line on the right, 3 by the addressee's name and post, 4 by the handwritten signature, 5 on the RECIBIDO stamp, 6 by the c.c.p. line at the bottom.

questions.explanation: The letterhead (el membrete) is at the top; the subject line (el asunto) sits on the right under the number; the addressee (el destinatario) is in capitals with PRESENTE; the signature (la firma) is above the sender's name; the RECIBIDO stamp is the acknowledgment of receipt; c.c.p. (con copia para) lists who gets a copy. An oficio on paper has no attachment icon.

questions.stem: Why does an oficio say "Por medio del presente" while a letter says "Por medio de la presente"?
choices: Presente agrees with the document: el oficio is masculine, la carta feminine.
Del presente is more formal than de la presente.
Del presente is the Mexican form and de la presente the Spanish one.
Presente refers to the reader, and the oficio is addressed to a man.
questions.explanation: The phrase means "by means of this one", and presente stands for the document: el (oficio) presente, la (carta) presente. It has nothing to do with the reader's gender or with formality or region.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I would be grateful if you sent me the invoice.
questions.explanation: "Le agradecería que me enviara la factura": the conditional agradecería is followed by que and the imperfect subjunctive. Envió is the preterite (he sent), which can't follow agradecería que.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: It would be discourteous not to answer.
questions.explanation: "Sería descortés no contestar" or "No contestar sería descortés": the infinitive phrase is the subject and can go first or last ("Descortés sería no contestar", with the adjective stressed, is also correct). Cortés means the opposite, courteous.

questions.stem: A Mexican friend says your Spanish is "muy coloquial". What does she mean?
choices: It is full of technical terms.
questions.explanation: Coloquial means informal, the language of conversation. Crude language is vulgar; the specialized register is full of technical terms.

questions.stem: In Mexico, what does "El taxi llegó hasta las tres" usually mean?
choices: The taxi drove as far as three blocks.
The taxi didn't arrive until three.
The taxi came at three at the latest.
questions.explanation: In Mexico, Central America, Colombia and coastal Ecuador, hasta often drops the no: llegó hasta las tres = it didn't arrive until three (DPD, hasta). In formal writing put the no back: No llegó hasta las tres.

questions.stem: Your trip was canceled and nothing can be done about it. Which reaction fits?
questions.explanation: Ni modo (oh well, nothing to be done) accepts what can't be changed. ¡Ándale! urges or confirms, ¿A poco? shows surprise, and ¡Sale! agrees to a plan.

questions.stem: "—Ya me pagaron la quincena. —¿A poco?" What does the second speaker express?
questions.explanation: ¿A poco? (really? no way?) shows surprise or disbelief, with a rise on po. Agreement would be ¡Sale!, and a request to repeat ¿Mande?

questions.stem: You are meeting a new client at your office. Which greeting would sound out of place?
choices: Buenos días, licenciado, pase por favor.
questions.explanation: ¿Qué onda? (what's up?) and el compa (pal) are very informal: fine among friends, odd with a client. The other greetings are polite and neutral or formal.

questions.stem: Which of these are fillers or backchannels? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Este… fills a pause; ajá and the tag ¿verdad? keep the speaker going or invite agreement. La botana is a noun (snacks) and luego luego an adverb phrase (right away).

questions.stem: Complete with the two-word Mexican expression for "right away": "Le escribí y me contestó ___."
questions.explanation: Luego luego means right away, immediately. A single luego means later or then.

questions.stem: Rewrite for a formal text, replacing nomás with one word: "Nomás tomé dos cervezas." → "___ tomé dos cervezas."
questions.explanation: Nomás (only) is informal and marked as American in the DLE. In a formal text use solo, solamente or únicamente. (The RAE now recommends solo without an accent; the accented form is accepted here.)

questions.stem: Match each colloquial Mexican word to a neutral equivalent.
choices: lo que se come con las bebidas
questions.explanation: La lana is money, la cruda a hangover, el antro a club, la botana snacks with drinks, and chafa shoddy. El trabajo matches none of them (its colloquial word is B1's la chamba).

questions.stem: The headings of this chart are hidden. Name each numbered column.

image.alt: The conversation chart from the lesson with its five headings hidden and numbered. Column 1: este, pues, bueno, o sea. Column 2: ajá, ¿en serio?, ¿no?, ¿verdad?. Column 3: y eso, o algo así, y cosas así, como que. Column 4: a short exchange, ¿Y la cartera? En la chamarra. ¿Fuiste? Obvio. Column 5: bien cansado, súper, de a tiro, requetebién.

questions.explanation: Este, pues, bueno and o sea are fillers (muletillas); ajá and the tags are backchannels (señales de escucha); y eso and o algo así are vague language; the short answers drop what is obvious (elipsis); bien, súper, de a tiro and requete- intensify. Courtesy formulas belong to formal writing.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I went for it and sang at the club.
questions.explanation: "Me aventé a cantar en el antro" (or "En el antro me aventé a cantar"): aventarse a + infinitive is to go for it. Me avento is the present (I go for it), not the past.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: My buddy lent me the money. (Mexico, informal)
questions.explanation: "Mi compa me prestó la lana", or with the subject after the verb, "Me prestó la lana mi compa" or "Me prestó mi compa la lana". Le prestó would mean he lent it to someone else.

questions.stem: What does the lesson advise about güey?
choices: Use it to sound natural with anyone you call tú.
It is an old word that young Mexicans no longer use.
Recognize it: it is very common among friends but rude in many settings.
questions.explanation: Güey is extremely common among friends, especially young men, in much of Mexico, but it is still an insult in many settings and never belongs with strangers, older people or at work. Recognize it; don't start using it.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows dequeísmo?
choices: Me alegro de que estés aquí.
questions.explanation: Dequeísmo adds a de the verb doesn't take: ¿Qué piensas? → Pienso eso → Pienso que… The other three need de: acordarse de algo, estar seguro de algo, alegrarse de algo.

questions.stem: Which version would you write in a formal report?
choices: Me di de cuenta que había un error.
Me di cuenta de qué había un error.
Me di cuenta de que había un error.
Me di cuenta del que había un error.
questions.explanation: Darse cuenta takes de (¿De qué te diste cuenta?), so careful writing keeps de que. Me di cuenta que (without de) is very frequent in speech; the other choices put de in the wrong place or add an accent or an article.

questions.stem: Which form do the academies recommend?
choices: Había muchas personas en la fila.
Habían muchas personas en la fila.
Habemos muchas personas en la fila.
Hubieron muchas personas en la fila.
questions.explanation: Existential haber is impersonal: muchas personas is its object, so the verb stays singular, as in hay and hubo. The plural habían is very frequent in Latin American speech, but the norm keeps the singular; habemos and hubieron are nonstandard.

questions.stem: A friend from Spain says checar is "wrong". What does the DPD (2005) say?
choices: It is a calque that should always be avoided.
It is the form used in Mexico; chequear can't be criticized either.
It is accepted only in informal speech.
questions.explanation: The DPD (entry chequear) explains that chequear adapts English to check, that its use can't be censured, and that Mexico uses the variant checar. It is accepted Mexican usage, not an error.

questions.stem: Which of these are calques of English expressions? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Hacer sentido (make sense), tomar lugar (take place) and aplicar a una vacante (apply for a vacancy) copy English structures with Spanish words. Tener lugar is the standard Spanish phrase, and fútbol is an adapted loanword, not a calque.

questions.stem: Complete as careful writing recommends (one word): "Me acuerdo ___ que llovía mucho."
questions.explanation: Acordarse takes de: ¿De qué te acuerdas? → Me acuerdo de eso → Me acuerdo de que… Leaving it out is queísmo, very common in speech.

questions.stem: Complete with the preterite of haber: "Ayer ___ dos accidentes en la autopista."
questions.explanation: Impersonal haber stays singular in every tense: hay, había, hubo, habrá. Dos accidentes is its object, not its subject.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the eso test for de que / que in order.
choices: Find the verb or expression before the que clause.
Replace the whole que clause with eso.
Check whether the verb needs de before eso.
Write de que if it does, que alone if it doesn't.
questions.explanation: Find the verb, replace the clause with eso, see whether de is needed (Me acuerdo de eso, Pienso eso), then write de que or que to match.

questions.stem: Match each term to its example.
questions.explanation: Pienso de que adds a needless de (dequeísmo); Me di cuenta que drops a needed one (queísmo); hacer sentido copies make sense (calque); escáner is an adapted loanword; haiga is a nonstandard form of haya. Me alegro de que is standard.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this dictionary entry.

image.alt: The dictionary card from the lesson with five numbered markers: 1 by the headword checar, 2 by the bracketed origin, 3 by the country mark Méx., 4 by the definition, 5 by the example sentence in italics.

questions.explanation: The headword (el lema) comes first; the origin (la etimología) is in brackets; Méx. is a geographic mark; the definition belongs to sense 1 (la acepción); the sentence in italics is an example. The card shows no synonym.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: There were two accidents on the highway.
questions.explanation: "Hubo dos accidentes en la carretera" (or "En la carretera hubo dos accidentes", "Hubo en la carretera dos accidentes"): impersonal haber stays singular. Hubieron is frequent in speech but nonstandard.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I'm sure you're right.
questions.explanation: "Estoy seguro de que tienes razón": estar seguro takes de (¿De qué estás seguro?), so de que is required. De qué, with an accent, is a question word.

questions.stem: A linguist records that "habían muchas personas" is very frequent in Mexico, without saying whether it is right or wrong. What kind of approach is that?
questions.explanation: Recording usage without judging it is descriptive. A prescriptive (normative) work would recommend the singular había; a purist would reject the plural as damage to the language.

questions.stem: After tasting your mole, your friend smiles and says "No está nada mal". What does she mean?
questions.explanation: No está nada mal (it's not bad at all) is litotes: denying the opposite to say something positive, often strongly. With a smile, it's praise.

questions.stem: A friend invites you to her birthday dinner, and you can't go. Which answer is most tactful?
choices: Te lo agradezco mucho, pero me temo que no voy a poder.
questions.explanation: A tactful refusal thanks first, softens the no (me temo que) and often adds a reason. No, gracias and No quiero ir are blunt, and Declino tu invitación belongs to formal writing, not to a friend.

questions.stem: Your bus breaks down in a storm, and the man next to you sighs "¡Qué oportuno!". What is he doing?
choices: Being ironic: the timing couldn't be worse
questions.explanation: ¡Qué oportuno! (how timely!) said of something that came at the worst moment is irony: it means the opposite of the words, marked by a flat, drawn-out intonation and the context.

questions.stem: Which phrase is a euphemism for layoffs?
questions.explanation: Un ajuste de personal (a staff adjustment) softens what it describes: people losing their jobs. La negativa is a refusal, la franqueza frankness and la mediación mediation.

questions.stem: Which of these soften (mitigate) what follows? Select all that apply.
choices: Será lo que tú digas, pero…
questions.explanation: The conditional (Yo diría que), the diminutive hedge un poquito and the future of concession (Será lo que tú digas, pero…) soften. Sumamente and infinitamente intensify; they belong with thanks and praise.

questions.stem: Complete the formula for giving bad news formally (one word, with le attached): "Lamento ___ que su solicitud no fue aprobada."
questions.explanation: Lamento comunicarle que… (I regret to inform you that…) is the standard formula; informarle, notificarle and decirle are also correct.

questions.stem: Complete with atenuar in the present: "El condicional ___ la crítica."
questions.explanation: Atenuar stresses the u in the singular and the third plural, with a written accent: atenúo, atenúas, atenúa, atenúan (like continuar).

questions.stem: Match each delicate speech act to a formula.
choices: Me temo que no voy a poder.
questions.explanation: Each act has its softener. Me dirijo a usted para… opens a formal letter by stating its purpose; it isn't one of these acts.

questions.stem: Put the parts of this refusal in the usual order.
choices: pero me temo que no voy a poder,
porque ese día viajo a Monterrey.
¿Te parece si lo dejamos para la próxima semana?
questions.explanation: Thanks first, then the softened refusal (pero me temo que…), then the reason (porque…), and finally an alternative. Pero must follow the thanks, and porque explains the refusal before it.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: With all due respect, I think the plan is risky.
questions.explanation: "Con todo respeto, creo que el plan es arriesgado": the softener goes first, set off by a comma. Creer takes que alone; creo de que is dequeísmo.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: It may be as you say, but I don't see it that way.
questions.explanation: "Será lo que tú digas, pero yo no lo veo así": the future of concession (será) grants the other side before disagreeing, and lo que tú digas takes the subjunctive (whatever you say).

questions.stem: What was the main idea of the Doctrina Estrada (1930)?
choices: Mexico would join every international treaty on trade.
Mexico would send ambassadors only to Latin American countries.
Mexico would not pass judgment on other governments by recognizing them; it would just keep or withdraw its diplomats.
Mexico would mediate in every conflict in the region.
questions.explanation: Genaro Estrada's doctrine, published on September 27, 1930, said Mexico would not grant or deny recognition to other governments and would simply keep or withdraw its diplomats, in defense of non-intervention and self-determination.

questions.stem: You ask a Mexican colleague to cover your shift on Saturday, and she answers warmly "A ver si puedo, te aviso". What is the most likely meaning?
choices: Probably not, but she doesn't want to say no directly.
She will call you back in five minutes.
questions.explanation: As the lesson notes, refusals in Mexico are often softened until they no longer sound like refusals: a ver si puedo and te aviso can mean "probably not". It is a tendency, not a rule, so the context matters.

questions.stem: How do plain-language organizations usually define plain language?
choices: A text with no word longer than three syllables
A text written in the colloquial register
A text whose readers can find what they need, understand it and use it
A text approved by a language academy
questions.explanation: Plain language is defined by its results for the reader: they can find, understand and use what they need. It isn't a word-length rule, and it isn't colloquial: a plain notice still uses usted.

questions.stem: When did Mexico launch its Lenguaje Ciudadano initiative, and under which agency?
choices: 2004, under the Secretaría de la Función Pública
1988, under the Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores
2023, under the International Organization for Standardization
questions.explanation: Lenguaje Ciudadano began in 2004 under the Secretaría de la Función Pública, as a federal manual circulated in 2021 describes it. 2011 is the year Spain's Ministry of Justice received its commission's report; ISO 24495-1 appeared in 2023.

questions.stem: Which is the best plain rewrite of "se llevará a cabo la suspensión del servicio de agua"?
choices: se efectuará la interrupción del suministro
se procederá a suspender el servicio
la suspensión del agua será llevada a cabo
questions.explanation: No habrá agua says what the reader needs in three words, with a verb instead of a noun. The other versions keep the nouns (la interrupción, la suspensión), the empty support verbs (efectuar, proceder a, llevar a cabo) or a passive.

questions.stem: The notice calls water "el vital líquido". What habit of bureaucratic Spanish is that?
choices: An ornamental synonym that adds nothing
A technical term that must stay
questions.explanation: El vital líquido is a decorative way of saying el agua. It adds length, not meaning, so a plain version uses agua. Technical terms and terms of art, by contrast, may need to stay.

questions.stem: Why does the plain version of the lease clause keep the word rescindir?
choices: Because plain language never changes verbs
Because it is a term of art with an exact legal meaning, so it is kept and explained
Because terminar would be too colloquial
questions.explanation: Rescindir means ending a contract because the other side broke it, not just ending it. Replacing it could change the legal effect, so the plain version keeps it and explains it with es decir.

questions.stem: Which simplification creates a new ambiguity?
choices: Dos o más mensualidades consecutivas → dos meses seguidos
Incurrir en mora → dejar de pagar
Saldo insoluto → la cantidad que deba
Dos o más mensualidades consecutivas → dos meses
questions.explanation: Dos meses alone could mean any two months, not two in a row. Dos meses seguidos keeps the meaning of consecutivas; the other two rewrites keep the meaning in plainer words.

questions.stem: Put the lesson's rewriting steps in order.
choices: Put the most important thing first.
Unpack the nouns and name the doer.
questions.explanation: Work from meaning to form: find what the reader needs, put it first, turn nouns into verbs with a visible doer, cut repeats, and only then design the layout.

questions.stem: Match each bureaucratic phrase to its plain version.
left: en el periodo comprendido entre… y…
se hace del conocimiento de los usuarios
questions.explanation: Each phrase has a short everyday equivalent. Rescindir is a legal term of art that a plain text keeps and explains, so it isn't the plain version of anything here.

questions.stem: Replace the support verb and noun with one verb (infinitive): "llevar a cabo la revisión" → ___
questions.explanation: Llevar a cabo la revisión is just revisar: the noun goes back to its verb (B2 18).

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: We recommend that you store water before Tuesday.
questions.explanation: "Le recomendamos guardar agua antes del martes": a visible doer (we) speaking to the reader (le), as plain language advises. The time phrase can also go first. Se recomienda hides the doer and doesn't say "we".

questions.stem: Which of these are plain-language techniques? Select all that apply.
choices: Short sentences with one idea each
Active voice with a visible doer
Explaining a technical term the first time it appears
Leaving out dates to keep the text short
Switching from usted to tú to sound friendly
questions.explanation: Short sentences, a visible doer and explained technical terms all help the reader. Dropping dates makes the notice useless, and plain official texts keep usted.

questions.stem: Spain's Comisión para la Modernización del Lenguaje Jurídico presented its report in 2011. What did it recommend?
choices: Replacing all legal terms with everyday words
Writing laws in the colloquial register
Ordering ideas, shorter paragraphs, fewer chained subordinate clauses and less abuse of gerunds and the passive
questions.explanation: The report noted that citizens found legal language cryptic and recommended better-ordered paragraphs, shorter ones, fewer chained subordinate clauses and less abuse of gerunds and the passive. It didn't propose dropping all technical terms.

questions.stem: Listen to the sentence, read by the app's Mexican voice. Which spelling imitates how many speakers in San Juan, Puerto Rico, might say it?

audio.text: Los chicos ya llegaron a la plaza.

choices: Lo' chico' ya llegaron a la plasa.
Los chicos sha shegaron a la plasa.
Los chicos ya llegaron a la platha.
Los chicos ya llegaron a la plaza, con r asibilada.
questions.explanation: Caribbean speakers often aspirate or drop an s at the end of a syllable: lo' chico'. The sh version is the Río de la Plata, platha (th for z) is Spain's distinción, and assibilation is an Andean feature of rr and final r, which this sentence doesn't have (llegaron has a single r between vowels).

questions.stem: Listen to the sentence in the app's Mexican voice. Which spelling imitates how many speakers in Buenos Aires would say it?

audio.text: Yo me llamo Lucía y llegué ayer.

choices: Yo me llamo Lucía y llegué ayé.
Sho me shamo Lucía y shegué ashé.
Yo me llamo Luthía y llegué ayer.
Yo me yamo Lusía y yegué ayer.
questions.explanation: In the Río de la Plata, ll and y sound like sh or zh: yo → sho, llamo → shamo, llegué → shegué, ayer → ashé (with the final r weakened). Luthía is Spain's distinción; the last choice is just yeísmo and seseo, which is how you heard it.

questions.stem: You heard this sentence with seseo, in the app's Mexican voice. How would a speaker from Madrid with distinción say it?
choices: With s in every case, exactly as you heard it
With th for every s and every z: thí, thiempre…
With th in gracias and in cerveza (twice), and s elsewhere
With sh in place of the ll and y sounds
questions.explanation: Distinción gives th only to z and to c before e, i: gra-THias, ther-VE-tha. The letter s stays s. What you heard is seseo; th for every s would be ceceo; there is no ll or y in the sentence.

questions.stem: A speaker from Santo Domingo says "ehtamo' cansao". Write it in standard spelling.
questions.explanation: Restore the aspirated or lost s (ehtamo' → estamos), and the -ado reduced to -ao, with its plural s (cansao → cansados, or cansadas for women).

questions.stem: What is seseo?
choices: Pronouncing z and c before e, i as s
Dropping the s at the end of a syllable
questions.explanation: Seseo makes casa and caza sound alike; it is the norm in Latin America, the Canaries and parts of Andalusia. Th for s is ceceo, ll = y is yeísmo, and dropping a final s is part of aspiration.

questions.stem: Where is ceceo heard, according to Ohio State University's Dialectos del español project?
choices: In many parts of southern Spain, and in parts of Nicaragua, El Salvador and Honduras
questions.explanation: The project describes ceceo as characteristic of many parts of southern Spain and records it in parts of Central America. Madrid uses distinción; Mexico and the Río de la Plata use seseo.

questions.stem: Match each feature to the area the lesson associates it with.
left: s at the end of a syllable aspirated or lost
sh or zh for ll and y
th for z and for c before e, i
ll and y kept apart by some speakers
choices: el centro y el norte de España
questions.explanation: Aspiration is the best-known Caribbean feature; sheísmo and zheísmo belong to Buenos Aires and Montevideo; distinción to most of Spain; some Andean speakers keep ll and y apart. Mexico City has none of these four (it uses seseo and yeísmo and keeps its s).

questions.stem: Which features does Mexican Spanish share with most of the Spanish-speaking world? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Seseo and yeísmo are the majority pronunciations, Mexico's included. Distinción is Spain's, sheísmo the Río de la Plata's, and central Mexico keeps its s firmly.

questions.stem: Why do this lesson's listening questions ask what a sentence would sound like elsewhere instead of playing other accents?
choices: Because other accents are not tested in the DELE C1
Because the app speaks with a Mexican voice, and no synthetic voice reproduces real regional speech
Because Mexican Spanish is the only standard
Because learners should imitate other accents
questions.explanation: The app's voice is es-MX, and device voices can't reproduce regional speech, so the questions use the Mexican voice and ask you to imagine the other variety. The DELE C1 does use at least three varieties, so listen to real radio and podcasts from each area.

questions.stem: Which word describes the Spanish of Spain, in Latin American usage?
questions.explanation: Peninsular refers to the Iberian Peninsula: el español peninsular. Caribeño is Caribbean, rioplatense is of the Río de la Plata, andino is Andean.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: In Madrid they use distinción.
questions.explanation: "En Madrid se usa la distinción", with the place, the verb or the noun first ("La distinción se usa en Madrid", "Se usa la distinción en Madrid"). Madrid has distinción, not seseo.

questions.stem: You hear "Mi'ja, ehtamo' cansao, vamo' a dehcansá un rato." What did the speaker say?
choices: Mija, estamos cansados, vamos a descansar un rato.
Mija, están cansados, van a descansar un rato.
Mija, estamos casados, vamos a descansar un rato.
Mija, estoy cansado, voy a descansar un rato.
questions.explanation: Restore the lost s sounds (ehtamo' → estamos, vamo' → vamos, dehcansá → descansar with its final r), and -ao → -ados. The verbs are first person plural, so it isn't están or estoy, and cansao is cansado, not casado.

questions.stem: Your friend Lucía wants you to come at five. Your roommate passes on her message: "Lucía dice que ___ a las cinco."
questions.explanation: Lucía is asking you to do something, so "decir" passes on a request and takes the subjunctive: "Dice que vengas a las cinco" (She says you should come at five). With "vienes" or "vendrás" the sentence reports a fact or a plan (she says you are coming / will come), which isn't her message. "Decir que" can't be followed by a bare infinitive here.

questions.stem: What does "Siento que no puedas venir" mean?
choices: I sense that you can't come.
I feel that I can't come.
I regret not being able to come.
questions.explanation: With the subjunctive ("puedas"), "sentir" means to regret: I'm sorry you can't come. "I sense that you can't come" would be "Siento que no puedes venir" (indicative: a perception or hunch). The other two change the subject: the one who can't come is "tú".

questions.stem: Which sentence politely announces bad news that the speaker already knows, instead of expressing a fear?
choices: Me temo que el vuelo está cancelado.
Temo que el vuelo esté cancelado.
Tengo miedo de que cancelen el vuelo.
questions.explanation: "Me temo que" + indicative ("está") is the polite way to give bad news: I'm afraid the flight is canceled. "Temo que" and "tengo miedo de que" + subjunctive express a real worry, and "ojalá" expresses a hope.

questions.stem: In "No sabía que estabas aquí", what does the indicative "estabas" tell the listener?
choices: The speaker doubts that you are here.
The speaker wishes you were here.
The speaker now accepts that you are here.
The speaker thinks you'll arrive later.
questions.explanation: After a verb of knowing, even a negated one, the indicative presupposes the fact: you are here, and the speaker simply didn't know. Doubt or a wish would need the subjunctive ("No creo que estés aquí"; "Ojalá estuvieras aquí").

questions.stem: Both "¿Crees que es verdad?" and "¿Crees que sea verdad?" are correct. Which one signals that the speaker doubts it?
choices: Neither: questions don't affect the mood.
questions.explanation: In questions with "creer", both moods are standard. The subjunctive ("sea") sounds more doubtful (Do you really think it could be true?); the indicative ("es") is an open question and may even lean toward yes.

questions.stem: In the article "Tres testigos, tres verdades", what did the street camera show?
choices: The light was yellow, the van was slow and the dog had crossed a minute earlier.
The taxi ran a red light, as Doña Teresa said.
The van was speeding, as Julián assumed.
There was no dog at all.
questions.explanation: The video showed that each witness was wrong about something: "el semáforo estaba en amarillo, la camioneta iba despacio y el perro existía, pero había cruzado un minuto antes".

questions.stem: According to the article, what happened in Loftus and Palmer's 1974 study?
choices: Students remembered the video perfectly a week later.
Witnesses who saw broken glass estimated lower speeds.
The students were asked to invent a childhood memory.
A more violent verb in the question raised speed estimates and reports of broken glass.
questions.explanation: Students who heard "se estrellaron" (smashed) estimated higher speeds and, a week later, more of them reported broken glass that wasn't in the video. The invented childhood memory (being lost in a mall) is the later experiment, published in 1995.

questions.stem: Which sentences pass on a request rather than report a statement? Select all that apply.
choices: Dice que la esperes en la entrada.
Me escribió que no me preocupara.
questions.explanation: A request takes the subjunctive: "que la esperes" (wait for her), "que no me preocupara" (told me not to worry), "en que lo acompañemos" (that we go with him). "Avísale que llegamos tarde" (let him know we're late) and "Dice que está cansada" (she says she's tired) report facts with the indicative.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to what it does.
left: Me temo que no hay boletos.
No admito que me hables así.
questions.explanation: "Sentir" + indicative perceives, + subjunctive regrets. "Me temo que" + indicative gives bad news politely. "No admito que" + subjunctive refuses to allow something. "Recuérdale que" + subjunctive asks someone to remind another person to do something. A hope would be "Espero que…" or "Ojalá…".

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of "llamar": "Mi mamá me dijo que ___ al plomero, porque ella no tenía tiempo." (She told me to call the plumber.)
questions.explanation: Your mother told you to do something, so "decir" passes on a request: subjunctive. The main verb is in the past ("dijo"), so the sequence of tenses gives the imperfect subjunctive: "llamara" (or "llamase"). If the call is still to be made, Latin American Spanish also often uses the present subjunctive ("Me dijo que llame al plomero"), so "llame" is accepted too. "Llamé" would report that you called.

questions.stem: Complete with "hablar" (tú): "No admito que me ___ así." (I won't allow you to talk to me like that.)
questions.explanation: "Admitir" meaning "to allow" takes the subjunctive: "No admito que me hables así". With the indicative, "admitir" accepts a fact ("Admito que me equivoqué").

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I'm sorry you can't come to the party.
questions.explanation: Regret: "sentir" + subjunctive, "Siento que no puedas venir a la fiesta". "No puedes" would turn it into a perception (I sense you can't come). The place phrase can also come earlier for emphasis: "Siento que a la fiesta no puedas venir".

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Remind him to bring the keys.
questions.explanation: "Recordar" meaning "to remind someone to do something" takes the subjunctive: "Recuérdale que traiga las llaves". "Recuérdale que trae las llaves" would remind him of a fact (that he's bringing them).

questions.stem: Which sentence means "Whatever you do, they'll criticize you"?
choices: Haces lo que haces, te van a criticar.
Hagas lo que hagas, te van a criticar.
Hagas lo que haces, te van a criticar.
Hicieras lo que hagas, te van a criticar.
questions.explanation: The reduplicated concessive repeats the same verb in the same tense and person, in the subjunctive: "hagas lo que hagas". Mixing moods ("hagas lo que haces") or tenses ("hicieras lo que hagas") breaks the pattern, and the indicative "haces lo que haces" doesn't mean "whatever".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "Whatever he said, nobody believed him"?
choices: Dijera lo que dijera, nadie le creía.
Diga lo que diga, nadie le creía.
Dijo lo que dijo, nadie le creía.
Dijera lo que dijo, nadie le creía.
questions.explanation: In past narration the repeated verb goes into the imperfect subjunctive (sequence of tenses): "Dijera lo que dijera" (or "Dijese lo que dijese"). "Diga lo que diga" belongs with a present or future main clause, and the pattern needs the same form twice.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "Not even if they paid me double"?
choices: Ni aunque me pagaban el doble.
Ni aunque me pagaran el doble.
Aunque ni me pagaran el doble.
Ni aunque me pagarían el doble.
questions.explanation: "Ni aunque" takes the subjunctive; for an unlikely case, the imperfect subjunctive: "ni aunque me pagaran" (or "pagasen"). The indicative "pagaban" and the conditional "pagarían" can't follow it, and "ni" goes before "aunque".

questions.stem: Complete: "Con lo ___ que está la renta, no sé cómo le hacen."
questions.explanation: In "con lo + adjective + que", "lo" never changes but the adjective agrees with the noun it describes: "la renta" is feminine singular, so "lo cara que está la renta" (given how expensive the rent is).

questions.stem: In much of Latin America you'll hear "No acepto, así me ofrezcan el doble." What does "así" mean here?
questions.explanation: "Así" + subjunctive is concessive, like "aunque": I won't accept, even if they offer me double. It's common in Mexico and much of Latin America; "aunque" is the safe choice in writing for any audience.

questions.stem: In the podcast, why did Mariana's café close?
choices: Her business partner left with the money.
She confused customers with profits and didn't check costs until rent and coffee prices rose.
A pandemic forced every café in Puebla to close.
An investor withdrew his capital after a year.
questions.explanation: Mariana says "yo confundía clientes con ganancias… nunca revisé los costos, y cuando subieron la renta y el precio del café, ya era tarde".

questions.stem: An investor told Mariana he wouldn't back someone who had gone bankrupt. What was her answer?
choices: That she had never really gone bankrupt.
That she didn't need his money.
That she would open another café.
That precisely because of it, she knew what not to do.
questions.explanation: She replied "que precisamente por eso yo sabía lo que no había que hacer": her failure taught her what to avoid.

questions.stem: Which sentences use the reduplicated concessive (the same verb repeated around a relative word)? Select all that apply.
choices: Vayas donde vayas, vas a encontrar competencia.
Venga quien venga, la junta empieza a las nueve.
Cueste lo que cueste, lo vamos a lograr.
questions.explanation: "Vayas donde vayas", "venga quien venga" and "cueste lo que cueste" repeat the same subjunctive around "donde", "quien" and "lo que". "Haz lo que quieras" and "Quiero lo que tú quieras" use a relative with the subjunctive, but with two different verbs and no concessive meaning.

questions.stem: Complete with "querer" (tú): "___ o no, mañana hay que firmar el contrato." (Like it or not, the contract has to be signed tomorrow.)
questions.explanation: "Quieras o no" (like it or not) uses two alternatives in the subjunctive: "quieras o no". The indicative "quieres" isn't used in this pattern.

questions.stem: Complete with "vender" (ustedes): "Por poco que ___, lleven las cuentas desde el primer día." (However little you sell, keep accounts from day one.)
questions.explanation: "Por poco que" + subjunctive covers any amount, however small: "Por poco que vendan". The indicative would present a known fact, which doesn't fit advice for the future.

questions.stem: Complete the past reduplicated concessive with "hacer": "Hiciera lo que ___, el negocio no despegaba." (Whatever he did, the business wouldn't take off.)
questions.explanation: Both halves repeat the same form. In the past, the imperfect subjunctive: "Hiciera lo que hiciera" ("hiciese lo que hiciese" is also correct, though the two halves usually match).

questions.stem: Match each structure to its meaning.
questions.explanation: "Hagas lo que hagas" is the reduplicated concessive; "quieras o no" sets two alternatives; "ni aunque" rejects even an extreme condition; "mal que bien" sums up a result reached with difficulty; "así" + subjunctive is the Latin American "even if". "As long as" is "siempre que" or "con tal de que".

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Whatever you decide, they're going to criticize you.
questions.explanation: Reduplicated concessive: subjunctive + "lo que" + the same subjunctive, "Decidas lo que decidas, te van a criticar". The indicative "decides" breaks the pattern. (Without the comma tiles, the clause could also follow: "Te van a criticar decidas lo que decidas".)

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: Not even if they paid me double.
questions.explanation: "Ni aunque" + imperfect subjunctive for an unlikely case: "Ni aunque me pagaran el doble" ("pagasen" is also correct). The indicative "pagaban" can't follow "ni aunque".
